# PanCode

> PanCode is one harness for the models and coding agents you already use. Panos, its orchestrator agent, routes work across providers, sandboxes commands, checks finished work against what ran, keeps memory and runs fleets of workers, in the terminal, in scripts and CI, in ACP editors and on the desktop (alpha). It installs on HPC login nodes without root and ships checks for numerical work.

PanCode is a harness for development work. Panos, its orchestrator agent, plans a task, runs it on the models you connect and hands parts of it to workers, including the coding agents you already have. It routes across providers, sandboxes commands, checks finished work against what ran and keeps memory, in the terminal, in scripts and CI, in ACP editors or on the desktop. PanHub packs and PanKit servers cover HPC and scientific software.

PanCode is a product of PanStudio. It needs no account and no root, and sends nothing home. It is free for individuals, small organizations (fewer than 100 people and under $1M revenue), and noncommercial research and teaching. Its source is available on GitHub under the PanCode License 1.0. Larger organizations get a 32-day evaluation, then a commercial license from PanStudio.

- Install on macOS, Linux, or WSL: `curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh`
- Install on Windows (best effort) in PowerShell: `irm https://pancode.dev/install.ps1 | iex`
- Install with npm (Node.js 22.19 or newer): `npm install -g @panstudio/pancode`
- Connect a model in a project: `pancode configure`; then run `pancode` for the terminal or `pancode gui --open` for the desktop alpha.
- Current release: v0.9.1. Source: https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode. License: PanCode License 1.0.

This file holds the public PanCode guides (documentation for v0.9.1), the PanHub catalog, tutorials, and research pages as Markdown. Each section names the page it comes from.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs.html

# Install PanCode

Install, update, and launch PanCode on your machine.

## Install

You need a model with tool calling. Linux, macOS and WSL are the primary platforms; native Windows is best effort. Every command below installs the latest release. Choose the tab for your system.

### macOS, Linux and WSL

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh
```

The installer needs no root, including on x64 HPC login nodes with glibc 2.17 or newer. It downloads one bundle for your platform, about 85 MB, that holds PanCode, the Node.js it runs on and every dependency, and checks the bundle's SHA-256 against the checksums published with the release before unpacking it. It installs under `~/.local/share/pancode-install` on Linux or `~/Library/Application Support/pancode/install` on macOS, and writes the launcher `~/.local/bin/pancode`.

On Linux, an install run from a terminal ends by offering the desktop app, which starts at login and appears in your app menu. The optional Claude Agent SDK, about 224 MB, is skipped; PanCode offers to fetch it the first time you need it.

Pass options after `sh -s --`. For example, `--modify-path` adds the launcher directory to your shell profile, `--gui` sets up the desktop app without asking, and `--include-claude-sdk` installs the SDK now:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- --modify-path
```

On a cluster, read [Install on a cluster](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html).

Commands PanCode runs are sandboxed with bubblewrap on Linux and WSL. On macOS they run under `sandbox-exec`, whose profile has not yet been verified on a real Mac. See [Sandbox and safety](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/sandbox-and-safety.html).

### PowerShell

Native Windows is best effort, so use the current stable release. Release checks only start the package on Windows, Windows has no command sandbox, and WSL with the macOS, Linux and WSL command is the better-tested route. The install needs no administrator rights, downloads a bundle that carries its own Node.js, and adds the launcher to your user `PATH`.

```powershell
irm https://pancode.dev/install.ps1 | iex
```

PowerShell shows `PS C:\>` at the prompt. If `curl ... | sh` reports that `sh` is not recognized, you are in Windows rather than WSL.

### CMD

The same best-effort install, started from CMD.

```bat
powershell -NoProfile -Command "irm https://pancode.dev/install.ps1 | iex"
```

CMD shows `C:\>` without the `PS`. If you see `'irm' is not recognized as an internal or external command`, you ran the PowerShell command in CMD; use the command above.

### npm

With your own **Node.js 22.19 or newer** on `PATH`:

```sh
npm install -g @panstudio/pancode
```

### bun

```sh
bun add -g @panstudio/pancode
```

bun installs the package, but `pancode` still runs on Node.js, so it needs **Node.js 22.19 or newer** on `PATH` too.

## Confirm the installation

Open a new terminal and run:

```sh
pancode --version
```

It prints the installed version. If the shell says `pancode: command not found`, the launcher directory is not on your `PATH` yet. Add the line the installer printed to `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, or install again with `--modify-path`:

```sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
```

`command -v pancode` shows which file the name runs. If it is not `~/.local/bin/pancode`, an older install comes first on your `PATH`; remove it or reorder `PATH`. `pancode doctor` checks the installation and connections.

## Open a project

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
pancode configure
pancode
```

On first launch, **Guided setup** asks what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file from your lab or team. It sends the model one short test request and saves when the model answers. PanCode has no account of its own; your provider may require credentials and charge for inference.

A new installation starts guided setup by itself, so `pancode configure` is optional. If you have used PanCode before and no chat route is saved, it looks for a route it can use, such as a provider key in your environment, and opens chat with it. A model server found on a local port is used only after you say yes.

`/config` opens your connections inside a session, where **Add a target** runs setup again.

Prefer the desktop alpha? It is served from your own machine, opens in your browser, and shares the terminal's saved connections and settings. See [the desktop app](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/gui.html):

```sh
pancode gui --open
```

The browser has its own **Guided setup**; configuring in the terminal first is optional.

## Update, roll back and remove

Installer installs update themselves in the background, at most once a day. On Linux and macOS, npm, pnpm, bun, and volta installs whose prefix you own update after an interactive session quits and no other process of that install remains. Set `interface.autoUpdate: false` or `PANCODE_AUTO_UPDATE=0` to keep only the notice. `/upgrade` reviews an update from inside the terminal. From the shell, update with the tool that installed it:

| Installed with | Update | Remove the program |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Installer | `pancode upgrade`. The new version, with the Node.js it runs on, installs beside the current one and must start before the launcher switches to it. | `pancode uninstall` |
| npm | `pancode upgrade` | `npm uninstall -g @panstudio/pancode` |
| bun | `bun add -g @panstudio/pancode@latest`, then `pancode upgrade --post-install` | `bun remove -g @panstudio/pancode` |

The installer keeps the previous version. `pancode upgrade --rollback` makes it current again. An install made with an exact `--version` stays pinned to that version until you run the installer with `--version latest`.

If an upgrade is refused over a setting the installed version cannot repair, the installer prints the new version's own `doctor --fix` command to run.

`pancode uninstall` removes your settings, credentials, sessions and caches, the launcher, the desktop app's background service, every installed version of an installer install, and the package of an npm global install. It previews what it will delete and asks first, and it stops with exit 1 while a session is open on this state directory. Add `--keep-binary` to keep the program, `--keep-config` to keep settings and credentials, or `--dry-run` to only look. Removing the program with npm or bun keeps those files. Project `.pancode/` directories are never removed.

If pancode.dev is unreachable, the latest GitHub release carries the installer, at `https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/releases/latest/download/install.sh`. Run it with `--version <x.y.z>`, because the file that says which version is latest lives on pancode.dev.

## Give PanCode a useful first task

Start with a read-only question:

> Explain how this repository builds and runs its tests. Do not change files.

Then ask for one change with a finish line, such as the test that must pass:

> The test in tests/test_solver.py fails. Make the smallest fix, run the tests, show me the diff, and tell me anything you could not verify.

`/view` shows the evidence for the change, `/usage` what it cost, and `/rewind` restores your files from the snapshot taken before it. The same task runs from a script, which prints the answer and exits with a status your CI can read:

```sh
pancode run --read-only "Summarize this repository and how to run its tests."
```

Follow the [desktop and terminal walkthrough](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/desktop-and-terminal.html), or try [a numerical change with seven tests](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html).

## Keep going

- [Connect a model](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html): setup, model selection, and saved settings.
- [Commands and shortcuts](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html): the controls you'll use most.
- [Tools and permissions](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html): understand changes and review checks.
- [Check your installation](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/doctor.html): diagnose a connection or setup problem.

## When you need more detail

These web guides cover the essentials. Detailed documentation ships with PanCode; ask it to look up the bundled guide for the feature you're using. Each page also links to its full source guide.

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html

# Install on a cluster

Install PanCode on a login node with an old glibc, a proxy, or no internet.

## Install without root

The installer downloads one bundle that holds PanCode, the Node.js it runs on and every dependency, so you do not need `module load nodejs`, a system Node or a package registry. It never uses `sudo` and refuses to run under it.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
pancode doctor
```

It needs `curl` or `wget`, `tar`, `gzip` and a SHA-256 tool. The installed versions go under `~/.local/share/pancode-install` and the launcher under `~/.local/bin`. Compute nodes that mount the same home directory run the same launcher.

## Work on the cluster

Ask for scheduler work in words, such as "submit job.sh and tell me when it starts". `sbatch`, `squeue` and the other Slurm, PBS, LSF and Flux clients run outside the sandbox with the same review as `ssh`: the safety judge decides first and asks you when it has no verdict, so name the action you want. Run them directly, not from a wrapper script, which stays inside the sandbox and fails.

Shell commands write to the project and temp folders without asking. Add scratch space with an absolute path:

```yaml
safety:
  scratchRoots: [/scratch/alice]
```

Keep results out of Git with `pancode store put results run-042.h5`; every checkout of the project on this host sees them.

## Old glibc, proxies, and quotas

The installer picks the bundle for the host. There are bundles for Linux on x64 and arm64 with glibc 2.28 or newer, for x64 hosts with glibc 2.17 to 2.27, the RHEL and CentOS 7 class, for Alpine on x64 and arm64, and for macOS. Linux arm64 with an older glibc has no bundle; use conda-forge Node and npm instead. `PANCODE_TARGET` forces a bundle when detection is wrong.

Export `https_proxy` before running the installer behind a proxy. An installed version takes about 330 MB, and the Claude Agent SDK, installed only with `--include-claude-sdk`, adds about 224 MB. The installer refuses to start with under about 488 MB free at the install root. On a small home quota, move the install root:

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- --install-dir /project/$USER/pancode
```

## Verified downloads

The installer compares the bundle's SHA-256 with the release's `SHA256SUMS`, and a mismatch stops the install. Every release file also has a GitHub build attestation, which `gh attestation verify <file> --repo PanStudio/pancode` checks on a machine with the GitHub CLI.

## Airgapped sites and your own Node

With no route out, download the bundle for the cluster and `install.sh` from the GitHub release on a connected machine, copy both over, and run `sh install.sh --bundle pancode-<version>-<target>.tar.gz`. Nothing else is fetched. A site that mirrors the releases sets `PANCODE_RELEASE_MIRROR` to the mirror's base URL, which can be a `file://` URL on a shared filesystem.

If the site already provides Node 22.19 or newer, you can install with its npm instead: `npm install -g @panstudio/pancode`. When an older `node` comes first on `PATH`, set `PANCODE_NODE` to the newer binary.

Pick versions with `--version` or `--channel`, and undo an upgrade with `--rollback`. The full guide covers the mirror layout; `sh install.sh --help` lists every option.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html

# Connect a model

Set up local models, institutional endpoints, and cloud connections.

## Connect the way you already work

Run `pancode configure`, or choose **Guided setup** in the desktop alpha. First-time setup asks what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file from your lab or team. When PanCode finds a route first, such as a provider key in your environment, it lists that route for you to choose.

1. Provide what the row asks for: paste a key, sign in to a subscription in the browser, or enter a server's address.
2. For a model server or gateway, PanCode checks reachability and reads the model list.
3. PanCode takes the provider's recommended model, or the only model a server lists. Otherwise you pick from the list. For a local server with no models, load one and choose **Check again**.
4. PanCode sends the model one short test request and saves when it answers. After a failure you can try again, change the key or address, or choose **Save anyway**. The first connection supplies the chat and worker defaults.

The test request shows that the model answers. It does not establish model quality or tool calling, and `--no-verify` skips it. Live, cached, and provider-catalog model lists are labeled separately. Choose a model that supports tool calling for repository work.

Already know the URL? Use `pancode configure --quick` for endpoint-first setup. A lab or team can publish one setup file: `pancode configure --import <path-or-https-url>` reads it, prints where prompts will go, and asks once before saving.

## Use a local model server

Start LM Studio, Ollama, llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang or Lemonade with a model that can call tools, then run `pancode`. It finds a server on its default port, such as Ollama on 11434, and offers it. On another address, run `pancode configure` and choose **A model server or gateway**. `pancode targets --probe --tools --target <id>` checks that the model really calls tools.

## Settings Center

Run `pancode configure --settings` or choose **Settings** on the desktop. Both use these sections:

| Section | What to change |
| --- | --- |
| Connections | Providers, credentials, endpoints, and model lists |
| Chat | The connection and model answering you |
| Fleet | Worker models, profiles, and capacity |
| Context & Memory | Context limits, compaction, and memory |
| Permissions & Limits | Approvals, autonomy, and spending limits |
| Appearance | Output style and interface preferences |
| Integrations | Agents, libraries, plugins, and Git |
| Advanced | Diagnostics and the full settings editor |

Terminal `/settings` groups the same controls into its own areas: Recent & Pinned, Models, Chat and display, Workers, Context and memory, Safety and limits, Workspace, and Advanced.

**Use connection default** lets a route inherit its connection's model. In the terminal, save to the session, project, or global scope where offered. Configure edits global defaults; desktop saved settings apply to new conversations. Active conversation controls have their own scope.

## Check the connection

```sh
pancode doctor
pancode targets --probe
```

If setup fails, check credentials, the endpoint address, and whether the local model is loaded. See [troubleshooting](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html) for the next step.

## Servers without a built-in runtime

Every connection names a runtime, which fixes how PanCode talks to the server. `pancode configure --list` prints the runtime ids you can choose. Amazon Bedrock is not in that list, but a `bedrock` connection in your configuration runs.

| Kind of server | Runtimes |
| --- | --- |
| Local model servers | `lmstudio`, `ollama`, `llamacpp`, `vllm`, `sglang`, `lemonade` |
| Cloud providers | `openai`, `anthropic`, `google`, `mistral`, `groq`, `deepseek`, `openrouter`, and others |
| Any compatible endpoint | `openai-compat`, `anthropic-compat`, `litellm` |
| Another agent's login | `claude-code`, `codex-cli`, `opencode-cli`, `pi-cli`, and others; workers only |

A server that speaks the OpenAI or Anthropic API but has no runtime of its own usually works through `openai-compat` or `anthropic-compat`, or through a LiteLLM gateway. Local runtimes probe the server, report the loaded models, and price usage as free; the compatible runtimes make no local-server assumptions and are priced as free only when the connection declares it.

When none of these fits, a developer can add a runtime as a plugin: a JavaScript file in the `runtimes/` folder of PanCode's config directory, or an npm package listed under `integrations.runtimePlugins`, which takes effect after a restart. A broken plugin is reported on stderr and never stops startup. The [provider adapter cookbook](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/0241470c83204f6dfb03baa5771a8d125fda3014/docs/architecture/provider-adapter-cookbook.md) describes the runtime descriptor a plugin exports.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html

# Commands and shortcuts

Navigate the terminal, choose models, and control a session.

## Launch and inspect

| Command | Use it to |
| --- | --- |
| `pancode` | Open the terminal in your project |
| `pancode gui --open` | Open the local desktop alpha |
| `pancode configure` | Connect a model with Guided setup |
| `pancode doctor` | Check installation and connections |
| `pancode upgrade` | Update PanCode |
| `pancode --help` | See installed commands; `--help --all` lists every command path |
| `pancode --resume` | Pick an earlier session to reopen; `--continue` opens the latest |
| `pancode session history` | List saved sessions from the shell |
| `pancode config get <path>` | Read one setting; `config set` and `config unset` change it |

For a single task without the interactive interface:

```sh
pancode run "Explain this project's test setup. Do not change files." --cwd /path/to/project
```

Add `--output-format json` for one machine-readable result, or `--output-format stream-json` for events as they happen. A request to avoid edits is task guidance. When execution must be constrained, add `--read-only` or limit tools with `--allow-tools <names>`.

## Everyday terminal commands

| Command | What it opens or does |
| --- | --- |
| `/help` | Commands and effective keybindings |
| `/model` | Model picker; apply to this session or save for the project or globally |
| `/settings` | Settings, grouped by area |
| `/config` | Connections in Settings; **Add a target** runs setup inside the session |
| `/hub` | PanHub: skills, prompts, agents, playbooks, plugins, and extensions |
| `/context` | Context usage and pending handoffs |
| `/usage` | Session usage and supported subscription quotas |
| `/rewind` | Preview and restore this session's file snapshots |
| `/rename [name]` | Name the session so `/resume` can find it |
| `/fork [name]` | Fork from an assistant turn into a new session, optionally named |
| `/loop <interval> <task>` | Repeat a task on an interval as a bounded job; bare `/loop` lists jobs and `/loop stop` ends one |
| `/reload` | Reload settings, PanHub packs, and extension runtimes |
| `/restart` | Save the session and restart into it |
| `/resume` | Previous conversations; `/resume <id>` reopens one directly |
| `/tree` | Conversation history and branches |
| `/new` | A fresh conversation |
| `/view` | Artifacts and recorded results |
| `/trust` | Review the project's own PanCode configuration and decide whether to activate it |
| `/poll <n> <question>` | Ask 2 to 5 independent agents the same question and see how they vote |
| `/report` | Draft a report for the maintainers; nothing is sent until you review it |

Familiar names work as aliases: `/clear` is `/new`, `/exit` is `/quit`, `/undo` is `/rewind`, `/cost` and `/status` open `/usage`, `/login` opens connections, and `/init` writes a project handbook. A mistyped command names the closest one and keeps your draft.

## A few keys to remember

Alt+letter runs a PanCode action, and **Ctrl+G** then the same letter runs it in any terminal, including ones that intercept Alt. The menu also lists a few actions with no Alt key; arrows and Enter work too, and Esc closes it. On an empty composer, `?` shows the keys; `/help` shows every binding, custom ones included.

| Default key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Enter | Send; while running, queue the message for the next pause between tool calls |
| Ctrl+J | Insert a newline |
| Alt+S | Send now: interrupt the run and submit the draft |
| Alt+Q | Open the queue to reorder, edit, or remove waiting messages; `a` puts them all back in the draft |
| Alt+M | Open the model picker |
| Alt+L | Open PanHub |
| Alt+O | Cycle the output detail level |
| Alt+W | Open Workers: the Fleet Runs board, or the workers dock in a session with panes |
| Alt+U | Open or close the one-page dashboard |

Ctrl+C closes an active overlay or cancels a running turn. When idle with no queued messages, two presses within 3 seconds exit; the first press keeps your draft.

For a course correction, type it in the composer and press **Alt+S** (or **Ctrl+G s**). Work already completed remains in the session record. In the queue, `t` switches a message between the next pause and the end of the turn.

A clean exit prints a summary of the session and the `pancode --resume <id>` line that reopens it. Inside the app, `/resume` does the same.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html

# Tools and permissions

Read, search, edit, and run commands with PanCode's repository tools.

## Ask for a bounded change

PanCode can read and search files, make edits, run shell commands, and execute declared project checks. Give it a concrete scope and an outcome you can review:

> Fix the parser's handling of empty input. Keep the public API unchanged, add the relevant regression test, and run the project's test check. Show the diff and result.

A useful sequence is **inspect → change → verify → review**. Inspect the actual diff before committing. The `git` tool can also run `add` and `commit`, and the safety rules judge those like the matching shell command.

## Understand permission requests

**default** follows one rule: containment first, judgment second, asking last. Workspace edits run. Shell commands run inside an OS sandbox when the host has one. In a Git work tree, PanCode snapshots your files before the first change of a turn, and `/rewind` restores them. A safety judge reviews what would otherwise ask against your own messages, and you are asked when it has no verdict or the decision is yours.

**yolo** is for long jobs you leave running: nothing waits for you. It is contained by default, so the sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge work as at `default`, and a call that would have asked you is refused back to PanCode. It needs a one-time acceptance. Set the level in Settings, with `--autonomy`, or with the leader key.

Unconfined yolo is the skip-permissions mode for a container or another disposable environment. Commands run unsandboxed as you, and only a short floor, your project rules, and the run's ceilings block. It takes effect only with `safety.yoloConfinement: unconfined` in your user settings and its own one-time acceptance. See [the containment tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html).

When a card reaches you, read the command and its working directory before approving it. A card nobody answers within `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) is denied and the turn continues. In the terminal, a shell approval card also shows an **Effect** line that says in plain words what the command would do. It is a reading aid; admission does not depend on it.

Asking for a plan or saying “do not edit” guides the task; it does not establish a technical read-only boundary. Use the explicit tool restrictions or read-only dispatch options when you need that boundary.

## What the sandbox hides

A sandboxed command writes only to your project, the temp directories, your scratch roots, a private tool cache and the repository's Git data. It cannot read your SSH keys, cloud and code-host logins, registry tokens or the project's `.env` and key files, and credential variables are removed. A push or a publish needs those credentials, and a cluster scheduler command needs a host daemon the sandbox blocks, so each leaves the sandbox only once the safety judge or you allow it.

## Verify using your project's checks

Ask PanCode to discover available checks, then run the relevant one with `verify`. It uses declared scripts and supported build/CI definitions rather than treating arbitrary output as a test result.

> Discover this project's verification checks. Run the test check through verify and report the exit status, failures, and anything you could not check.

The agent can end a turn by declaring how it went with the `finish` tool: `done`, `partly_done` or `not_done`, with its limitations. PanCode records that claim beside its own assessment. A `done` that left unvalidated changes, a failing check or an open task is assessed as partly done, and the terminal shows one line that begins `declared done, assessed partly done`.

On the desktop, the Session column's **Artifacts** card lists tool output and session records, and **Changes** lists the files a turn changed. In the terminal, use `/view` to browse artifacts and run records.

For checks that must accompany specific changes, add a [project quality policy](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/quality-policy.html). For a worked example, follow [the temperature-calibration tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html).

## How tools reach the model

A main session starts with a small set of tools attached: `read`, `bash`, `edit`, `write`, `grep`, `code_nav`, `verify`, `ask_user`, `finish`, and `gateway`. `dispatch` joins when workers are available, `consult` when a decision model is configured, and `memory_note` while the agent writes memory notes, which is the default.

The model finds every other capability through `gateway`, which can search the catalog, describe a tool's arguments, and call it. This keeps the request small while search, Git, web reading, data inspection, and MCP server tools stay one call away. Workers instead receive the tools their agent recipe admits.

Tool results are bounded. Each reading tool has a size cap per call, and all of them share a budget per turn that grows with the model's context window. A cut result ends with one notice line that says how much was shown and gives the exact argument for the next page. When the cap cut content that was already collected, the notice also names a read-only overflow copy in PanCode's state directory, outside your workspace. The permission rules above apply to every tool, whether it is attached or reached through `gateway`.

## Limit what the agent may use

Run `pancode --allow-tools read,grep,find,ls` to limit the main agent to those tools, and `--delegate-tools` to limit its workers. Both take a comma-separated list or `none`. A prompt, skill or worker recipe can narrow these limits but never widen them. `/view` shows what the tools produced, a cut result in full included.

The full guide lists every tool and its limits. Developers can read [how the prompt and tool surface are assembled](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/0241470c83204f6dfb03baa5771a8d125fda3014/docs/architecture/prompt-envelope-and-tools.md).

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/sandbox-and-safety.html

# Sandbox and safety

What a sandboxed command may do, what it hides, and when PanCode asks you.

## Check your machine first

Run `pancode doctor` and read the `shell sandbox` row. `OK` means shell commands run inside an OS sandbox: bubblewrap on Linux and WSL, `sandbox-exec` on macOS (not yet verified on a real Mac). `WARN` means they run uncontained, so more of them ask first. Windows has no sandbox.

Then work at the `default` level. In your request, name anything that reaches beyond the project, such as "push the branch when the tests pass".

## What a sandboxed command may do

A sandboxed command can read your files and use the network. It writes only to the project, the temp directories, any directory in `safety.scratchRoots`, a private tool cache and the repository's Git data. Git hooks and Git config stay read-only, because they run later outside the sandbox.

## What the sandbox hides

The command cannot read SSH and GPG keys, the SSH agent, cloud and cluster logins, code-host and registry tokens, password stores, browser profiles, shell histories or other agents' logins. Secret files in the project, such as `.env` and `*.key`, are hidden too. Variables whose names or values look like credentials are removed. List one a build needs in `safety.sandboxPassEnv`.

## Commands that leave the sandbox

`git push`, `gh`, cloud CLIs, `ssh`, publishing commands and the Slurm, PBS, LSF and Flux clients need your credentials, so they run outside the sandbox. At `default` the safety judge reviews each one against your own messages first, and you are asked when it has no verdict. Contained yolo runs one only when your message names it.

## Stricter or looser

`safety.sandbox` is `auto` by default. `required` refuses workers' commands on a machine without a sandbox and keeps unconfined yolo sandboxed; `srun`, `salloc` and `flux` then stay inside it. `off` never sandboxes. Unconfined yolo, for containers only, runs commands as you with your credentials.

A short floor holds at every level. It blocks wiping `/`, your home directory or a system tree, formatting disks, and writes into PanCode's own settings and credentials. The floor also reads the shell scripts a command runs by path or with `source`. A change only you may make, such as project trust, is refused with a message that sends the agent to you.

## Project configuration and /trust

A repository's own PanCode settings, safety rules, hooks and packages are ignored until you approve their exact contents. A card lists them when you open the project, and `/trust` reopens it. Even approved, project settings can only make PanCode more careful: they cannot raise the autonomy level, loosen the sandbox, raise limits or carry credentials.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/context-continuity.html

# Save and resume work

Resume conversations, manage context, and prepare a handoff.

## Pick up a conversation

In the terminal, use `/resume` to choose a previous session, or `/rename` first so you can resume it by name. On the desktop, open a saved conversation from **Overview** or **Sessions**. Saved history lets you continue with the context of earlier work.

Use `/tree` to inspect terminal conversation branches and `/fork [name]` to fork from an assistant turn into a new session, optionally named. `/tree` rewinds the conversation; `/rewind` restores files. On the desktop, open **Branches** in the Session column. Branches let you explore another direction while preserving the earlier conversation.

## Find sessions from the shell

`pancode session list` shows open sessions on this state directory, from any host that shares it, with host, pid, and last heartbeat. `pancode session terminate <id>` asks the owning process to exit. `pancode session history` lists saved sessions, `pancode --resume <id or prefix>` reopens one, and `pancode --continue` reopens the most recent session for the project.

## Keep long work focused

Open `/context` to inspect context usage, output reservation, remaining headroom, and any pending handoff. PanCode compacts a long native session automatically when context use crosses its configured threshold, or you can request a focused summary:

```text
/context compact Keep the objective, decisions, changed files, test results, and remaining work.
```

For a fresh session with a stated goal, use `/handoff <goal>`. When moving work between agents, make sure the handoff includes evidence and unresolved questions, then review what the receiving agent does.

To keep a session well under the model's window, start it with `pancode --max-context-tokens <N>`. `pancode run` takes the same flag. It caps the context budget and never enlarges the server's window.

## Recover an interrupted handoff

If `/context` shows a pending handoff, use its exact ID:

```text
/context recover <handoffId> reduce
/context recover <handoffId> deliver
```

Choose `reduce` when the reduction has not committed and another attempt remains; choose `deliver` when a validated commit exists. If the continuation still cannot fit, compact more history first.

A restarted process records an interrupted handoff as paused and waits for your recovery command. A fork receives earlier notes as recall; it does not inherit permission to resume the parent's handoff.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/proactive-memory.html

# Memory and lessons

See what PanCode remembers, approve lessons, or turn memory off.

## What memory does

Memory is on by default and needs no setup. PanCode keeps task memory for a session: requirements, environment facts, failed attempts, and diagnoses. By default it runs on rules, with no automatic model calls. The model steps are opt-in, and they use your chat route unless you give memory a route of its own.

## Notes have to be demonstrated

What PanCode keeps across sessions is a note: a claim bound to a command that succeeded or a file that was read. The agent writes one with the `memory_note` tool, and a failed command followed by its fix is filed by rule. A note becomes a lesson only after two other sessions demonstrate it, or after you approve it.

A stored lesson is checked once per session before it is delivered. If its command no longer resolves, or the text it quotes has left the file, PanCode withholds it. A lesson you approved keeps its approval and is named in a notice.

## See and approve lessons

Open `/memory` to see the lessons this session can reach, pending and rejected records beside approved ones, and what each one concerns. From the shell:

```sh
pancode memory list
pancode memory approve <memoryId>
pancode memory reject <memoryId>
pancode memory prune --stale
pancode memory consolidate
```

`memory consolidate` merges records of the same claim, demotes lessons that no longer hold and drops automatic notes with no evidence. It makes no model call and never touches a record you approved or rejected. `memory list --approved-by operator` or `--approved-by guardian` lists approved records by who approved them.

`/memory` also shows the current tier, the live bank, and the last twenty memory steps with their trigger, decision, and latency. That history is the only place a skipped step or a timeout appears. In `/memory`, press `p` on a selected row to propose it for review at repository scope, or `g` for global scope.

A lesson reaches the agent in the `# Memory` section of the prompt and, by default, as a reminder at a decision point: a failed command, a missing check, a touched file or the task of the turn. Reviewing earlier sessions for new lessons is off by default; set `context.memory.surfaces.history: on` to turn it on.

## Turn it off or route it elsewhere

Set `context.memory.enabled: false`, or use `/settings` → **Context and memory** → **Proactive memory**. Off means off: the `# Memory` section leaves main and worker prompts, and history review reads nothing from a session that ran with memory off. To run memory on its own route, set both `context.memory.target` and `context.memory.model`.

## Settings

All keys live under `context.memory` in `settings.yaml`, and `/settings` → **Context and memory** has rows for them.

| Key | Default | Effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `enabled` | `true` | Turns memory on or off. |
| `target`, `model` | `null` | Dedicated memory route; unset uses the chat route. |
| `surfaces.lessons` | `agent` | Who writes notes: `off`, `rules`, `agent` or `side`. |
| `surfaces.delivery` | `decision` | How lessons reach the agent: `off`, `section`, `decision` or `broadcast`. |
| `surfaces.correct`, `surfaces.bank` | `rules` | `model` adds a model step for corrections or bank upkeep. |
| `surfaces.history` | `off` | `on` reviews earlier sessions for lessons while idle. |
| `sideShare` | `0.15` | Caps automatic memory calls at a share of the session's main output; `0` removes the cap. |
| `thinkingLevel` | `off` | How much the memory side call reasons. |
| `cadenceToolCalls` | `10` | Completed tools between model steps under `surfaces.bank: model`. |
| `trajectorySteps` | `8` | Recent tool steps a background step reads. |
| `maxOutputTokens` | `2000` | Bounds the bank context and the reminder. |
| `timeoutMs` | `60000` | Time limit for one background step. |

## Choose a cheap or local background model

Memory reads a short trajectory and writes a bounded result, so a small model usually suffices. The route's thinking level is `context.memory.thinkingLevel`, which defaults to `off`.

```yaml
context:
  memory:
    target: memory-dedicated
    model: memory-profile/qwen3.5-4b
```

These IDs are examples; check yours with `pancode targets --probe`. Locally, both models and their caches must fit in memory.

## Cost and budget

A step is checked against its route's cost before any request leaves, so a skipped step costs nothing. Metered routes stop at `safety.limits.sessionCostUsd`, subscription routes wait out a near-full quota window, and free routes need an open request slot. After a session's first three automatic memory calls, `sideShare` also holds memory output to 15% of main output. Steps appear as `memory steps` in `/usage`.

Memory gives reminders; it does not replace reading the code or running the checks. See the full guide for how reminders are selected and when a lesson is promoted.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html

# Files and terminal panes

Attach files and open companion terminal panes.

## Add a file browser or companion shell

The terminal can open a files pane, a live workers dashboard, logs, a shell, music, or an installed coding peer beside the conversation.

Bare `pancode` in an interactive terminal opens its own private pane host with no question to answer. The host is a pinned copy of **Herdr** that the installer provisions. When the host is not installed, PanCode starts in the plain terminal without a notice, and `/panes`, `/files`, and Alt+E name `pancode panes install`.

After an npm or bun install, add the pane host yourself. The file browser is a separate install either way:

```sh
pancode panes install
pancode tools install yazi
```

To join a Herdr session of your own as a guest, open a pane in your project, then run:

```sh
pancode --with-panes
```

The option joins the current Herdr session. It does not create a pane host from a plain terminal. For the files pane, also enable it in your PanCode settings:

```yaml
interface:
  panes:
    files:
      enabled: true
```

Check `pancode doctor` if the host or files engine is unavailable.

## Use the files pane

`/files` or **Alt+E** opens the file browser and gives it keyboard focus. Select a file and press **Ctrl+Y** to insert it as an `@file` mention and return focus to PanCode. `/files` or Alt+E then hides the pane: the browser keeps running and keeps its directory. Press the key twice quickly, or run `/files close`, to end it.

## Docks hide instead of closing

The files, workers, and music panes are docks with fixed places. **Alt+E**, **Alt+W**, and **Alt+A** show or hide them, and a second press within a moment closes one. Alt+W opens a dashboard with a card for each worker in the session; Enter follows one worker's live stream.

`/music` plays focus radio through cliamp in a thin dock once `integrations.music.enabled` is on and `pancode tools install cliamp` has run. `/music pause`, `/music next`, `/music station <name or url>`, and `/music off` control it.

| Command | Companion pane |
| --- | --- |
| `/panes open shell` | A login shell in the workspace |
| `/panes open logs` | The newest dispatched run's event journal |
| `/panes show <run-or-agent>` | A live worker view |
| `/panes peer <agent> [brief]` | An interactive coding-agent handoff |

A session started inside tmux, Zellij, or screen stays in the plain terminal without panes. For editor and agent connections, see [interoperability](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/interop.html).

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/gui.html

# The desktop app

Open the desktop alpha, keep tasks in one window, and read the Session column.

## Open the desktop app

The desktop app is in alpha. It is a local web application: PanCode serves it from your own machine on `127.0.0.1`, and it opens in your browser. It shares the terminal's saved connections and settings and covers a subset of terminal workflows.

```sh
pancode gui --open
```

Started this way, the app runs while that terminal stays open. On Linux with a systemd user session, including WSL, you can keep it running in the background instead. It then starts at login and appears in your app menu, or in the Windows Start Menu under WSL:

```sh
pancode gui background install --open
```

The installer offers the same step. The background app listens on port 4343, or 7373 when another program holds 4343. It uses saved credentials, so store a key that lives only in your shell with `pancode auth login <target>`.

`pancode gui` prints one link ending in `#ticket=`. The ticket opens one browser window once, within 60 seconds, and the browser then keeps its own short-lived sign-in. If a window shows the reconnect prompt, for example after the background app restarted, run `pancode gui` again or paste the new link into the prompt's **Launch link** field.

## One window, many tasks

Launching again brings the open PanCode window forward under WSL, when the app is installed through Chrome or Edge, and on a Linux desktop with `wmctrl`, `xdotool` or sway when the background app is running. Otherwise it opens a new browser tab. Open a second window on purpose with **Open in new window** in a task's menu.

Any number of tasks can be open. Up to four turns run at once by default, and the `interface.guiTurnCapacity` setting allows 1 to 16. A further turn shows **Waiting for a slot** and starts when one frees. A task with no running turn that no window has shown for five minutes is paused. Its conversation stays readable, and **Resume task** continues it.

## Read the Session column

Beside each conversation, the Session column shows the workspace's path, branch and Git state, the model and its health, context, tokens and cost, the plan, artifacts, changed files, branches, agents, and evidence from run records. It updates as the task runs. **App activity** counts working, queued, and approval-waiting tasks across workspaces.

Type `/` in the composer for session commands such as `/context`, `/usage`, `/tree`, `/fork`, and `/handoff`.

## Approvals

With **Ask first**, reads, edits, and recognized commands run, and unrecognized shell commands, large dispatch plans, and anything that publishes outside the project wait on a card. The card states what the call is, what allowing it authorizes, and what it can affect. Choose **Allow once** or **Reject**.

**Run without approvals** stops the cards for one task after a second confirmation. By default the sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge stay on, and a call that would have waited for you is refused back to PanCode. It lasts until the task closes or is paused.

If a project carries settings, hooks, safety rules, extensions, or plugins you have not approved, the app lists the ignored files above the conversation with the command that reviews them.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panstore.html

# Keep results in PanStore

Keep datasets and results outside the working tree, with a record of where each came from.

## Keep results out of your working tree

Long analyses produce files you want to keep but not commit: datasets, model outputs, figures. PanStore, the project store, holds them outside the working tree. The main session, its workers and every linked worktree of the project see the same store, and each file keeps a record of where it came from.

A tag is a named container, classed input, output, cache or archive. A blob is a file in a tag. A reference reads `<tag>:<blob>`, such as `results:summary.parquet`.

## Store a file from your shell

```sh
pancode store put results out/summary.parquet --note "baseline run"
pancode store tags
pancode store ls results
pancode store stat results:summary.parquet
```

`put` creates a missing tag as an input tag. `stat` shows the record and whether the bytes have drifted since: `none`, `changed`, `missing` or `unrecorded`. `get` prints the path of a read-only copy, or copies the blob elsewhere with `--to <path>`. Every command takes `--json`. `pancode store where` prints the store's folders and ends with the `pankit serve store` line that serves this store over MCP to another agent on this machine.

## Ask PanCode to use it

> Run the analysis script on `data:measurements.h5`, put its summary into the `results` tag, and tell me whether the stored baseline has drifted.

The agent reaches the store through its `store` tool. Reads run without asking. Creating a tag, a put and a note are judged as writes. Removing a blob, or a put that replaces one, asks first and names the blob; a replacing put also states its size. The store keeps no earlier versions.

When a `run_script` run declares a store blob as an input and its output is put back, the record names the script and that input.

## Let workers write

Dispatched workers read the store. They write only into the tags their dispatch grants, and a granted tag must exist first. The built-in coder, researcher and scout workers use the store without extra setup.

## Limits

- The store lives in PanCode's data directory on one host; `pancode store where` prints its folder. A worker on an SSH fleet node sees that node's own store.
- `put` copies bytes, and the store keeps no earlier versions of a blob.
- `pancode reset --data`, `reset --all` and `uninstall` without `--keep-data` delete the store for good.
- The store has been exercised on Linux only.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panhub.html

# Packs from PanHub

Find, install and manage skills, plugins, extensions and other packs.

## Find a useful skill

PanHub holds installable packs, each of one kind: **skill, agent, prompt, playbook, plugin, or extension**. Open `/hub` or press **Alt+L**. Switch categories with left/right, search with `/`, and open a pack with Enter.

`pancode hub update --all` updates eligible copies, `pancode hub package <directory>` turns a skill directory into a pack, and `pancode hub validate` checks what you author.

Use **Browse** to find available content and **Installed** to manage your copies. Choose **User** for tools shared across projects or **Project** for resources specific to this workspace.

`install` uses user scope unless you pass `--project`; `s` switches scope in PanHub. Project packs live under `.pancode/plugins/`.

For example, preview and install the test-driven-development skill:

```sh
pancode hub install skill:tdd --project --dry-run
pancode hub install skill:tdd --project
```

Then activate it in the terminal:

```text
/skill tdd Add coverage for this parser before changing its behavior.
```

## Write your own prompts and skills

A file such as `.pancode/prompts/bugfix.md` runs as `/bugfix`. A `SKILL.md` with a `description` in `.pancode/skills/<name>/` loads with `/skill <name>`. Prompts and skills that Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode keep in your home folder are found without copying; copies inside a project wait until you trust them.

Move your prompts, skills and settings to another machine with a share archive:

```sh
pancode share export --out project.pancode-share.json --project
pancode share import project.pancode-share.json --dry-run
```

## Command reference

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `hub search [query] [--kind <kind>]` | Find packs in the index |
| `hub list` | Show packs in both scopes |
| `hub install <ref> [--dry-run]` | Review and install a pack |
| `hub update <ref>\|--all` | Bring installed copies forward |
| `hub enable`, `disable`, `remove <ref>` | Change one installed copy |

Prefix each with `pancode`. A reference is `kind:name`, such as `skill:tdd`, or an unambiguous bare name. `update --all` skips extensions, which each need their own review.

## Review before installing

The install review shows the destination, dependencies, and verified pack pin. In PanHub, the selected row offers install, update, enable/disable, and remove actions when applicable. Management actions name the owning pack and selected scope.

Project packs take precedence over matching user packs. A disabled project copy also suppresses the user copy, so a project can explicitly keep a resource unavailable. A project pack set you have not approved for the workspace is listed but not loaded, and does not override your user copy; see [plugins](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/plugins.html).

## Trust project packs

A project copy comes from the repository, so its digest proves integrity, not your consent. Approve project packs per workspace:

```sh
pancode config trust plugins
pancode config trust plugins --hash <sha256>
```

The first is a read-only review; the second approves what you reviewed, and `--revoke` withdraws it. `/reload hub` applies it to a running session. A changed pack identity needs a new review, and an import never approves one.

## Refresh a running session

After changing recipes through another process, run:

```text
/reload hub
```

Disabling a pack prevents subsequent discovery; it does not stop an in-flight tool or erase instructions already read. Disable deletes no files; `hub enable <ref>` restores the pack. Disabling and removal apply without a reload, while installs from another process need `/reload hub`. `/skill off` clears an active skill's armed tool surface without erasing earlier context.

For bundles of related resources, see [plugins](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/plugins.html). To review resources from other coding agents, see [interoperability](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/interop.html).

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/pankit.html

# Tool servers with PanKit

Run PanKit's MCP tool servers in PanCode or in any other MCP host.

## What PanKit gives you

PanKit is PanCode's agent toolkit, shareable with other agents over MCP: seven tool servers for HPC and scientific work. PanCode installs it as the `pankit` command. PanCode loads every server as a builtin MCP server, and any other MCP host can launch one with `pankit serve <server>`.

| Server | What it answers |
| --- | --- |
| `node` | This machine's CPU, memory, disks, network interfaces, NVIDIA GPUs and top processes, read-only. |
| `modules` | The site's software modules, and the `module load` lines a batch script needs. |
| `spack` | Installed Spack specs, package details, prefixes, concretization and environments. |
| `darshan` | What one Darshan log says about a job's I/O. |
| `scidata` | The structure, a bounded slice and summary statistics of HDF5, NetCDF, Zarr, Parquet, CSV and JSON files. |
| `catalog` | Search, describe and stage datasets from the catalogs an operator lists. |
| `store` | A project's [PanStore](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panstore.html) tags and blobs, writing only to the tags it was started with. |

Each tool has an action class: `read` tools only read, and `execute` tools change something or run work with side effects.

## Check what runs on this host

```sh
pankit list
pankit doctor
pankit manifest
```

`doctor` prints `<id>: available` or `<id>: unavailable: <reason>` for each server and starts none of them. `manifest` prints every tool's class and path arguments, the policy PanCode ships for these servers.

## Use the servers inside PanCode

PanKit servers are trusted by authorship: their classes come from the shipped manifest, and they need no `pancode mcp trust`. List them and call one tool:

```sh
pancode mcp list
pancode mcp test node --call node_memory
```

PanCode starts `scidata` with its reader cache, `catalog` with `pankit/catalog.json` in your PanCode config folder, and `store` with the session's store and the tags the session may write. A sandboxed fleet worker starts a server without network until you grant it once, for example `pancode mcp trust catalog --network`.

## Use them from another MCP host

A host launches a server over stdio. Without a global install, `npx` fetches the `@panstudio/pancode` package and runs its `pankit`:

```json
{
	"mcpServers": {
		"node": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "-p", "@panstudio/pancode", "pankit", "serve", "node"] }
	}
}
```

A server's own description of its tools is a hint; each host decides the policy it enforces. Another host can review and adopt the output of `pankit manifest`.

## Limits

- `catalog` ships no sources and reads public CKAN portals only, with no credentials and no proxy support.
- `scidata` keeps its own reader cache, separate from PanCode's `data` tool, and has no SQLite reader.
- No `modules` tool loads a module, and `node_gpus` reports NVIDIA GPUs only.
- A fleet worker that may write the project starts a builtin server without its network grant.
- PanKit servers on macOS and Windows are unverified beyond one `pankit serve node` handshake.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html

# Workers and fleets

Assign focused tasks and combine workers into a workflow.

## Delegate a focused task

A worker handles a bounded task while PanCode keeps the main conversation. Start with an explicit goal, files it may change, and the checks it should report.

```sh
pancode agents
pancode run "Inspect the parser's test coverage and report gaps. Do not edit files." --agent verifier
```

Use an agent ID from your installed catalog: `coder` makes changes, `tester` adds tests, `reviewer` judges a diff, and `debugger` and `verifier` only check. Add `--worktree` to `/run` to give an editing worker its own branch, or `--read-only` to make sure it changes nothing. A worker's answer stays out of the conversation until you run `/fleet share <runId>`, or start it with `--share`.

In the terminal, `/run <agent-id> <task>` starts a worker. The same command with a configured ACP peer's id, or `acp:<id>`, delegates to that peer. The **Workers** area of `/settings` chooses worker defaults without changing the chat model.

## Follow the work

Alt+W opens the **Fleet Runs** board to inspect active runs. Select a running worker and use the displayed steer or cancel action. In a session with panes, Alt+W opens the workers dock instead, a live dashboard beside the conversation. You can also send an addressed message:

```text
@<agentId-or-runId-prefix> Focus on empty input and report the existing tests.
```

A steering message first reports queued, then received when the worker acknowledges it. Some external runtimes have no live steering channel; the interface identifies that limit. Review each run's recorded result before using its conclusions.

## Permissions, sandbox, and merges

Native workers run their shell, script, and verification commands in an OS sandbox: bubblewrap on Linux, or an experimental `sandbox-exec` profile on macOS. With the default `safety.sandbox: auto`, they run unsandboxed on a host with no sandbox backend; `required` refuses them instead, and `off` disables it. `safety.sandboxNetwork: true` allows network access.

Your own session's shell commands run in the same kind of sandbox at `default` and at contained `yolo`, which is yolo's default. At unconfined `yolo` they do not, and workers keep theirs. A worker's ordinary asks go to the safety judge by default (`fleet.permissions.mode: judge`).

When a worker's task branch would merge with a failing or unrun check, the terminal asks first with a **Merge task branch?** card showing the branch, changed paths, and the check. The card opens on **Keep branch**. Headless runs keep the branch, and so do ACP sessions whose client cannot answer questions. `pancode fleet land` lists the branches finished runs kept, previews one, and lands it.

## Run a playbook when you need one

```sh
pancode playbook list
pancode fleet run sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
pancode fleet status
```

For a script, `fleet run --output-format json` prints one result document. `fleet run --detach` returns once the fleet is recorded, `pancode fleet wait <fleetRootId>` prints the result and exits with its code, and `pancode fleet list` shows this project's fleets.

A playbook combines workers into a workflow such as a review gate, competing solutions, or a council. The fleet runs it. Copy a built-in playbook with `pancode playbook new <name> --from sdlc`, check it with `pancode playbook validate <name>`, and inspect the approval preview before starting. Its steps work and commit in your checkout, so there is nothing to land afterwards. See [the playbook tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-a-playbook-and-land-it.html).

## Give workers MCP tools

A recipe names exact `mcp_<id>__<tool>` capabilities, and admission refuses an untrusted or stale server. Grant one project server with `pancode mcp trust <id>`, then check it with `pancode mcp test <id>`, which launches only a trusted server. Add `--network` to `mcp trust` to allow it network inside the worker sandbox.

## Run workers on another machine

Remote native workers use SSH and need the same PanCode version and the project at the same absolute path on each node. Add a node with `pancode fleet nodes add`, or in the terminal under `/settings fleet`, which opens the Workers area.

A node receives work only after `pancode fleet nodes test <id> --record` passes for this project; the record lasts one day. Adding a node moves nothing by itself: unpinned work stays local.

Start locally with one worker. Use the full guide for remote-node configuration, capacity, recipes, and failure recovery.

## When a worker stops or fails

A worker has no operator watching it, so `fleet.permissions.mode` decides what happens when it needs an approval. The default, `judge`, sends a local worker's ordinary request to the main session's safety judge while that session runs at `default`; elsewhere it denies. A refused shell command goes back to the worker as a tool result, and the third refusal ends the run with exit 3 and outcome `permission_required`. The reason names every refused command. Under `fail`, the first refusal ends the run.

Some failures retry automatically and some never do:

- A provider 429 retries on another target after at least one second; a 401 or 403 also moves to another target, and a 408 retries.
- Other provider 4xx errors, cancellation, policy and permission refusals, and deterministic outcomes such as `worker_no_work` never retry.
- Every role owes evidence: an explorer what it observed, a builder a change or a stated reason, a checker executed checks, a reviewer cited evidence. A worker that returns without it is retried once on another model.
- No attempt retries automatically after it ran a state-changing call, or when its records cannot prove the checkout unchanged.
- Backoff starts at 500 ms, doubles, and stops at 60 seconds.

A remote node that fails its channel twice in a row is marked offline. Its in-flight runs settle as `stalled` and retry without that node, and each reroute is recorded on the run. Read the stop reason in **Workers** or with `pancode fleet status` before retrying by hand. The [dispatch mechanics reference](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/0241470c83204f6dfb03baa5771a8d125fda3014/docs/architecture/worker-dispatch-mechanics.md) gives the full failure taxonomy and exit codes.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/plugins.html

# Install plugins

Add reusable resources to your PanCode installation.

## Install a bundle of resources

Plugins keep related skills, prompts, agents, playbooks, and supporting files together. Browse the shipped catalog and preview an installation before writing it:

```sh
pancode hub list --kind plugin
pancode hub install plugin:hpc --dry-run
pancode hub install plugin:hpc
```

The catalog ships with PanCode, but its content is not installed automatically. Add `--project` to keep a package in the current workspace; otherwise installation uses user scope.

Project packages load only in a workspace you have approved. A project install you run approves the packages it writes. Any other change to the project's package set, including one that arrives with a clone or a pull, stays listed but unloaded until you review it with `pancode config trust plugins` and run the approval command it prints.

A local bundle uses the same review flow:

```sh
pancode hub install ./my-plugin --project
```

## Keep the installed copy under control

```sh
pancode hub inspect hpc --json
pancode hub drift hpc
pancode hub disable hpc
pancode hub enable hpc
```

Installation records a verified pin covering the complete package tree. Drifted content is blocked from loading; `pin` verifies the recorded pin rather than approving edits. Review an update before replacing a modified copy.

In the terminal, open **PanHub → Plugins** to browse members and review lifecycle actions. Run `/reload hub` after changing recipes externally.

## Choose the right kind of extension

A plugin carries content. An extension is code that runs in its own process, declares everything it may do, and loads only after you approve those capabilities; manage it with `pancode extensions`. The runtime is sandboxed where the host has a backend. Project extensions also need `pancode config trust extensions`. See [the extension tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html). Adding or changing an extension's command tool needs a restart; `/reload hub` refreshes plugin content and never changes tool schemas.

See [PanHub](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panhub.html) for everyday PanHub controls. The full plugin guide covers private catalogs and package authoring.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/harness-extensions.html

# Write and install extensions

Install and write extensions that declare what they may do.

## Plugin or extension

A plugin carries content such as skills, prompts, and playbooks. An extension is code that runs in its own process, declares everything it may do, and loads only after you approve those capabilities.

## Manage extensions

```sh
pancode extensions list
pancode extensions install <path>
pancode extensions disable <id>
pancode extensions remove <id>
```

`install` prints what the package would be allowed to do and records the digest of that declaration. If the manifest changes between review and apply, the install refuses and asks for a fresh review. In a session, `/extensions` shows each package's state, commands, and confinement.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `init <id> [--template <name>]` | Scaffold a manifest, entrypoint, and test |
| `validate <path>` | Check the manifest; print the envelope and its digest |
| `test <path>` | Run the package's `*.test.ts` files |
| `install <path> [--user\|--project]` | Review and install; user scope by default |
| `enable`, `disable`, `remove <id>` | Change one installed copy |
| `run <id> <command>` | Run one extension command headlessly |

Prefix each with `pancode extensions`. `enable`, `disable`, and `remove` act on the project copy when one exists, unless `--user` or `--project` selects one.

## Where packages live

User packages live under `<configDir>/extensions/<id>/`, project packages under `.pancode/extensions/<id>/`. A project package shadows the user package with the same ID, even when disabled, but only once you approve project extensions for the workspace:

```sh
pancode config trust extensions
pancode config trust extensions --hash <sha256>
```

The first is a read-only review; the second approves it. Until then a project copy lists as `untrusted` and the user copy keeps loading.

## What an extension can add

Hooks at prompt submit and around tool calls, runtime tools the model can call, status lines, panels, and work on a timer. A `before_tool` hook can refuse a call. At `api: 2`, a hook can pin one small context block that stays in the conversation, a tool can return a short `summary` with a `detail_ref` the model pages through on demand, and `runtime.promote` attaches up to four of the package's tools to every request. The runtime runs inside bubblewrap on Linux or Seatbelt on macOS when a backend exists; without one, it runs with your permissions.

Approval covers the manifest's `runtime` block, the capability envelope: commands, hooks, tools with their action class, interface slots, content the runtime may see (`prompt`, `tool-args`, `tool-results`, `assistant-text`), file roots, and whether it may run programs or use the network.

Command tools under `capabilities.tools` run a `node` or `python3` script per call. The command runs inside your session's OS sandbox when admission contains the call, as it contains `bash` at `default`; otherwise it runs with your access. Prefer a runtime tool when confinement matters.

## Write one

```sh
pancode extensions init <id> --template status
```

The templates are `status`, `hook`, `panel`, `tool`, and `workspace`. Follow [the extension tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html) for the whole path. A project's own extensions also need `pancode config trust extensions`.

The manifest, `pancode-extension.yaml`, requires `id`, `version`, and `description`:

```yaml
id: lab-guard
version: 1.0.0
description: Refuse writes to protected paths.
runtime:
  api: 2
  entrypoint: runtime/extension.ts
  commands:
    - { name: protect, description: Protect a path against write and edit calls. }
```

The code must register exactly what the manifest declares, and PanCode never installs dependencies. Run `validate` and `test`, then `install`; a running session picks it up after `/reload extensions`.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/sdk.html

# Extension API (unstable)

Scaffold, validate and test extensions, and write MCP tool servers.

## What the extension API holds

The extension API is how you write PanCode extensions, packs, tools and MCP servers. It is unstable: its imports, types and limits can change in any release, so pin the PanCode version an extension is tested against. It ships inside the `@panstudio/pancode` npm package, licensed Apache-2.0, as five imports:

| Import | Holds |
| --- | --- |
| `pancode/sdk/extension` | The types an extension runtime is written against. |
| `pancode/sdk/pack` | The validators and limits PanCode applies to a pack's manifest and to what its runtime returns. |
| `pancode/sdk/testing` | A test host that runs a runtime in process, under the same rules. |
| `pancode/sdk/tool` | `defineTool`, `defineServer` and `policyManifest`, for MCP tools with a declared policy. |
| `pancode/sdk/mcp-server` | `serveStdio`, which serves a defined server over MCP stdio. |

The [PanKit](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/pankit.html) servers are built on the last two.

## Start an extension

A scaffolded extension needs no `npm install`: its tsconfig points at the installed PanCode.

```sh
pancode extensions init lab-hello
pancode extensions validate .pancode/dev/extensions/lab-hello
pancode extensions test .pancode/dev/extensions/lab-hello
```

`init` writes a package from a template (`status`, `hook`, `panel`, `tool` or `workspace`). `validate` prints `Valid` or `Invalid` with each diagnostic and the capability envelope you will approve, and checks that the runtime registers exactly what its manifest declares. `test` runs the package's tests. See [extensions](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/harness-extensions.html) for the runtime API.

## Write a tool server

Any other Node project adds the package as a dependency with `npm install --save-dev pancode@npm:@panstudio/pancode` (Node 22.19 or later) and imports the subpaths:

```js
import { serveStdio } from "pancode/sdk/mcp-server";
import { defineServer, defineTool } from "pancode/sdk/tool";

const echo = defineTool({
	name: "echo",
	description: "Echo the text back.",
	input: { type: "object", properties: { text: { type: "string" } }, required: ["text"] },
	actionClass: "read",
	run: (args) => ({ text: args.text }),
});

await serveStdio(defineServer({ id: "notes", version: "1.0.0", tools: [echo] }));
```

`actionClass` is `read`, `execute` or `destructive`; a tool that writes files names its write paths in `pathArguments`. A wrong definition throws when the server starts. Log through `context.log`, because stdout carries only protocol frames.

To use the server from PanCode, declare it in `<config>/mcp.yaml` with its classes, since PanCode does not take them from the server, then review it with `pancode mcp trust notes --surface`.

## Limits

- A scaffolded package resolves only `pancode/sdk/extension` and `pancode/sdk/testing` without `node_modules`.
- The scaffold's tsconfig names the installed PanCode by its absolute path, so moving PanCode leaves it pointing at the old place.
- `pancode/sdk/mcp-server` serves tools only, over stdio only, and refuses an inbound line over 4 MiB.
- A server's declared classes are a hint; PanCode applies the classes its operator declares or the policy it ships.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/interop.html

# Editors and other agents

Use supported agent connections and editor integrations.

## Bring an installed coding agent

PanCode can dispatch a focused task to a configured coding peer or open an interactive handoff pane. Install and authenticate that peer's own CLI first, then inspect what is available:

```sh
pancode interop inspect --json
pancode configure --interop
```

In the terminal, `/hub interop` shows available connections. Supported managed modes vary by peer: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, GitHub Copilot, and the Antigravity CLI have ACP recipes; other peers may use a headless CLI or a pane.

- `/run <agent-id> <task>` uses a configured ACP connection; `/run acp:<id> <task>` names one explicitly.
- `/run --target <target> <agent> <task>` uses a configured headless target.
- `/panes peer [--cwd <path>] <agent> [brief]` opens an interactive pane beside the conversation.

Managed ACP and headless runs record results in sealed run records. A pane is an interactive handoff and does not produce a run record. For a headless task, `--worktree` preserves a Git task branch for review; it does not confine the peer's filesystem or network access.

A peer that runs its own tool loop is refused write-capable work unless you trust it with `trustedUnmediated: true` in your user settings: on the target for a headless peer, or on its external-agent entry for an ACP peer.

## Delegate to the Antigravity CLI

The Antigravity CLI (`agy`) is a built-in ACP target with the id `antigravity`. Sign in with `agy`, add the connection with `pancode configure --interop`, then run `/run antigravity <task>`. PanCode uses the `agy` login already on the machine and needs `agy` 1.5.1 or later.

A dispatch can name a model and a thinking level, and a `<model>-<level>` id selects both. When `agy` does not offer the choice, the run fails and lists the values it does offer. A question from `agy` appears as a card headed "Delegated agent"; with no operator attached, it is cancelled.

A steer reaches `agy` as its own prompt while the turn keeps running. When the `agy` quota runs out, the run fails with the reset time and the retry moves to another target. PanCode judges each `run_command` and `run_workflow` call by the command it runs.

## Review resources from another agent

PanHub can discover supported foreign resources and review their origin, scope, trust, and actual availability before adoption. It identifies unsupported components rather than treating an entire foreign package as compatible.

Run `pancode interop adopt <host> --dry-run`, for example with `claude-code`, `codex`, or `copilot`, to see the plan. Run it again without `--dry-run` to approve it into user scope, or add `--project`. In the terminal, `o` in `/hub` opens the same review.

## Connect an ACP frontend

To use PanCode from an editor that speaks the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), point the editor's ACP agent entry at `pancode acp`. The editor then exchanges JSON-RPC with that process over stdio, with session listing, resume, fork, modes, and model selection.

```sh
pancode acp --cwd /path/to/project
```

These launch options are the operator's limits; a client can narrow them but never widen them:

| Option | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--cwd PATH` | Pins the workspace. Without it, the editor's first session request selects it. |
| `--permission-timeout MS` | Longest wait, in milliseconds, for one permission answer from the editor; defaults to `integrations.externalAgents.defaults.permissionTimeoutMs`, 120000. |
| `--autonomy LEVEL` | The highest autonomy any session may use, `default` or `yolo`; it never raises your configured level. |
| `--allow-tools NAMES` | Limits the session's tools to these comma-separated names, as `pancode run` does; `none` disables all. |
| `--delegate-tools NAMES` | Limits the tools the session's dispatched workers may hold. |
| `--read-only` | Holds every session at the read-only ceiling. No file outside PanCode's own home changes. |

`pancode acp auth login` opens the interactive Quick Connect setup, so an editor's terminal sign-in step can create a connection. Stdout carries only protocol messages; diagnostics go to stderr. The [ACP protocol reference](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/0241470c83204f6dfb03baa5771a8d125fda3014/docs/architecture/acp.md) covers capabilities, authentication, permissions, and telemetry in detail. Consult the full guide for peer-specific setup and for installing PanCode's portable skills and plugins in other agents.

## Built on the Pi SDK

PanCode's model connections, agent loop, and terminal interface are built on the Pi SDK. PanCode pins the Pi 1.5.2 packages to exact versions and bundles the one terminal package it patches, so an npm install needs no patch step. PanCode owns everything above that layer: permissions, workers, sessions, run records, and its own handling for local model servers.

Pi's coding agent is also a delegation peer. With the `pi` command installed and signed in, a target on the `pi-cli` runtime runs headless worker tasks under Pi's own login. Like other peers that run their own tool loop, it needs `trustedUnmediated: true` on the target before it may take write-capable work. Developers upgrading the SDK can read the [Pi SDK boundary](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/0241470c83204f6dfb03baa5771a8d125fda3014/docs/architecture/pi-boundary.md).

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/doctor.html

# Check your installation

Diagnose installation and connection problems with doctor.

## Start with the standard check

Run doctor from your project:

```sh
pancode doctor
```

It checks the installation, configured connections, model-list evidence, local worker capacity, and relevant tools. Standard doctor is read-only, uses passive probes, and sends no model generation request. In the terminal, `/doctor` shows the findings in your session.

Read three rows first: `chat` names your route and what is missing, each `connection <id>` row says whether the key is there and the endpoint answered, and `shell sandbox` says whether commands run in an OS sandbox. Fix `!!` rows first; a `WARN` row still lets PanCode work.

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--verbose` | Print every row, including the checks that passed |
| `--json` | Emit findings as JSON on stdout |
| `--deep` | Add the live tool probe and validation dry run |
| `--tools-timeout <seconds>` | Bound each tool probe; default 120, needs `--deep` |

Doctor exits 0 when no row is an error, 1 when one is, and 2 on a usage error.

## Read the findings

| Badge | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| OK | The check passed |
| INFO | A fact that usually needs no action, such as an HPC compiler that is not on `PATH` |
| WARN | Worth attention; PanCode can still work |
| !! | A broken requirement; doctor exits with an error |

A live model list, a cached list, and a provider catalog are distinct evidence. A reachable endpoint does not establish that a model will answer well or call tools. The capacity row reports CPUs and available memory; it does not measure GPU memory or model fit.

## Common rows and their fix

The first row, `chat`, says whether chat can run and what to run when it cannot.

| Row | Usual cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `settings.yaml` | Invalid keys, named in the row | Edit those keys |
| `credentials` | `credentials.yaml` is missing or not `0600` | `pancode doctor --fix` |
| `lifecycle migrations` | Migrations are pending after an update | `pancode upgrade --post-install` |
| `connection <id>` | Missing credential or no endpoint answer | Check the target and sign-in |
| `model <id>` | The role model is missing from a live list | Pick a listed model |
| `external tool <id>` | A pinned helper is missing | `pancode tools install <id>` |

## HPC toolchain rows

`toolchain <name>` rows cover compilers, MPI, `nvcc`, build tools, `python3`, and `sbatch`. An absent tool is `INFO`. It is `WARN` when your validation contract's validators need it, or when a tool's `--version` fails, as with an unconfigured Slurm client.

## Repair or investigate further

`pancode doctor --fix` creates missing directories and template files, makes `settings.yaml` and `credentials.yaml` owner-only, rewrites retired setting values such as `safety.autonomy: auto-edit` and YAML `on` and `off` booleans while keeping your comments, and records fleet preflight results. Plain `doctor` previews the settings rewrite. Version migrations still run through `pancode upgrade`.
