The `shell sandbox` row says whether this host contains your commands and where they may write.

For a live tool-use probe and validation-contract dry run:

```sh
pancode doctor --deep
```

Deep checks send model requests and may consume tokens. Allow more time for a cold local model with `--tools-timeout <seconds>`. Use `--json` for structured findings.

A `tools <target>` row is `OK` when the model streamed a valid tool call and `WARN` when the call was malformed or the target did not answer. A `validator <n>` row says whether each validator command would run without an approval ask; nothing is executed. In a session, use `/doctor --deep`.

If a connection remains unavailable, follow [troubleshooting](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html).

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html

# Troubleshooting

Resolve common connection, terminal, and runtime problems.

## First problems

| You see | Do this |
| --- | --- |
| `pancode: command not found` after installing | Open a new shell, or run the `export PATH=...` line the installer printed last. |
| `<target> at <url> did not answer (...)` | Start the model server, or change the address with `/config`. |
| `<provider> has no key or sign-in stored.` or HTTP 401 | Run the `pancode auth login` command it names, or fix the key in `/config`. |
| `... reports no tool support` | Pick a model that calls tools with `/model`. |
| `shell sandbox` is `WARN` in doctor | On Linux, install `bubblewrap`. PanCode still works; more commands ask first. |
| A call was denied because nobody answered | Name the action in your request, or set `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds: 0` to wait for you. |

## A connection is unavailable

Start with these diagnostics:

```sh
pancode doctor
pancode targets --probe
```

Check that the selected endpoint is reachable, required credentials are present, and the model is loaded. A local server with an empty model list usually needs a model loaded before setup can finish. In **Connections**, reopen Guided setup or repair the saved connection.

For slow first responses from a local model, check the server's load state and capacity. Live tool-use behavior can be investigated with `pancode doctor --deep`; it makes generation requests.

## Settings fail to load

PanCode uses a strict version-2 settings schema. Invalid or retired keys produce a diagnostic naming the path. `pancode upgrade` applies the registered migration and preserves the original version-1 settings as a backup. Plain `pancode doctor` previews the fix for a retired value, and `doctor --fix` applies it.

Use [Configuration essentials](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-reference.html) to find the settings layers and the full reference.

## A terminal shortcut does not arrive

Open **Ctrl+G** and choose the corresponding menu action. A terminal or multiplexer may intercept Alt shortcuts. **Ctrl+J** is the portable newline; `/help` shows your effective bindings.

If a files or companion pane is unavailable, run `pancode doctor` and read its `panes` and `external tool` rows. `pancode panes install` adds a missing pane host, and `pancode tools install yazi` adds the file browser. See [files and terminal panes](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html).

## Work stopped or a check failed

Read the recorded command and output in the desktop's **Artifacts** card or terminal `/view`. A failed test can point to a useful next task; ask PanCode to explain the failure before changing the test's acceptance criteria.

For an interrupted context handoff, inspect `/context` and follow [save and resume work](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/context-continuity.html).

## Report a problem to the maintainers

`/report` in the terminal and `pancode report` in a shell draft a bug report, a feature request or a question. `--last` adds what PanCode observed in the newest session in this folder.

```sh
pancode report bug --title "footer flickers on resize" --last --dry-run
```

You review the draft exactly as it will be posted. Local paths, user, host, project and branch names, e-mail and IP addresses, and secrets are masked first, and a draft that still holds this machine's names is refused. Nothing is sent until you press `s` in the terminal, answer the prompt in a shell, or pass `--yes`. `--dry-run` stops after the preview.

With a signed-in `gh`, PanCode searches GitHub for the same problem, then posts a public issue under your account. Without `gh` it opens a prefilled form in the browser. A diagnostic bundle is opt-in, encrypted for the maintainers, and shared only from your own shell. PanCode never sends anything on its own.

## Exit codes

Every `pancode` command uses the same exit codes, so a script can tell why a run stopped:

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | Success, including `--help`, `--version`, and a `--dry-run`. |
| `1` | Operational failure: an unreachable model, unresolved doctor findings, or a worker whose changes were withheld or who did no work. |
| `2` | Usage error: an unknown command, flag, target, or agent, or a global flag placed after the subcommand. |
| `3` | A dispatched worker was stopped by its permission refusal limit (`permission_required`), or a headless yolo run ended after too many safety-judge blocks (`judge-streak`). |
| `4` | The priced spend ceiling was reached: `safety.limits.sessionCostUsd` (5 USD by default) or `run --max-cost-usd`. A headless yolo run that reaches its autonomous tool-call, time or token cap also exits 4. |
| `5` | `pancode run --answers <file.yaml>` met an author question the file does not script. |
| `75` | An install or upgrade is busy; nothing changed, so retry later. |
| `124` | `pancode run --timeout` elapsed. |
| `141` | The reader of a `pancode run` stdout closed, as in `pancode run ... \| head -1`. |
| `129`, `130`, `143` | Stopped by SIGHUP, SIGINT, or SIGTERM. |

A few commands, such as `fleet events`, `telemetry verify`, `research start`, and `arena run`, give small codes their own meaning; the full guide lists them. In a headless `pancode run`, the answer or JSON stream goes to stdout, while progress and diagnostics go to stderr. [Automate with pancode run](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html) has the details.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/quality-policy.html

# Require project checks

Choose the declared checks a change requires and inspect verification freshness.

## Tell PanCode what “checked” means in your project

A quality policy names the declared checks required when particular files change. Your repository supplies the standards; PanCode records verification and assesses whether the results still match the current inputs.

At a Git workspace root, create `.pancode/quality.yaml`:

```yaml
version: 1
rules:
  - id: source
    paths: ["src/**", "tests/**"]
    inputs: ["src/**", "tests/**", "package.json", "package-lock.json"]
    checks: [test]
    allowLimitations: false
```

This example assumes the root `package.json` declares a `test` script. Adapt the paths, lockfile, and check IDs to your project. Include configuration, fixtures, and helper files that affect the result. PanCode does not create or modify this policy automatically.

## Run the declared checks

Ask PanCode to discover verification checks, then run each required ID through `verify` without argument or working-directory overrides. For a subproject, declare a root script or a verifier-catalog entry with its working directory.

The policy names existing checks; it cannot introduce shell commands or bypass approval. A narrowed test run or an unrelated passing command cannot satisfy a required full check.

## Review freshness

PanCode compares source, check-declaration, and policy fingerprints. Edits after a passing run can make the result **stale**; a later failing run supersedes an earlier pass. Missing or unavailable evidence remains unverified.

A valid policy selects high rigor by default, which requests continuation for outstanding checks when recovery is possible. Setting `PANCODE_RIGOR=normal` makes the assessment advisory. Neither mode grants additional execution authority. A turn the agent declared `partly_done` or `not_done` through `finish` settles as declared, and a declared `done` with a required check still open is assessed as partly done.

Snapshots need Git and a workspace at the repository root. They cover tracked and nonignored untracked source, not external datasets, installed dependencies, or running services. Use domain-specific checks for those requirements. The full guide explains bounded snapshots and permitted limitations.

Try [the calibration example](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html) to see a declared check and its actual result.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html

# Climb a metric, compare models

Improve a measured number with verified research campaigns, and compare models blind in the arena.

## Improve a number, and keep only real gains

`pancode research start` runs PanCode's agent repeatedly to move one measured number in your project, such as the wall time of a benchmark. The number is a key in the JSON that a check in `.pancode/verifiers.yaml` prints. Correctness checks run as gates.

```yaml
version: 2
checks:
  - id: bench
    description: Wall time of stats.py on 3000 values (min is better)
    kind: command
    command: [python3, bench.py]   # prints {"wall_ms": 12.3}
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
    tags: [benchmark]
  - id: correct
    description: stats.py answers match the reference on a holdout input
    kind: numeric-compare
    command: [python3, check.py]
    reference: tests/reference/stats.json
    tolerance: { relative: 1.0e-9 }
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
    tags: [correctness]
```

Commit this file so every research worktree contains it.

```bash
pancode research start --check bench --metric wall_ms --direction min \
  --max-iterations 5 --gate correct --scope stats.py --max-wall-minutes 30
```

Each attempt runs in its own Git worktree. Before the first attempt, an A/A check of the base against itself refuses a noisy measurement unless `--allow-noisy`. A change is kept only when it clears both measurement tests and every gate passes:

- **Measurement:** across interleaved trials, the median improves by at least 5% and a seeded bootstrap interval excludes zero.
- **Gates:** every gate check passes in the change's worktree.

Kept changes go to the branch `pancode/research/<id>`; your own branch is never touched. Unknown spend never counts as zero. `pancode research report <id>` regrades every verdict from the stored samples.

## Budgets and stopping

| Flag | Effect |
| --- | --- |
| `--max-iterations <N>` | Required hard stop on iterations |
| `--max-wall-minutes <M>` | Deadline that also ends the step in flight |
| `--max-cost-usd <X>` | Spend cap; an unpriced run stops the campaign unless you pass `--allow-unpriced` |
| `--min-improvement <frac>` | Relative gain to clear; default 0.05 |
| `--trials <N>` | Interleaved base and candidate pairs; default 5 |

## Where results go

Campaigns live in `.pancode/research/<id>/` and arena matches in `.pancode/arena/<match-id>/`. Check progress with `pancode research status` or `research list`.

| Exit code | `research start` |
| --- | --- |
| 0 | A budget cap ended the campaign |
| 1 | An error, a noisy A/A check, or unenforceable spend |
| 2 | Usage error |
| 130, 143, 129 | Stopped by Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, or SIGHUP |

## Compare models blind

`pancode arena run` gives one prompt to 2 to 4 target/model pairs, each in its own worktree. `arena show` hides which model produced which answer until you vote with `arena vote`. `arena standings` counts the votes and adds an Elo rating once a model has 5 votes. PanCode never grades a contender. The desktop app's Arena page runs the same commands.

```sh
pancode arena run --check unit \
  --contender copilot/claude-haiku-5.5 --contender ollama/qwen3-coder \
  -- "Fix the bug in calc.py so test_calc.py passes."
pancode arena show <match-id>
pancode arena vote <match-id> A --note "smaller diff"
pancode arena show <match-id> --reveal
```

Before a vote, `show` hides each target, model, cost, and duration, and `--reveal` is refused. Vote with a label, `tie`, or `both-bad`; `--replace` changes your vote.

To run one seeded project against several models, `pancode campaign run --fixture <dir> --roster <roster.yaml> --answers <answers.yaml> --prompt <text> --out <dir>` runs it once per roster entry and reports how each run ended, its tokens, and its wall time.

With `--autonomy yolo` both run contained yolo: the sandbox, the safety judge, and your autonomous caps stay on, and unconfined yolo is refused. `pancode research resume <id>` continues a stopped campaign from its journal with the same spec and budget.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html

# Automate with pancode run

Run one task from a script or CI job, read its exit code, and parse its JSON output.

## Run one task from a script

`pancode run` does one task without opening the terminal interface, then exits. The answer goes to stdout; progress, warnings and errors go to stderr, so a script can capture the answer alone.

```sh
pancode run --timeout 15m --max-cost-usd 2 "Run the test check and fix the failing parser test."
echo "exit $?"
```

Nobody is there to approve anything, so a request that would ask you is denied, and PanCode continues another way or reports what it could not do. Name the actions the job needs in the prompt, such as "commit the fix", because the safety judge decides from your words.

Stdin is read only when you pass `-`. `pancode run -` takes the task from stdin, and `pancode run "<task>" -` appends stdin after the task.

## Read the exit code

| Code | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The run finished. |
| `1` | The task failed, including a run that changed nothing because its actions were refused. With `--fail-on-verify`, a failed check also exits 1, and with `--exit-code`, so does a run the agent declared unfinished. |
| `2` | Nothing started: an unknown flag, target or agent, an empty task, a session open in another process, or a refused admission or capability request. |
| `3` | A worker was stopped by permission refusals, the safety judge kept blocking, or `--on-permission fail` met a request nobody could approve. |
| `4` | A limit stopped the run: a spend ceiling, `--max-requests`, `--max-tool-calls`, or a `yolo` run's autonomous tool-call, time, or token cap. |
| `5` | A `--answers` file did not script a question only the author may answer. |
| `124` | `--timeout` ran out. |
| `129`, `130`, `143` | A signal stopped the run (SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGTERM). |

The full guide lists the codes other commands use.

## Bound the run

- `--timeout <duration>` stops the run and exits 124. It takes `90`, `90s`, `15m` or `2h`, and a bare number is seconds.
- `--max-cost-usd <n>` caps what the run may spend on priced models, and `--require-priced` refuses routes with no price.
- `--max-requests <n>` and `--max-tool-calls <n>` cap the main agent's model requests and tool calls.
- `--verify "<cmd>"` runs an acceptance check after the turn, and `--fail-on-verify` turns a failed check into exit 1.
- `--dry-run` prints what the run would do and exits 0 without calling a model.
- `--read-only` leaves every file outside PanCode's own folders unchanged.
- `--answers <file.yaml>` answers the questions only the author may answer, such as extension interview steps; any other question is still refused.
- `--autonomy yolo` lets an unattended job continue without waiting. It stays contained by default, and a call that would ask you is refused back to PanCode, which continues without it.

## Read structured output

`--output-format json` writes one JSON document on stdout: a `run_end` result with the answer in `result.text`, the `exitCode`, the `outcome`, the `causes` that ended the run, and usage. `-o <path>` also saves the final answer to a file when the run exits 0.

`--output-format stream-json` writes one JSON event per line: the session, the model's text and each tool call, then the same `run_end` result as the last line. Dispatch on each frame's `type` and ignore kinds you do not know, because new ones are added.

JSON output is chosen only with `--output-format json` or `--output-format stream-json`; `run --json` is refused as an unknown flag. `pancode schema run-result` prints the JSON Schema of the result, and `--output-schema <file.json>` makes the answer itself one JSON object checked against your schema.

Continue an earlier session with `--resume <id>` or `--continue`. Add `--fork` to branch a new session and leave the original untouched.

`pancode doctor --json`, `pancode targets --json`, `pancode models --json` and other commands print one JSON document for scripts as well.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-reference.html

# Configuration essentials

Find settings layers, save scopes, and the full configuration reference.

## Prefer the Settings Center

Use `/settings`, desktop **Settings**, or:

```sh
pancode configure --settings
```

Configure and desktop Settings share eight sections: Connections, Chat, Fleet, Context & Memory, Permissions & Limits, Appearance, Integrations, and Advanced. Terminal `/settings` groups the same controls into its own areas and lists the settings people change; every key still works in `settings.yaml`. The guided controls help you select a discovered model instead of typing a model ID. See [Connect a model](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html) for the walkthrough.

## Know where a change is saved

| Layer | File or scope |
| --- | --- |
| User defaults | `settings.yaml` in PanCode's configuration directory |
| Shared project settings | `.pancode/settings.yaml` |
| Local project settings | `.pancode/settings.local.yaml` |
| Active session | The session/project/global choices offered by supported terminal controls |

Find the resolved locations on your machine:

```sh
pancode paths --json
```

`safety.sandbox` (`auto`, `required`, `off`) controls the OS sandbox for dispatched native workers' commands and for your own session's shell commands at `default`. `safety.sandboxNetwork` lets sandboxed worker commands reach the network; the session sandbox keeps network access. Objects merge by key; arrays and scalars replace the lower layer. Credential-bearing keys in project settings are ignored. Project saves require trusted project settings.

Saved routes seed a new session. A settings write from another process does not redirect a conversation already running; use that session's model controls.

## Look up an exact key

The full reference covers supported settings keys, defaults, CLI flags, project file ownership, and MCP trust. Use **Read the full guide** above or ask PanCode to retrieve the relevant bundled documentation before editing YAML.

Settings validation is strict. For an older installation, `pancode upgrade` applies the registered migration and preserves a version-1 backup. For connection and installation diagnostics, use [doctor](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/doctor.html).

A session started in a repository subdirectory reads the repository's `.pancode/` settings, agents, skills, rules, hooks, and MCP servers. PanCode writes an allow-list `.pancode/.gitignore`, so authored files can be committed while generated files stay out. A blanket `.pancode/` rule in your own `.gitignore` still hides them.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/environment-variables.html

# Environment essentials

Use directory overrides and existing provider credentials when needed.

## Use settings for ordinary preferences

Choose models, permissions, output style, and context behavior in [Settings](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html). Environment variables are useful when a script, container, or separate installation needs a different directory or an existing credential.

## Locate or separate installation state

```sh
pancode paths --json
```

| Variable | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `PANCODE_HOME` | Set a shared root for PanCode's directories |
| `PANCODE_CONFIG_DIR` | Override the configuration directory |
| `PANCODE_DATA_DIR` | Override the data directory |
| `PANCODE_STATE_DIR` | Override the state directory |
| `PANCODE_CACHE_DIR` | Override the cache directory |
| `PANCODE_BIN_DIR` | Choose where the installer puts the `pancode` launcher (default `~/.local/bin`) |
| `PANCODE_RELEASE_MIRROR` | Read releases and the channel files from a mirror, for the installer and the update check |

Individual directory overrides take precedence over the shared root. Separate state is useful for an isolated evaluation or a dedicated automation environment.

## How each directory is resolved

PanCode resolves the config, data, state, and cache directories one at a time. The first match wins:

| Order | Source | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | The per-role variable | `PANCODE_CONFIG_DIR` |
| 2 | The shared root | `PANCODE_HOME` |
| 3 | Platform defaults | `XDG_CONFIG_HOME` on Linux, `APPDATA` or `LOCALAPPDATA` on Windows |

So you can keep everything under one root and still move only the cache elsewhere:

```sh
export PANCODE_HOME="$HOME/pancode-eval"
export PANCODE_CACHE_DIR=/scratch/pancode-cache
pancode paths --json
```

`pancode paths` creates nothing, so it is a safe way to confirm a layout before the first run. Scripts should parse its `--json` output rather than repeat these rules. With `PANCODE_HOME` set, the installer root defaults to `$PANCODE_HOME/install`; `PANCODE_INSTALL_DIR` overrides it.

An isolated root still reads other coding agents' user skills and prompts from your real home. Set `PANCODE_INTEROP_HOME=none` to read none of them, or a path to read another home.

## Credentials and terminal behavior

Supported providers can read their conventional credential variables, such as `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, or `OPENROUTER_API_KEY`, when that provider is selected. Prefer PanCode's managed authentication flow for normal interactive setup, and keep secrets out of project settings and transcripts.

| Variable | Used for |
| --- | --- |
| `OPENAI_API_KEY` | OpenAI |
| `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` | Anthropic |
| `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` | OpenRouter |
| `GEMINI_API_KEY` or `GOOGLE_API_KEY` | Gemini |
| `AWS_*` | Credentials for an existing Amazon Bedrock connection |
| `OLLAMA_API_KEY` | An Ollama target at `https://ollama.com` |

The managed alternative is `pancode auth`, with `auth login` and `auth status` per target.

`HTTPS_PROXY`, `HTTP_PROXY`, and their lowercase forms apply to model requests, discovery probes, sign-in refreshes, and web fetches. `localhost` and `127.0.0.1` always go direct; name any other local model server in `NO_PROXY`. `pancode doctor` shows the proxy in effect.

`VISUAL` and `EDITOR` select an external editor, with `VISUAL` taking precedence. Terminal variables such as `TERM` and `COLORTERM` describe the environment; they do not grant tool permissions.

## Collect a trace

Debug toggles are off by default and turn on with `1`. `PANCODE_TRACE_BOOT=1` turns on a boot-phase timing trace for a slow startup. The render trace takes a file path instead, and records timing but no conversation text:

```sh
PANCODE_RENDER_TRACE="$PWD/render.jsonl" pancode
```

Setting it to `1` writes a file named `1` in the working directory.

The full guide lists provider-specific inputs, behavior overrides, and diagnostic switches. Use it when preparing automation or collecting a trace; most installations need no environment variables.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/system-one.html

# System One decision models

Bring a decision model, name a route, and read its limits.

## What it is

System One is an experimental way to bring a fast decision model to PanCode. It is off by default and sends nothing until you name a route. The main agent then gets one tool, `consult`, and the route also drives a screen beside the safety judge and, when you turn it on, triage of queued messages. System One never answers you, never edits anything, and never removes a confirmation.

## Name a route

```sh
pancode systemone use jev
pancode systemone status
pancode systemone check jev --live
pancode systemone off
```

The choice takes effect on the next start. A list such as `jev,memory` is a failover order, and a route you did not name is never used. `run --systemone <route>` sets one headless run, and `/usage health` shows the status in a session.

| Route | What answers | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `jev` | A hosted engine | `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` |
| `memory` | The model in `context.memory`, as labels | A memory target and model |
| `main` or a chat target | A chat route, as labels | That route's credentials |
| A declared engine | A decision server you run, with a named profile | An entry under `systemOne.engines` |

## The two consult forms

Only the main session gets `consult`, at most 3 calls per turn.

| Form | What the agent sends | What comes back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filter | Up to 256 files or items and one criterion | Ids and scores of matches |
| Questions | One to four `yesNo`, `pick`, or `rate` questions | Probabilities, or a label on an LLM route |

A filter sees a file as its path and a digest; use `grep` for behavior inside a body.

## The judge screen

When the safety judge reviews a call, System One asks whether the newest web and MCP results direct an AI agent. A positive reading can only turn a judge allow into a park on the approval card. LLM routes never screen.

## Declare an engine

```yaml
targets:
  - id: decider-gpu
    runtime: systemone
    url: http://127.0.0.1:13306/v1
    capabilities:
      contextWindow: 4096
systemOne:
  use: decider
  engines:
    decider:
      kind: systemone
      target: decider-gpu
      profile: strands-decider
```

You run the server. Name a profile: a `generic` engine never screens.

## When it fails

A failed ask returns nothing and the agent proceeds alone. Three timeouts in a row open a five-minute breaker; see `/usage health`.

## What to expect

`consult` filters a list against one criterion or asks typed questions, and the agent decides what to do with the answer. Between a third and more than half of filter matches can be wrong on the query sets tried so far, and nothing yet shows that `consult` helps. A hosted route receives what these uses send, including web and MCP result text at judge time. Redaction is best effort, so use a route you run yourself when that matters. An [information flow](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/information-flow.html) rule that excludes the engine's target ends that route as `flow-denied`, and nothing is sent.

Read [the research page](https://pancode.dev/research/system-one-decisions.html) for what has been measured and what is still open.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/information-flow.html

# Information flow

Keep named files away from destinations you did not choose.

## What it does

Information flow keeps named content, such as files under `secrets/`, away from destinations you did not choose. A source rule labels content when a session observes it, and the restrictions are checked before bytes leave for a model or a mediated outbound tool. It does nothing until a project declares rules and you approve them.

This controls where observed content may go. The safety model still decides whether a read or tool call may run.

## Declare and approve

Put `informationFlow` in the project's `.pancode/safety.yaml`, with each source naming its paths or tools and its allowed recipients. Then review and approve those exact bytes:

```sh
pancode config trust safety
pancode config trust safety --hash <reviewed-sha256>
pancode config trust safety --revoke
```

Restart PanCode after approving. An unapproved edit can only forbid more.

Recipients can be a pinned model target, an exact endpoint, an origin, a pinned MCP server, or a named group. Follow [the tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/information-flow-rules.html) for a complete worked policy.

## Example policy

This policy keeps content under `secrets/` on one local model target:

```yaml
version: 1
informationFlow:
  targets:
    local:
      runtime: llamacpp
      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1
  recipients:
    private-models: ["target:local"]
  sources:
    - id: secrets-local
      paths: [secrets/]
      recipients: ["group:private-models"]
```

After approval and restart, reading `secrets/notes.txt` labels the session. Requests to the `local` target still go out; switching to a cloud target refuses the next request before it sends. `recipients: []` forbids every transfer.

The first `config trust safety` command is read-only and prints the digest to approve. After `--revoke`, rules left in the file label content without allowing any recipient.

## What acquires a label

Read tools such as `read`, `grep`, and `find` label matching paths, including sources below a directory they walk. Bash commands and `@file` references label the paths they name; reads hidden in scripts or variables are not reliably seen.

Labels belong to the session and survive compaction, resume, handoffs, and worker results. Changing the policy, the model, or the autonomy mode does not clear them. Files the session writes carry no label.

## Read a refusal and recover

A refusal names the rule, the source path or tool, the requested destination, and any allowed recipients.

| Refusal | Recovery |
| --- | --- |
| Destination is outside the rule's recipients | Switch to an allowed destination, or start a new session |
| Rule was unapproved when content was read | Approve the exact bytes and restart |
| Approved rule names no recipient | Start a new session for work that must leave |
| Runtime cannot admit its own model requests | Use a native HTTP target, or add its pinned target to every rule |

Claude Code, Codex, and other external runtimes are refused whenever a rule does not allow their pinned target. At `yolo`, mediated outbound tools skip the label check, but model requests are still checked.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/glossary.html

# Glossary

Plain-language meanings of the words PanCode uses, from target to worktree.

## Words you meet first

Each term below in a sentence or two, with the guide that explains it. The full guide then gives the precise definitions, mapped to the source types that own them.

## Sessions and models

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Session | One conversation with PanCode in a project. It is saved, so you can resume it later. See [Commands and modes](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html). |
| Target (connection) | A place PanCode sends prompts to: a provider account or a local model server, with its default model. Settings call it a connection. See [Configuration and targets](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html). |
| Chat route | The target and model your main conversation uses right now. |
| Compaction | Shortening a long conversation into a summary so it fits the model's context window. See [Context continuity](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/context-continuity.html). |
| Handbook | `PANCODE.md` at the repository root: the project's name, conventions and rules, written by you and kept in Git. |
| Memory | Notes PanCode keeps while you work, such as your requirements and what failed, so it can remind the agent later. See [Proactive memory](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/proactive-memory.html). |
| Doctor | `pancode doctor`, a read-only check of your install, connections and sandbox. See [Doctor](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/doctor.html). |

## Safety

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Autonomy level | How much PanCode may do without you: `default` asks when something is risky, `yolo` never waits for you. See [Sandbox and safety](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/sandbox-and-safety.html). |
| Sandbox | An operating-system wall around shell commands. Inside it a command can write only to the project and scratch folders and cannot read your credentials. |
| Contained | A command that runs inside the sandbox. At `default` most contained work runs without asking. |
| Safety judge | A model that checks a risky call against what you asked for, before you are asked. It allows it, refuses it, or passes it to you. |
| Approval card | The question PanCode shows when a call needs your answer. One nobody answers is denied after a timeout. |
| Snapshot | A private copy of your files that PanCode takes before it changes them. `/rewind` restores one. |

## Workers and results

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Worker | A separate agent that does one task for the main session, often on its own branch. See [Fleet dispatch](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html). |
| Fleet | The workers available to you and the routes they run on. |
| Dispatch | Handing a task to a worker, with `/run` in a session or `pancode run --agent` from a shell. |
| Worktree | A separate checkout of your repository on its own branch, where a worker can change files without touching yours. |
| Run record | The sealed record of a finished worker run: what it did, what it changed and which checks passed. `/view verify <runId>` checks it. |
| Check (verifier) | A command in `.pancode/verifiers.yaml` that decides whether work is right, such as a test suite or a benchmark. |
| Peer | Another coding agent, such as Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, that PanCode hands a task to. See [Coding agent interoperability](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/interop.html). |
| Store | A place outside your working tree for result files and datasets, shared by every checkout of the project. See [Store](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panstore.html). |
| Research campaign | A loop where the agent tries one change at a time and keeps it only when a measured number improves and every check still passes. See [Research and arena](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html). |
| Arena match | The same task given to several models, each result run through the same check, so you can compare them and vote blind. |
| Sweep | A set of run directories for one experiment, each checked on its own. See [project checks](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html#verify-using-your-projects-checks). |

## Packages

| Term | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| Skill | Written instructions for a procedure, in a `SKILL.md` file, that the agent loads when the task needs it. |
| Prompt template | A saved prompt you run as a slash command, such as `/bugfix`. |
| PanHub | The installable packs PanCode knows about, browsed with `pancode hub` or `/hub`. See [PanHub](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panhub.html). |
| Plugin | A package of content only: skills, prompts, agents and playbooks. Installing one never runs code. See [Plugins](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/plugins.html). |
| Extension | A package of code that changes PanCode itself. It runs in its own process, after you review what it may do. See [Extensions](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/harness-extensions.html). |

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/semantic-context.html

# Semantic context

Search your project by meaning with a local embedding route.

## What it does

Semantic context is a beta local search index for code maps, wiki pages, approved memory, authorized evidence, recorded worker output, and folders you register. It uses a separate embedding target. It starts disabled, and ordinary startup scans and embeds nothing until you configure it.

## Set it up and search

Create a target for an embedding route you already run. PanCode does not start a server for it. Then configure, refresh, and search:

```sh
pancode semantic configure --help
pancode semantic inbox preview ./experiment-data
pancode semantic inbox add ./experiment-data --id experiments
pancode semantic refresh
pancode semantic status
pancode semantic search "Which run produced the delayed oscillation?" --limit 5
```

`--qualify` checks that a route accepts requests and returns vectors of the right shape. It does not check retrieval quality. A result is a candidate to read, and it does not prove anything by itself.

Follow [the tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/semantic-context-and-recordings.html) for a full walkthrough.

## Configure the embedding model

`configure` pins a target, model, and asset identity. Prefer a `sha256:<hash>` of the model file; a plain label is reported as unverified.

```sh
pancode semantic configure \
  --target embeddings --model embeddinggemma-300m \
  --asset-identity sha256:<gguf-sha256> \
  --modality text --modality image \
  --qualify
```

`--background`, off by default, allows refreshes at session start and after code map changes. Run `pancode semantic qualify` again after changing the serving build or model.

## Register inboxes

`inbox add` previews the work before saving a folder, which stays private to its project unless you pass `--scope user`. Ignore files and the project's read policy apply, and symlinks and credential-shaped files are refused. `inbox list` and `inbox remove <id>` manage them. An interrupted `refresh` keeps the last complete generation.

## Search and ask

| Filter | Narrows to |
| --- | --- |
| `--kind` | `code`, `wiki`, `memory`, `evidence`, `inbox`, or `recording`; repeatable |
| `--run <id>` | One parent run |
| `--since`, `--until` | Source dates, inclusive |
| `--media-type <MIME>` | One media type |

Search returns five results by default and at most 20, each with a path and a line, page, or timestamp. In a session, ask a specific question; the agent searches the same index, then reads the source. Worker output saved with `pancode run --agent <id> --record` is searchable as `recording`.

## Change the model

A new profile gets its own index. `pancode semantic reembed --profile <id>` rebuilds it; add `--from <old-profile-sha256>` to embed the previous profile's records. Old vectors are never copied.

## When something fails

If the embedding route is down, search returns lexical candidates from the last complete generation. Video frames need a qualified image route and `ffmpeg` on PATH. Scanned PDFs, raw video, and audio other than mono 16 kHz WAV are not indexed.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/built-in-agents.html

# Built-in and custom agents

See the agents you can dispatch and add your own.

## See the agents

PanCode dispatches focused agents from Markdown recipes. Each recipe declares the agent's tools, budget, and the result it must return.

```sh
pancode agents
pancode agents validate
pancode run --agent coder "<task>"
```

`pancode agents` lists the agents you can run, including `architect`, `coder`, `debugger`, `documenter`, `git-master`, `reviewer`, `tester`, and `verifier`. `/run` dispatches one from a session. Add `--read-only` to keep one dispatch from changing anything; work it delegates is read-only too.

Helper agents such as Scout are dispatched by the main agent, and `pancode agents --all` lists them. You cannot start them directly.

## Shipped agents

| Agent | Use it to | Edits files |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `architect` | Design a change or cut a plan into a sprint | Plan file only |
| `coder` | Make a bounded change, repair, or refactor | Yes |
| `debugger` | Diagnose failing code, tests, or runs | No |
| `documenter` | Write docs and examples from source | Yes |
| `git-master` | Commits, worktrees, merges, pull requests | Yes |
| `reviewer` | Judge one diff or change against its acceptance criteria | No |
| `tester` | Add deterministic regression tests | Yes |
| `verifier` | Run test, lint, build, and review gates | No |
| `wiki-writer` | Plan a wiki or write one page | Yes |
| `wiki-repair` | Fix one wiki draft's diagnostics | Yes |

When the main agent dispatches without naming an agent, the job picks one: inspecting goes to `scout`, reviewing a diff to `reviewer`, running checks to `verifier`, diagnosing a failure to `debugger`, adding tests to `tester`, implementing to `coder`, and documentation to `documenter`.

## Add your own

Put a recipe at `.pancode/agents/<id>.md` for one project, or in the `agents` folder of your PanCode config directory for yourself. The file name is the agent's id, and when a user recipe and a project recipe share an id, the project one wins. Run `pancode agents validate` after an edit.

A recipe must declare every required key, and `audience` must be `custom`:

```md
---
version: 1
name: My Agent
description: Focused local review helper.
tools:
  required: [read, artifact]
  optional: [grep, find, ls, git]
skills: []
audience: custom
category: quality
capabilityClass: artifact-write
latencyClass: balanced
projectContextTier: bounded
budget: {toolCalls: 20, readReserve: 4, synthesis: true}
resultContract: {kind: artifact-report}
tags: [review]
---

You are My Agent. Inspect only the requested area. Never edit files.
```

The body is the agent's instructions. Model and target are chosen at dispatch, not in the recipe. Start it with `pancode run --agent my-agent "Review the parser change."`. A user recipe may replace a shipped agent such as `coder`; a project recipe cannot.

## What validation rejects

`pancode agents validate` checks project and user recipes and skills, and the fleet bindings in `.pancode/settings.local.yaml`. It prints each problem as a `file: field: message` line and exits 1 when there is any. It rejects an unknown or missing key, an audience other than `custom`, a `budget` whose `readReserve` is not below `toolCalls`, a skill that does not resolve, and tools that break the `capabilityClass`, such as a `verification` agent that uses `bash`. A rejected recipe is not loaded.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/hub.html

# PanHub

> The PanHub marketplace: every pack in the index bundled with this PanCode release, with its tier, licence, source and the command that installs or serves it.

The 52 packs listed in the index bundled with PanCode v0.9.1, from `hub/index.yaml` (sha256 833411c8c5eecfd29937b806ddf606d9424890bf553895b778b54e88ea2a5fee). A skill, plugin or extension installs with the command on its row, for your user; add `--project` to install it into the current project. A server is built into PanCode, so there is nothing to install: its row gives the command that serves it to another agent host over MCP, and that command takes no install flags. A listing at any tier is not an endorsement.

# Your first session with PanCode

> Connect a model, open a repository, and ask PanCode to explain how it builds and runs its tests.

PanCode works in the repository you open. For your first session, give it a small, concrete task: explain how the project builds and runs its tests. That lets you see how it reads code and uses tools before asking it to make a change.

**Version scope**

The recordings on this page come from a small JavaScript project with one failing test and GPT-6 Luna through a GitHub Copilot subscription. The first starts with no model configured and one stored sign-in. The install step was not recorded.

## 1. Install PanCode

The installer brings its own Node.js and needs no root. Linux, macOS, and WSL are the primary platforms. Native Windows is best effort, so use the current stable release. On Linux, the installer offers to add the desktop app when it finishes.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh
```

## 2. Connect a model

Open a terminal in a repository you know and start PanCode:

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
pancode
```

With no model configured, setup starts on its own:

```text
No model target is configured. PanCode needs a model before it can do anything else, so setup starts now.
```

Setup looks for a provider key in your environment, a stored sign-in and a local model server, and lists what it found. Pick one, or choose **Set up something else** and answer what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file from your lab or team. Use a model that supports tool calling.

PanCode sends the model one short test request and saves only when it answers; a browser sign-in you complete is the exception. In the recording of `pancode configure` on a fresh profile, setup found the stored GitHub Copilot sign-in and recommended gpt-6-luna. Choosing it printed these lines:

```text
◇  Testing copilot-sdk / gpt-6-luna ... answered in 3.2 s.
◇  target copilot-sdk saved, runtime copilot-sdk
◇  chat runs on copilot-sdk, model gpt-6-luna
◇  fleet default is copilot-sdk
◇  settings written to ~/.config/pancode/settings.yaml
◇  Saved. Chat and workers use this model. Change it any time with /model or /config.
```

![Guided setup in the terminal after choosing GitHub Copilot SDK: it notes that researcher's GitHub Copilot subscription on github.com is used under the organization's Copilot policies, tests copilot-sdk / gpt-6-luna (answered in 3.2 s), saves target copilot-sdk as the chat and fleet default, writes ~/.config/pancode/settings.yaml, and ends with how to start pancode and change the setup later with pancode configure.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-configure-saved.webp)

*Accepting the offer tests the recommended model and saves it as the default for chat and workers.*

`pancode configure` runs setup again at any time. Its **Connect by endpoint** is the shortcut when you already know the URL. LM Studio commonly serves at `http://localhost:1234`; Ollama commonly serves at `http://localhost:11434`. The [connection guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html) covers setup and credentials.

If you have used PanCode before, you can skip this step. A chat route you already chose stays in use, and PanCode will not swap it for another when it stops working.

If a connection fails, run:

```sh
pancode doctor
```

## 3. Open a workspace

When setup saves, the terminal workspace opens in the same folder. In the recording, its status line read `✓ ready` and ended with `copilot-sdk · gpt-6-luna`. Later, `pancode` opens the workspace directly.

Or open the desktop alpha in your browser:

```sh
pancode gui --open
```

In the desktop, open a workspace folder and start a task. If you have not configured a model, **Guided setup** is also available in the browser; terminal configuration is optional. For this tutorial, either interface gives you a place to enter the first request.

## 4. Ask a focused question

Try this request:

> Explain how this repository builds and runs its tests. Identify the main entry points and suggest one verification task. Do not change files yet.

Follow the tool activity as PanCode reads the repository. In the recording, the agent read `package.json`, `README.md`, `temperature.mjs` and `calibration.test.mjs`, then named `npm test` as the test command and the two files as the main entry points. If an approval card appears, read the call before allowing it. If the answer misses an important directory or build system, name it in a follow-up.

## 5. Make the next task specific

Once you understand the project, ask for one change you can check. Name the problem, what to do and how to verify it. The recording below gave this request for the project's one failing test:

> The absolute-zero test fails. Find the cause, fix it, and run the test check.

![Terminal recording of a first task on copilot · gpt-6-luna: asked to fix the failing absolute-zero test, Panos searches the project (19 matches), reads temperature.mjs and calibration.test.mjs, changes if (kelvin <= 0) to if (kelvin < 0) on line 21 of temperature.mjs, and runs the test check, which exits 0 with pass 7 and fail 0. It reports that all 7 tests passed (Done · 12s · 8 calls), and a notice says checks passed but coverage of the change was not measured.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cast-first-task.webp)

*A first task at default autonomy: the agent finds the guard that rejects 0 K, edits one line, and runs the project's declared test check without asking.*

[Recording (asciicast)](https://pancode.dev/assets/casts/cast-first-task.cast), 0:22. Transcript:

```text
A first task in PanCode: fix a failing test and verify
Recorded with PanCode 0.9.1. Each section is the terminal screen at that moment.

== ready

   ██████  ██    ██ ███   ██
   ██   ██ ████████ ████  ██
   ██████  ██    ██ ██ ██ ██
   ██      ██    ██ ██  ████       ▐∀▌ PanCode 0.9.1 · Systems software for coding agents
   ██       ██████  ██   ███         awareness  not indexed yet · /context init
                                     last here  no earlier session here
 ██████  ██████  ██████  ███████
██      ██    ██ ██   ██ ██          /view shows every tool call and its full output.
██      ██    ██ ██   ██ █████
██      ██    ██ ██   ██ ██
 ██████  ██████  ██████  ███████

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
 Ask Panos…
```

The agent changed `kelvin <= 0` to `kelvin < 0` in `temperature.mjs`, ran the declared test check (`checked test · exit 0`), and ended its report with `The test check passes: all 7 tests passed.`

Use your project's real test name. Read the diff and the check output yourself before you commit the change.

## Keep going

In the terminal, `/help` lists commands, `/model` selects a model, `/settings` opens the settings center, and `/config` opens your connections, where **Add a target** runs setup again without leaving the session.

When you quit, PanCode prints a summary of the session and a `pancode --resume <id>` line. Run that line to return to the conversation, `pancode --continue` to reopen the most recent one, or `pancode --resume` alone to pick from a list.

The [commands guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html) covers shortcuts and session controls. The [tools guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html) explains the repository tools and their permissions.

**Next steps**

- [Let PanCode work without watching every call](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)
- [A numerical change, checked with PanCode](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html)
- [Commands and modes](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/desktop-and-terminal.html

# Desktop or terminal: find your workspace

> See both interfaces, learn how to launch them, and choose where to start your next coding session.

PanCode has two interfaces to the same runtime. The terminal offers the primary workflow. The desktop alpha opens locally in your browser and gives you a visual workspace for projects and conversations.

## PanCode in the terminal

Open your repository and launch PanCode:

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
pancode
```

![PanCode terminal at start: the PanCode wordmark beside the version, health ready with the copilot target healthy, sandbox auto edits, the Ask Panos composer, and a status bar with the calibration-lab workspace on main and copilot · gpt-6-luna.](https://pancode.dev/assets/tui-boot.webp)

The terminal combines the conversation, tool calls, permissions, and worker activity. Type `/help` to see available commands, or `/model` to choose a model.

![PanCode in the terminal changing one line of temperature.mjs to fix a failing test, then running the declared test check through verify with exit 0](https://pancode.dev/assets/tui-verify.webp)

Each tool call stays on its own line with its result, so you can see what ran before you read the answer. `/view` opens the recorded calls and their output.

![Fullscreen terminal recording of PanCode on gpt-6-luna: the question why the absolute-zero test fails is typed into the composer and sent with a request to fix it and run the test check; Panos explores the project with 5 searches and 2 files, runs the test check and sees 6 pass and 1 fail, edits one line of temperature.mjs, runs the test check again with exit 0, and explains that kelvinToCelsius rejected 0 K because its check used <= 0 and that all 7 tests passed, in 11s.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/anim-fix-a-test.webp)

*A short task on GPT-6 Luna through GitHub Copilot: the agent finds the off-by-one guard, edits it, and runs the project's test check.*


During a turn, **Enter** queues a message that PanCode reads at the next pause between tool calls, **Alt+S** sends it now, and **Escape** cancels the run.

On a permission card, **Enter** allows the call. **Esc** denies it, which skips that call and leaves the run going. **Alt+X** stops the turn.

## PanCode on the desktop

From a terminal, run:

```sh
pancode gui --open
```

The command opens the local application with its access link. Open a workspace folder, describe a task, and choose a model and thinking level from the composer.

The rail on the left groups tasks by workspace. The Session column on the right shows the workspace's Git state, the model, context, usage, the plan, artifacts, changes, and run records as the task runs.

You can keep any number of tasks open in one window. Launching again brings that window forward under WSL, when the app is installed through Chrome or Edge, and on a Linux desktop with `wmctrl`, `xdotool` or sway when the background app is running. Otherwise it opens a new browser tab.

Up to four turns run at once by default, set by `interface.guiTurnCapacity` from 1 to 16, and later ones wait for a slot. A task with no turn running and no window showing it for five minutes is paused with its conversation kept, and opening it again brings it back. A task you never typed into closes instead.

With the default **Ask first** setting, PanCode reads, edits files in the workspace, and runs commands it recognizes, such as read-only inspection and the project's test runners, without stopping. An unrecognized shell command, a large dispatch plan, or anything that publishes outside the project waits for you. The approval names the call, what allowing it authorizes, and what it can affect.

The same control can be switched to **Run without asking** for one task after a second confirmation. The cards stop, and by default the sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge stay on. A turn that changed files ends with a card that opens the changes for review. Type `/` in the composer to list session commands.

A first run with no model connection opens on guided setup, which asks the same questions as `pancode configure`.

![PanCode desktop app Start a task page: a prompt box bound to the calibration-lab workspace, gpt-6-luna with thinking low, and three starting points: Build something, Fix a problem and Explore a project. The earlier task is listed under the workspace in the sidebar.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/gui-home.webp)

*Start a task in a workspace; earlier tasks stay under it in the sidebar.*

![PanCode desktop app, version 0.9.1, with the calibration-lab workspace in the sidebar. A finished task: two collapsed tool groups (3 searches; then 2 file reads, a folder listing and a command), with Panos reporting it deleted dist/, rebuilt it and that npm test passed all 7 tests, then listing the reference temperatures calibration.test.mjs checks: freezing, boiling, absolute zero and the round-trip inputs 25, −10, 36.6, 100, 273.15, 0 and −40°C. The footer reads Done, 12s, 7 tool calls; the composer shows Ask first, gpt-6-luna and Thinking low.](https://pancode.dev/assets/gui-task.webp)

*A finished task in the desktop app: the tool groups, the answer and the turn footer.*

![PanCode desktop app approval card for git push origin main: an Approval needed banner with the time left and a Needs your approval badge, the exact command, and rows for authorization, consequence, the effect Publishes to origin, reversibility not guaranteed, why it asked, the task, who requested it and the target, above Reject, Reject and stop the turn, and Allow once.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/gui-approval.webp)

*An outward command waits for you; the card says what it would change and nothing runs until you answer.*

![PanCode desktop app on a fresh profile with no model: guided setup opens on Welcome to PanCode, with the steps Provider, Connect, Model, Test and Workspace across the top, the PanCode logo beside a note that Panos works in the folders you choose, three numbered steps (pick a provider, connect and choose a model, open a folder), and the buttons Get started and Explore without a model.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/gui-setup.webp)

*With no model connection, the desktop app opens on guided setup.*

The desktop from a new task to a finished one: the composer, the answer with its tool calls, a waiting approval, and guided setup.

The desktop is in alpha and covers a subset of terminal workflows. Treat it as an optional way to use PanCode, and keep the terminal available for commands that the desktop does not yet expose.

On Linux with a systemd user session, you can install the optional background application, which starts at login and appears in your app menu. The installer offers the same step, and `--gui` accepts it without asking:

```sh
pancode gui background install --open
```

For an optional Linux desktop entry, run `pancode gui launcher install`. The background service and launcher each have an `uninstall` command. The [desktop app guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/gui.html) covers those options.

## Choose where to begin

Start in the terminal if you work mostly from a shell or need the primary set of PanCode workflows. Start on the desktop if you prefer browsing projects and working with attachments in a visual interface.

Both launch commands use the installed PanCode package. You do not need an account on this website. Your model connections use your own local server, institutional endpoint, or cloud provider.

Try [a temperature-calibration example with recorded checks](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html), or follow [your first session](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/first-session.html) for a concrete task to try in either workspace.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html

# Let PanCode work without watching every call

> Check the sandbox, undo a change with /rewind, tell the safety judge about your machine, and know when yolo is the right call.

Most of a coding task should not need you. At the `default` level, PanCode runs shell work inside an OS sandbox, snapshots your files before it changes them, and has a safety judge review what escapes the sandbox. You are asked only when the judge has no verdict or the decision is yours.

This guide shows how to check that setup, undo a change, and choose when to step up to `yolo`.

**Version scope**

The sandbox needs bubblewrap on Linux; on macOS it uses an experimental `sandbox-exec` profile. Snapshots need a Git work tree. Native Windows has neither guarantee, so read what `doctor` reports on your host.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository you can experiment in, with a clean working tree.

### Check what this host can contain

```sh
pancode doctor --verbose
```

Plain `doctor` lists only the rows that need attention; `--verbose` prints every row. Look for the `shell sandbox` row. It names the backend and where contained commands may write. If no backend exists, commands outside the recognized set go to the judge and then to you, so the rest of this guide still holds with more questions.

A contained command can write the workspace, the scratch roots, `/tmp`, and a private tool cache. Your own `~/.cache` and `~/.npm` stay read-only. Credentials, credential variables, secret files such as `.env`, and the SSH agent are hidden, new local Unix sockets are refused, and the network stays on. A directory your scripts must always write belongs in `safety.scratchRoots`.

A secret path is also refused before any sandbox is involved. In the recording below, asked how many bytes `.env` holds, the agent tried `wc -c .env` with bash, and PanCode stopped it before it ran:

```text
rule: secret_path_bash
This is a hard block; confirmation cannot override it.
```

![Terminal recording in which the user asks PanCode on gpt-6-luna how many bytes .env holds, using wc -c .env with bash. The bash call is marked blocked under rule secret_path_bash as a hard block that confirmation cannot override, and Panos reports that the command did not run, so it cannot give the byte count.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cast-sandbox.webp)

*A command that names the project's .env is refused before it runs; confirmation cannot override the block.*

```text
 ▐∀▌ default · projects/calibration-lab · main* │ ✓ ready                          ctx ▰▱▱▱▱▱ 4% · low · gpt-6-luna · ?
```

### Give it a task and watch what happens

On a scratch branch, type this:

```text
Delete the build output directory, regenerate it, and run the project's test check. Report what you ran.
```

Workspace edits and contained commands run without a card. A delete inside the workspace runs after a snapshot is taken. Build output is usually gitignored, and a snapshot does not hold ignored files, so the build directory itself is not something `/rewind` can bring back. A push or a command that leaves the sandbox goes to the judge first.

### Undo it with /rewind

```text
/rewind
```

The list shows this session's snapshots, newest first, with how many files each differs by. `Enter` previews a restore before anything is written. Confirming takes one more snapshot, so the rewind itself can be rewound. `Esc` goes back without writing anything.

In the recorded session behind this guide, the regenerated build was gitignored and nothing tracked had changed, so the preview read:

```text
The workspace already matches this snapshot. Nothing would change.
```

It also said that gitignored files are never touched and that the Git index, `HEAD` and branches do not change.

### Tell the judge about your machine

The judge reads your typed messages and the proposed call. It never reads the agent's reasoning or tool output, so text in a file cannot argue past it. Name what is yours in your user settings, the `settings.yaml` file in the folder that `pancode paths` prints on its `config` line:

```yaml title=settings.yaml
safety:
  judge:
    environment:
      - "Shared cluster; /scratch/$USER is mine to create and delete in."
    allow:
      - "restarting the dev containers this project's compose file defines"
```

**What you should see**

Contained work runs without a card, and `/rewind` lists a snapshot from before the first change of the turn. This shows the controls work on your host. It does not show that the agent's change is correct, so review the diff and the check results.

## What still reaches you

Some decisions never go to the judge: `ask_user` questions, PanCode's own settings, a plan-scale dispatch, and a model edit of project settings. An approval card nobody answers within `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) is denied, never approved, and the turn continues. A question nobody answers takes its recommended option, and `/decisions` shows what was chosen for you.

## When to use yolo

`yolo` is for long jobs you leave running: nothing waits for you. It is contained by default. The sandbox, snapshots, and safety judge work as at `default`, and a call that would have asked you is refused back to PanCode, so the job keeps going without it.

```sh
pancode --autonomy yolo
```

The first interactive activation shows a one-time acceptance card, and yolo is refused as root outside a detected container. A short floor still blocks deleting your home directory or a system tree, `mkfs`, writes to a block device, fork bombs, and reads of PanCode's credential store. Your project's approved rules and the run's ceilings also hold. Snapshots stay on.

After 600 tool calls since you last spoke, set by `safety.limits.autonomousToolCalls`, the session pauses until you continue.

Unconfined yolo is the skip-permissions mode for a container or another disposable environment: nothing asks, and commands run unsandboxed with your credentials. It takes effect only with `safety.yoloConfinement: unconfined` in your user settings and its own one-time acceptance. The footer shows which one is active.

To keep unconfined yolo inside the sandbox, also set `safety.sandbox: required`. Commands then run contained, and a retry with `unsandboxed: true` is refused. An outward command such as `git push` or `gh pr create` leaves the sandbox only as one literal command on that tool's short option list, with no pipe, redirect, or substitution. `doctor` reports which rule applies.

| | `default` | `yolo`, contained | `yolo`, unconfined |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shell commands | In the OS sandbox when a backend exists | As at `default` | Unsandboxed as you, unless `safety.sandbox: required` |
| Would-be approvals | Judge first, then you | Judge first, then refused back to PanCode | None |
| Your questions | Wait, then resolve after the timeout | Answered at once | Answered at once |
| Workers | Own sandbox, asks go to the judge | Dispatched as at `default` | Own sandbox, run the yolo way in their scope |
| `/rewind` | Available | Available | Available |

**What this does not protect**

- The sandbox contains `bash`, `run_script` and checks that run commands through `verify`. Typed `write` and `edit` calls follow the rules instead.
- Ignored files, untracked files over 16 MiB, and nested repositories are not in a snapshot.
- `/rewind` restores files. It never moves refs: it prints the commands that bring a moved branch back.
- The judge is a model. It can be wrong, and a route error means no verdict, so the call parks or is denied.
- Stronger isolation needs an external sandbox such as a container.

**Next steps**

- [Check a change against your repository](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Tools and permissions](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html)
- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)
- [How protection works](https://pancode.dev/research/protection.html)
