Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-a-playbook-and-land-it.html

# Run a playbook from plan to commit

> Run the built-in sdlc playbook on one task, watch it work, and read the three commits it makes on your branch.

A playbook is a sequence of workers and code steps that the fleet runs for you. The built-in `sdlc` playbook plans, builds, tests with a bounded fix loop, reviews with a bounded revise loop, and documents, with three commits along the way. This guide runs it on one task and reads what it committed on your branch.

**Version scope**

Run time and cost depend on your repository and the model you connect, so start with a small task.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, with a connected model that supports tool calling.
- A clean Git repository with a test command.
- A small, specific task you could review by hand.

### See what is available

```sh
pancode playbook list
```

`sdlc` shows as `setup` until the project declares the two commands it runs, `test` and `commit`.

### Declare the commands it runs

```sh
pancode playbook commands init
```

This drafts `.pancode/playbooks/commands.yaml` from your project's declarations, fully commented out, because uncommenting an entry confirms its exact command. Edit it to name what this project runs:

```yaml title=.pancode/playbooks/commands.yaml
version: 1
commands:
  test:
    argv: ["npm", "run", "test"]
  commit:
    argv: ["git", "commit", "-m", "{{commitMessage}}"]
```

### Check before you run

```sh
pancode playbook validate sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
pancode playbook graph sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
```

`validate` runs the execution preflight and `graph` prints the compiled waves, loops, scopes, and write boundaries, both without side effects. It resolves agents, targets, and profiles, and checks the session budget and write boundaries. A failed preflight during a real run exits 2 before anything dispatches.

### Run it

```sh
pancode fleet run sdlc --var task="Add empty-input handling to the parser"
```

The first line, on stderr, names the fleet root and plan hash. Each settled step prints one line. In another terminal, `pancode fleet status` shows the board and `pancode fleet events <root> --follow` follows the journal.

To keep your terminal, add `--detach`: the command returns once the fleet is recorded and prints its root id. `pancode fleet wait <root>` then prints the result and exits with the fleet's code. For a script, `--output-format json` prints one result document.

The steps work in your checkout, one after another, not in separate worktrees. The `suite` loop runs your `test` command inside the sandbox, rooted at the checkout, up to three times, and hands each of the first two failures back to the coder.

The command exits 0 only when every required step succeeded, no step was skipped, and every loop resolved. Any other finished run exits 1. A failed preflight, or an error in the scheduler itself, exits 2.

### Read what it committed

```sh
git log --oneline -3
git show --stat HEAD~2 HEAD~1 HEAD
```

The three `commit` steps commit the plan, the code, and the docs on the branch you have checked out, so there is nothing to merge or land afterwards. If you do not want the result, reset the branch to where it was before the run.

`pancode fleet land` is for something else: the task branch a worker dispatched with its own worktree keeps when its change was not merged.

![Terminal output: playbook validate sdlc reports 8 declared steps, 6 code steps, 4 agents and 14 plan steps with the plan hash; playbook graph lists waves 1 to 14 with each step's kind, agent or command, and scope, then the suite and review loops.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cli-playbook-graph.webp)

*validate runs the preflight and graph prints the compiled waves and loops, both without side effects.*

**What you should see**

A summary with each loop's terminal reason and any steps that need your decision, and three new commits on your branch. A finished run shows the playbook ran and its checks passed. It does not show the change is right, so read the diff.

## Make it yours

```sh
pancode playbook new parser-fix --from sdlc
```

This copies the built-in playbook to `.pancode/playbooks/parser-fix.md`, where you can change steps, agents, and limits. A resumed run replays a completed prefix of the same plan: `pancode fleet run <name> --resume <runId>`.

**Boundaries**

- Under `fleet run` nobody is attached, so a worker's ordinary ask is denied, not judged.
- One lock per Git checkout keeps two fleets out of the same workspace.
- `pancode telemetry verify --run <run-id>` checks the record of a run. The journals are hash-chained and unsigned, so they show consistency, not who wrote them.

**Next steps**

- [Workers and fleets](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)
- [How scheduling works](https://pancode.dev/research/scheduling.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html

# Run it unattended within limits

> Start a headless run with a cost ceiling and a timeout, ask read-only questions, schedule turns, and know what stops each one.

You can start a task and leave. Headless `pancode run` does one turn with nobody attached, and the limits you set are enforced. This guide covers a bounded headless run, a read-only one, the timeouts that apply when you walk away from an open session, and scheduled turns.

**Version scope**

A headless run has no one to ask: it denies whatever the safety judge does not allow, and `ask_user` is not available.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository, and a task you can state completely in one prompt.

### Put your decisions in the prompt

The judge reads only your prompt in a headless run, so name the actions the job needs:

```sh
pancode run --max-cost-usd 2 --timeout 30m \
  "Fix the failing parser test, run the test check, and commit on this branch. Do not push."
```

`--max-cost-usd` caps the priced spend this run adds. Reaching it stops the run and its workers with exit 4. Calls already in flight can pass the cap, and unpriced routes cannot be bounded, so pair it with `--timeout`, which exits 124 on expiry. The session ceiling, 5 USD by default, still applies.

`--require-priced` refuses a run that could reach a route with no price. `--max-requests <n>` and `--max-tool-calls <n>` cap the main agent's model requests and tool calls, and each exits 4 when reached. `--dry-run` prints the route, tools, and limits the run would use, then exits 0 without calling a model.

### Ask a question that cannot change anything

```sh
pancode run --read-only "Which modules have no tests? Report paths."
```

`--read-only` is an enforced ceiling on the main agent, not a request. No file outside PanCode's home changes: writes are refused, and shell commands run only in a read-only sandbox.

### Stream it to another program

```sh
pancode run --output-format stream-json "Summarize the last five commits."
```

The stream opens with a `session` frame carrying its schema version and ends with one `run_end` frame. That frame holds the answer in `result.text`, the `exitCode`, the `outcome`, and the `causes` that ended the run. Read the result from it.

When you want only the result, `--output-format json` prints that `run_end` document alone, and `-o answer.txt` also saves the answer to a file when the run exits 0. `run --json` was removed; use `--output-format stream-json`.

Continue later with `--continue` or `--resume <id>`. Add `--fork` to branch a new session and leave the original as it was.

### Walk away from an open session

In the terminal, an unanswered approval card is denied after `safety.unattendedAfterSeconds` (300 by default) and the turn continues. A question takes its recommended option. Any key stops the countdown. When you return, `/decisions` shows what was chosen, and the exit summary counts it on an `Unattended` line.

### Schedule turns while idle

```text
/loop 30m Check the nightly build log and report anything new.
/loop 5m --command make check
/loop
```

A bare `/loop` lists the jobs. A loop runs only while its conversation is idle and never replays missed runs. The `--command` form polls a program directly, with no shell.

**What you should see**

A finished turn with its exit code, not a parked prompt. An exit of 4 means a limit such as the cost ceiling stopped it. `pancode telemetry why-stopped <session>` explains a stop afterward.

## Read how a run ended

Stderr names the session and prints an `observed:` line that counts tool calls, refusals, writes, and checks, plus a one-line summary of the outcome, requests, tokens, and cost. A script should read the exit code or the `run_end` frame, not the prose answer.

When `--max-cost-usd` meets a route with no price, stderr says the cap cannot bound it; declare `targets[].pricing` to fix that.

In a separate run of the first step, made for this guide apart from the session at the top of the page, Claude Haiku 5.5 on the `anthropic-max` route worked on a repository with one failing parser test. It split each line at the first `=`, ran the test check, committed on the branch, and pushed nothing.

That route carries a price estimate, so `--max-cost-usd` could bound it and stderr printed no unpriced-route notice. Stderr read:

```text
pancode run: session n5iuvnc76u7o
pancode run: observed: 8 tool calls, 0 refused · 1 write · checks passed: npm run test, git status
```

On a route with no price, such as a gateway target without `targets[].pricing`, the same command first prints `pancode run: --max-cost-usd does not bound unpriced routes: <target>/<model>; declare targets[].pricing to bound them`.

The `run_end` frame of the third step has this shape. `causes` is empty on success and lists every reason, most important first, when the run failed or was stopped:

```json
{"type":"run_end","schemaVersion":2,"mode":"main","sessionId":"<id>","exitCode":0,"outcome":"succeeded","causes":[],"result":{"text":"<answer>","artifacts":[]}}
```

The real frame carries more fields, such as usage, timings, and tool counts. `pancode schema run-result` prints the full JSON Schema.

| Exit | What it means |
| --- | --- |
| `0` | The run settled and succeeded |
| `1` | It failed: the model was unreachable, a worker did not deliver, or a refused call left the task undone. `--fail-on-verify` adds a failed `--verify` check |
| `2` | A usage error, including `--autonomy yolo` as root outside a container |
| `3` | At `yolo`, the safety judge blocked too many calls in a row; review the run, then `--continue`. Also `--on-permission fail` at the first request nobody could approve |
| `4` | A cost ceiling, `--max-requests`, `--max-tool-calls`, or at `yolo` an autonomous cap on tool calls, minutes, or tokens, stopped it; `--continue` resumes |
| `124` | `--timeout` expired; the run still settled and sealed |
| `130`, `143` | Ctrl+C or a SIGTERM stopped it |

## Pick the right tool

| When you want | Use | What still stops it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One bounded task | `pancode run` at `default` | Judge, sandbox, cost ceiling, timeout |
| A long job you leave running | `pancode run --autonomy yolo` | Contained by default: the sandbox and judge stay on, and a call the judge does not allow is refused back to the run. Ceilings, timeout, the loop guard, and the tool budget also stop it |
| A recurring check | `/loop` in an open session | Pause or stop it; needs the session to stay open |

**Boundaries**

- A contained command starts without credential variables and cannot open secret files, so name tools that need them. PanCode may rerun with `unsandboxed: true`, which the judge reviews. At unconfined `yolo` under `safety.sandbox: required`, that retry is refused.
- `yolo` does not carry over from `settings.yaml` to a headless run. It comes only from that run's own `--autonomy yolo`, and it exits 2 as root outside a detected container.

**Next steps**

- [Let PanCode work without watching every call](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)
- [Report a problem without leaking your machine](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/report-a-problem-without-leaking-your-machine.html)
- [Commands and shortcuts](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html)
- [How protection works](https://pancode.dev/research/protection.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/script-pancode-in-ci.html

# Script PanCode in CI

> Build a CI job on one JSON result, typed exit codes, run limits, a dry run, and an answer validated against your schema.

A CI job needs three things from a coding agent: a result it can parse, an exit code it can branch on, and limits it can rely on. `pancode run` gives a script all three. This guide builds one job step by step, then puts it in a GitHub Actions workflow.

**Version scope**

The output contract is schema version 2, and `pancode schema run-result` prints its JSON Schema for the version you have installed.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed on the runner, with a model connection whose key comes from an environment variable.
- A repository with a test command.
- `jq`, to read the result.

### Preview the run without calling a model

`--dry-run` prints what the run would do and exits 0. It opens no session, calls no model, and runs no check.

```sh
pancode run --dry-run --output-format json \
  --max-cost-usd 2 --timeout 15m \
  --verify "npm test" \
  "Fix the failing parser test." | jq '.plan'
```

The plan names the route, the tools the agent may use, the sandbox mode, the limits, and the checks. Put this in a pull request job to catch a bad flag before anything is spent. Check that `.plan.route.target` is set.

### Ask for one result document

`--output-format json` prints one `run_end` document on stdout when the run is over. Progress and notices go to stderr, so stdout is the document alone.

```sh
pancode run --output-format json \
  --max-cost-usd 2 --timeout 15m \
  "Fix the failing parser test." > result.json
```

Use `--output-format stream-json` instead when another program should follow the run live. It prints one JSON event per line and ends with the same `run_end` document.

### Bound the run

Each limit is a flag, and each one stops the run with its own cause code.

```sh
pancode run --output-format json \
  --max-requests 40 --max-tool-calls 120 \
  --max-cost-usd 2 --require-priced \
  --timeout 15m --sandbox required \
  "Fix the failing parser test." > result.json
```

`--max-requests` and `--max-tool-calls` cap the main agent's model requests and tool calls. `--max-cost-usd` caps priced spend, and `--require-priced` refuses the run when a route it could reach has no price. `--sandbox required` refuses to start on a runner with no OS sandbox.

### Make the job fail when the work is not finished

By default a run that ends normally exits 0, whatever the agent says about its own work. Two flags turn an honest "not finished" into a failed job.

```sh
pancode run --output-format json \
  --verify "npm test" --fail-on-verify \
  --exit-code \
  "Fix the failing parser test." > result.json
```

`--verify` declares an acceptance check that PanCode runs itself after the turn, and `--fail-on-verify` exits 1 when it fails. `--exit-code` exits 1 when the run was assessed as partly done or not done.

The agent declares how the turn ended, and PanCode records that claim beside its own assessment. A claim of done that left unvalidated changes or a failing check is assessed as partly done, so `--exit-code` fails it.

### Get a structured answer

When the next step needs data instead of prose, pass a JSON Schema. The answer must be one JSON object that matches it, and PanCode validates the object before the run exits 0.

```sh
cat > summary.schema.json <<'EOF'
{
  "type": "object",
  "required": ["fixed", "files"],
  "properties": {
    "fixed": { "type": "boolean" },
    "files": { "type": "array", "items": { "type": "string" } }
  }
}
EOF

pancode run --output-format json \
  --output-schema summary.schema.json \
  "Fix the failing parser test and report which files changed." \
  | jq '.result.structured'
```

A mismatch gets one repair turn with no tools. If the answer still does not match, the run exits 1 with cause `schema_mismatch`. The schema's root must be an object, and a schema PanCode cannot enforce exits 2 before any model request.

### Read the result

Branch on the exit code first, then read the fields you need.

```sh
jq -r '.outcome' result.json            # succeeded, failed, canceled, timed_out
jq -r '.causes[].code' result.json      # why, most important first
jq -r '.result.text' result.json        # the answer
jq '.verify.checks' result.json         # each --verify check and whether it passed
jq '.usage.total' result.json           # tokens and cost
```

`causes` is empty on success. On a failure or a stop it lists every reason as a code, usually with a message. `-o answer.md` also writes the answer to a file when the run exits 0.

**What you should see**

One JSON document on stdout, an exit code that matches its `exitCode` field, and a `causes` list that names the reason whenever that code is not 0.

## Exit codes a job can branch on

| Exit | Meaning | Typical cause codes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `0` | The run settled and succeeded | none |
| `1` | The run failed, or a flag you set turned an unfinished result into a failure | `verify_failed`, `schema_mismatch`, `context_overflow` |
| `2` | A usage or setup error, before any model request | `empty_task`, `schema_unsupported`, `session_live` |
| `3` | A request nobody could approve, with `--on-permission fail` | `permission_required` |
| `4` | A limit stopped the run | `max_requests`, `max_tool_calls`, `max_cost_usd` |
| `124` | `--timeout` expired | `deadline` |

Retry on 124 or 4 only after you raise the limit, because the same run will stop at the same place. An exit of 2 is a mistake in the job itself, so fail fast and fix the command.

## A GitHub Actions job

This workflow installs PanCode, connects a model from a repository secret, previews the run, then runs it with limits. The job fails when the run does not finish the work.

```yaml
name: agent-fix
on: workflow_dispatch

jobs:
  fix:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 30
    env:
      ANTHROPIC_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Install PanCode
        run: |
          curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh -s -- --no-gui
          echo "$HOME/.local/bin" >> "$GITHUB_PATH"

      - name: Connect a model
        run: |
          pancode configure --id ci --runtime anthropic \
            --model <model> --api-key-env ANTHROPIC_API_KEY --set-orchestrator

      - name: Preview
        run: |
          pancode run --dry-run --output-format json \
            --verify "npm test" "Fix the failing parser test." | jq '.plan'

      - name: Run
        run: |
          pancode run --output-format json \
            --max-requests 40 --max-cost-usd 2 --timeout 15m \
            --verify "npm test" --fail-on-verify --exit-code \
            "Fix the failing parser test." > result.json

      - name: Report
        if: always()
        run: |
          jq -r '"outcome: \(.outcome)", "causes: \([.causes[].code] | join(", "))"' result.json
          jq -r '.result.text' result.json >> "$GITHUB_STEP_SUMMARY"
```

Replace `<model>` with a model id from `pancode models --target ci`. The key stays in the secret: `--api-key-env` names the variable, and PanCode reads it when it calls the model. If the installer put the launcher somewhere else, `command -v pancode` after the install step shows where.

## Limits to know

A headless run has no one to ask. Requests that would need approval are denied, and the turn goes on without them unless you pass `--on-permission fail`.

`--max-cost-usd` bounds priced routes only. On a route with no price, stderr says the cap cannot bound it, and `--require-priced` turns that into a refusal.

Pass the task as an argument. `run` reads stdin only when you pass `-`, so a pipe into `run` without it is ignored.

## Next

[Run it unattended within limits](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html) covers read-only runs, yolo, and scheduled turns. The [exit codes and output guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html) lists every field and cause.

**Next steps**

- [Run it unattended within limits](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html)
- [Automate with pancode run](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html)
- [How accounting works](https://pancode.dev/research/accounting.html)

# See what a session cost and what a run did

> Read session cost and stop reasons from local journals, verify a sealed record, and prepare an archive that uploads nothing.

PanCode records what each process, session, and worker run did in local journals, and every usage figure in every interface comes from those journals. This guide shows how to read a session's cost, find out why it stopped, check a run's record, and prepare an archive for the maintainers.

**Version scope**

Costs are shown with their provenance: a measured figure, an estimate, and an unknown value stay separate. An unknown stays unknown rather than becoming zero.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, and at least one finished session in a repository.
- The session id, which the exit summary prints. `/resume` also lists them.

### Read it in the session

```text
/usage
/context
/usage health
```

`/usage` covers session usage and supported subscription quotas. `/context` shows context use and the newest call's cache evidence. `/usage health` shows process health and route state.

### Read it from the shell

```sh
pancode telemetry inspect <session>
pancode telemetry cost <session> --by model
pancode telemetry calls <session> --limit 20
pancode telemetry cache <session>
```

Each takes `--json` and returns the same data the terminal, editors, and desktop app read. For a repository over time, use `pancode telemetry cost --repo . --days 30 --by model`.

### Ask why it stopped

```sh
pancode telemetry why-stopped <session>
pancode telemetry timeline <session>
pancode telemetry explain <ref>
```

`explain` shows how a figure was derived. `--run <run-id>` points `inspect` and `cost` at one worker run instead of a session.

### Check a record

```sh
pancode telemetry verify <session>
pancode telemetry verify --run <run-id>
```

A sealed scope directory is self-contained, so you can copy it and verify it on another machine. `verify` checks journal segments, objects, and seals.

### Share it deliberately

```sh
pancode telemetry share --session <id> --profile content-free --dry-run
pancode telemetry share --session <id> --profile content-free --out report.tar.gz
```

Without `--send`, `share` writes an archive and uploads nothing. `content-free` is the default profile, with structural records and no objects or content. `structural` adds objects that hold structure, such as prompt manifests. Read the dry run before you send anything.

![Terminal: telemetry why-stopped says the session closed after a normal last turn, with spend not measured over 147,026 tokens; telemetry verify reports the session sealed with 127 lines in 1 segment and 3 objects and its head hash; telemetry cost --by turn shows one turn with 10 calls and 147,026 tokens, cost not measured, and an economy line of 0.3362 credits.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cli-telemetry-session.webp)

*The session's record: why it stopped, whether it verifies, and what each turn used.*

**What you should see**

Figures labelled by provenance, and a `verify` result that names any gap. A clean verify shows the journals are internally consistent. The chain is unsigned, so it does not show who wrote them, and it says nothing about whether the work was correct.

## Control what is kept

`telemetry.mode` defaults to `standard`, which keeps accountability and operational records without prompt content. `research` mode, `telemetry.research.content: true`, and `pancode telemetry consent` for the workspace are all required before prompts and request bodies are kept. Consent is stored in your own state directory, keyed by the workspace's real path, so a file committed to a repository cannot grant it.

`pancode telemetry prune` is a dry run unless you pass `--apply`.

**Boundaries**

- Figures depend on what the provider reports. Calls with unknown usage are counted separately.
- Quota rows are what a provider account reports, shared across sessions, and are separate from session spend.
- `pancode usage report` is experimental.

**Next steps**

- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)
- [Run it unattended within limits](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html)
- [Check your installation](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/doctor.html)
- [How accounting works](https://pancode.dev/research/accounting.html)

# A numerical change, checked with PanCode

> Follow a temperature-conversion example through a floating-point test failure, a correction, and recorded verification.

A small numerical task makes it easy to follow a change from code to a recorded check. This example converts temperatures between Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit, validates inputs, and tests physical boundaries without adding dependencies.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, with a connected model that supports tool calling.
- Node.js 18.1 or newer and npm on your `PATH`. The installer's private Node.js is not added to `PATH`, so install them yourself.
- The example archive below, extracted into a project you can open.

## Open the example

Download the [runnable temperature-calibration example](https://pancode.dev/assets/temperature-calibration.zip). It includes the actual implementation, seven tests, and a private package manifest. It uses only the built-in Node.js test runner and has no dependencies.

Extract the archive into your project's `examples/` folder, so the files live in `examples/temperature-calibration/`. Open the project in the terminal:

```sh
pancode
```

Select a model that supports tool calling. You can also use the desktop alpha with `pancode gui --open`. To reproduce the authoring task in your own project, ask:

> Create four temperature conversion functions for Celsius, Kelvin, and Fahrenheit. Reject non-numeric and non-finite inputs with TypeError, and temperatures below absolute zero with RangeError. Use 273.15 for the Celsius/Kelvin offset. Add Node.js tests for freezing, boiling, absolute zero, round trips within 1e-10, and invalid inputs. Use no dependencies. Run the tests and report the actual result.

Choose a new example directory when creating files. In the supplied example, the implementation and tests are already present; start by asking PanCode to read them.

## Check the numerical boundaries

These reference temperatures cover ordinary values and the physical lower boundary:

| Reference | Celsius | Kelvin | Fahrenheit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Freezing point | 0 °C | 273.15 K | 32 °F |
| Boiling point | 100 °C | 373.15 K | 212 °F |
| Absolute zero | −273.15 °C | 0 K | −459.67 °F |

When PanCode first wrote this example, the first run exposed an exact-equality assertion for the Fahrenheit value at absolute zero. JavaScript produced `−459.66999999999996`; the test expected `−459.67`. The agent changed that assertion to an absolute tolerance of `1e-10` and reran the tests. Review a tolerance against your domain’s numerical requirements before applying it elsewhere.

## Run a declared check

The example’s private `package.json` declares its test command. With the archive extracted into the folder above, ask PanCode:

> Use verify with check test and cwd examples/temperature-calibration, then show the reference temperatures from examples/temperature-calibration/calibration.test.mjs as a table. Do not edit files.

If an approval card appears, read the command before allowing it. In the recorded run, the check exited 0 with seven passing tests, and PanCode read the test file for the table. Naming the file keeps a fast model from searching the project for it.

![PanCode in the terminal running the declared test check through verify with exit 0, then showing the reference temperatures from the test file as a table](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-verify-table.webp)

To run the same tests yourself from the repository root:

```sh
node --test examples/temperature-calibration/calibration.test.mjs
```

## Inspect the recorded result

In the terminal, open `/view` and select the `checked test` row. The preview shows the check, its working directory, the exit status, and the output, so you can compare the answer with what ran. On the desktop alpha, **Artifacts** in the Session column lists the same record.

![Terminal /view with the checked test row selected under Diffs & checks: the preview shows check test, cwd examples/temperature-calibration, exit 0 with 19 lines of output, the npm test script running node --test calibration.test.mjs, and passing tests for freezing point, boiling point, absolute zero, round trips and non-numeric input; the list also holds transcript details, message delivery, accountability, prompt manifests and 14 safety audit rows.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-view-result.webp)

*/view: the recorded check, with its working directory, exit status and output.*

Passing tests establish the behavior covered by those tests. This small example does not establish the scientific validity of a larger application. For project-specific requirements, see [quality policies](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/quality-policy.html) and [tool usage](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html).

**Next steps**

- [Check a change against your repository](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Quality policy guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/quality-policy.html)
- [How accounting works](https://pancode.dev/research/accounting.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html

# Choose a model for your project

> Connect a local server, a cloud API, or a supported subscription route, then choose models separately for conversation and delegated work.

PanCode lets you choose the model connection around your project. Start with the place your code is allowed to go, then choose a model and runtime that can do the task. A local GPU, a model server, an institutional gateway, and a cloud API are different deployment choices.

If you already connected a model, skip to **Separate conversation from worker models** below.

**Version scope**

A working connection does not establish a model's coding quality, and routes differ in the tools and images they carry.

## Before you start

- Linux, macOS, or WSL. The installer supplies Node.js.
- A repository you know, so you can judge the first answer.
- One model route you are allowed to use for this code: an app on your computer, a model server, an AI subscription, or a provider account.

## Decide where inference may run

On first setup, Guided setup asks what you have. Choose by where the model input may go, then by what you already run.

| Answer | Where inference runs | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An API key | The provider | Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, OpenRouter, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, and others |
| A subscription | The provider | ChatGPT Plus or Pro, Claude Pro or Max, or GitHub Copilot |
| A model server or gateway | The server you name | Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, LiteLLM, or any OpenAI-compatible address |
| A setup file from my lab or team | The targets the file names | A path or https address someone gave you |

When setup finds a route first, such as a provider key in your environment or a model server on a default local port, it lists that route before asking. A subscription-backed route has its own authentication and usage conditions; it is not interchangeable with an API account. The [connection guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html) covers each route.

**Where each part runs**

1. PanCode and its tools (Your computer): The session, repository tools, and approvals run where you start PanCode.
2. Inference (The route you choose): A local app, a model server, a subscription, or a provider API. Moves from the previous stage: model requests.
3. Worker tools (Where a worker runs): On this computer by default, or on an SSH node you configure. Moves from the previous stage: delegated work.

*PanCode, its tools, and inference can run in different places. Choosing a remote model does not move your files or tools there.*

## Connect one model

### Install PanCode

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh
cd /path/to/your/project
```

### Start guided setup

```sh
pancode configure
```

Choose **Guided setup**. The desktop alpha offers the same wizard after `pancode gui --open`. In a terminal session, `/config` opens your connections, where **Add a target** runs the wizard without leaving the session.

### Pick the route and the model

Answer what you have, then provide the key, sign-in, or server address it asks for. Setup takes the provider's recommended model, or the only model a server lists; otherwise you pick from the list. For a local server with no models, load one and choose **Check again**.

### Test the connection, then save

Setup sends the model one short test request and saves when it answers. After a failure you can try again, change the key or address, or choose **Save anyway**. The first connection supplies the chat and worker defaults, and `/model` changes the model later.

![Guided setup in the terminal on a fresh profile: the welcome text says one short test message is sent before saving, and PanCode found a way to reach a model, offering GitHub Copilot SDK, signed in, with model gpt-6-luna recommended, or Set up something else for an API key, a subscription or a server.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-configure-detected.webp)

*When setup finds a stored sign-in it offers that first; Set up something else leads to the other routes.*

![Guided setup in the terminal asking what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file from your lab or team, with the providers behind the first three and a path or https address for the setup file; the welcome text above says one short test message is sent before anything is saved.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-configure-source.webp)

*Guided setup asks what you have: an API key, a subscription, a model server or gateway, or a setup file.*

![Guided setup in the terminal after choosing GitHub Copilot SDK: it notes that researcher's GitHub Copilot subscription on github.com is used under the organization's Copilot policies, tests copilot-sdk / gpt-6-luna (answered in 3.2 s), saves target copilot-sdk as the chat and fleet default, writes ~/.config/pancode/settings.yaml, and ends with how to start pancode and change the setup later with pancode configure.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-configure-saved.webp)

*Accepting the offer tests the recommended model and saves it as the default for chat and workers.*

Guided setup in the terminal: a stored sign-in it found, the routes it offers, and the saved connection.

After setup, `/model` lists the models of every connected target and switches the conversation between them:

![Fullscreen terminal recording of the /model picker in PanCode on GitHub Copilot: the session starts on gpt-6-luna, the picker lists 26 models on the copilot target, and claude-sonnet-5.5 and gemini-4-argon are chosen in turn by typing part of the name, each changing the status bar's model and context size, before the session returns to gpt-6-luna.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/anim-model-switch.webp)

*One subscription, many models: /model lists what the connected target offers and switches the session without leaving the conversation.*

```text
 ∀  PanCode 0.9.1

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
 Ask Panos…  ? keys · / commands
━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━
  ∀  default · calibration-lab · main │ ✓ ready                     ctx 272k · low · gpt-6-luna · ?
```

**What you should see**

When setup shows a model list, the list says whether it is live, cached, or the provider's catalog; a server that lists one model skips the list. The test request shows that the model answers; it does not test tool calling. An answer is useful, but it is not a coding benchmark.

## Ask one question you can check

**Ask PanCode**

> Explain this project's build and test entry points. Do not change files. Identify one check I could run to confirm your explanation.

Read the tool activity and compare the answer with the project. If it fails, check the endpoint, the loaded model, the credentials, and the selected runtime before giving it a larger assignment. `pancode doctor` provides diagnostics; it does not certify model quality.

## Separate conversation from worker models

The model answering you need not handle every delegated task. The terminal `/settings` groups its rows into seven areas below **Recent & Pinned**, with the conversation model under **Models** and worker defaults under **Workers**.

`pancode configure --settings` opens the shell menu, which uses eight sections instead: the conversation model is under **Chat** and worker defaults under **Fleet**. On the desktop, Settings has a **Models** page and a **Fleet routes** tab. Select a connection and model for conversation, then use worker defaults or profiles for delegated work.

![Terminal Settings open on Models: the copilot connection is healthy and used by chat+fleet, with Add a target and Connect by URL below it; the chat connection is copilot, the chat model gpt-6-luna and the thinking level Low, and the side panel shows copilot's default model gpt-6-luna.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-settings-models.webp)

*Settings: the model answering you, under Models.*

![Terminal Settings open on Workers: the default fleet connection is copilot, the default fleet model gpt-6-luna, the thinking level Off and the worker location Automatic, followed by Profiles, Agent routes, Automatic routing and Machines; the side panel says the selected value comes from the user settings.yaml.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-settings-workers.webp)

*Settings: the default worker's connection, model and thinking level, under Workers.*

Terminal settings keep the conversation model and the worker defaults apart.

This helps when exploring a repository and changing code have different requirements, or when you want to keep a workflow while evaluating another model. The benefit depends on the task and environment; this guide makes no claim that a particular combination is cheaper or faster.

A worker running on your machine against a remote model server is still a local worker: inference and tool execution are separate choices. To run the worker process on another machine, use the [fleet configuration](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html).

## Choose capabilities deliberately

PanCode supports more than one kind of model interaction. Its Inception runtime serves [Mercury diffusion language models](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/diffusion-models.html) as chat models with tool calling. Optional, experimental [System One routes](https://pancode.dev/research/system-one-decisions.html) answer typed questions an agent asks through `consult`. Neither replaces a chat model or is required to get started.

Vision support depends on the model and the route. A model advertised as multimodal is not enough if the bridge does not carry images: the managed Codex, Pi, OpenCode, Claude Code, and Antigravity CLI bridges are text-only. Check what the route accepts before attaching a screenshot.

**Know where information goes**

- PanCode runs locally, but a configured cloud model receives the input sent to that provider.
- Local inference keeps inference on the selected server; tools, peers, plugins, and commands can still make network requests.
- PanCode is free for individuals, small organizations (fewer than 100 people and under $1M revenue), and noncommercial research and teaching. Inference hardware, provider usage, and subscriptions can still cost money.

**Next steps**

- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)
- [Connection guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Install PanCode](https://pancode.dev/#start)
- [How the drivers work](https://pancode.dev/research/drivers.html)

# Coordinate the coding agents you already use

> Hand a bounded task to a coding agent you have installed, tell a managed run from an interactive handoff, and review what comes back before you combine it.

You can use PanCode to coordinate the coding agents you already have installed. Give a peer a focused assignment, follow a managed run where the connector supports it, and review its output before accepting the change.

**Version scope**

The supported peers are Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and Antigravity. Their modes and controls differ. Install and authenticate each peer's own CLI before configuring it in PanCode.

## Before you start

- PanCode with one working model connection. The [first session](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/first-session.html) covers it.
- A peer's CLI installed and signed in under its own account.
- An assignment whose answer you can check against the repository.

## See which peers PanCode can use

```sh
pancode interop inspect --json
pancode configure --interop
```

The first command reports what PanCode can find; the second configures interoperability. In a terminal conversation, `/hub interop` shows the available connections. The [interoperability guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/interop.html) covers the mode for each peer.

![Terminal Local coding agents panel with 4 proposed and 0 connected: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and GitHub Copilot are listed as not configured with their launch commands, and the detail for Claude Code shows its path under /home/researcher, [a] connect, which appends exactly this entry to delegation.agents, [x] decline, and the start of that entry.](/assets/guides/tui-interop.webp)

*/hub interop lists the coding agents PanCode detected and the entry that connecting would add.*

![Terminal interop inspect report: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and GitHub Copilot present with their versions, each with its ACP, headless and pane status and the next step, no inventory found, and Antigravity CLI absent because its agy CLI is missing.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cli-interop-inspect.webp)

*interop inspect: each coding agent PanCode detected, how far it is wired, and the next step.*

What PanCode detected on a machine with peer CLIs installed but not signed in.

## Choose managed work or an interactive handoff

The three commands answer different needs. Pick by whether you want a recorded run or a place to work with the peer yourself. An ACP peer is one PanCode drives over the Agent Client Protocol; a headless target runs the peer's own CLI once for the task.

| Command | What happens | What PanCode records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `/run <agent-id> <task>` | A configured ACP peer such as `antigravity` runs the task; `acp:<id>` names one explicitly | The result and a sealed run record |
| `/run --target <target> <agent> <task>` | A configured headless target runs it | The result and a sealed run record |
| `/panes peer <agent> [brief]` | A pane opens beside the conversation for you to work in | No run record |

The [panes tutorial](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/panes-and-docks.html) covers the pane host. Do not infer that a pane completed a task because it opened. Do not infer that a run record contains every internal reasoning step or mediates every operation inside a peer-owned loop.

## Give one bounded assignment

**Assign to a peer**

> Inspect the parser's handling of empty input. Identify the existing tests and propose a regression test. Do not edit files.

That last sentence is a task instruction, not an enforced boundary. For an enforced one, put `--read-only` before the task, as in `/run --read-only <agent> <task>`; an option typed after the task text becomes part of the task. PanCode admits a read-only run only on a peer whose own sandbox refuses every write, and refuses it before launch on every other peer, ACP peers included.

## Keep worker authority separate

A native worker, one of PanCode's own agents, inherits the main session's level inside its own permit and OS sandbox. At contained `yolo`, which is yolo's default, workers are dispatched as at `default`; at unconfined `yolo` a mediated worker runs the yolo way within its dispatch scope. A read-only worker stays at `default`.

Managed peer dispatches run at default permissions, even when the main session uses `yolo`, and each external agent runs its own tool loop.

A read-only run must leave every file outside PanCode's home unchanged. It is admitted only where the peer's own sandbox guarantees that, so check the peer before you rely on it.

| Peer | Read-only headless run |
| --- | --- |
| Codex | Runs under its read-only sandbox mode |
| Claude Code | Refused before launch |
| Antigravity | Refused before launch |
| Pi | Refused before launch |
| OpenCode | Refused before launch |

ACP peers may own their tools. Explicitly permitting peer-owned tools changes what PanCode can observe and mediate, so read the guide's permission limits before using such a peer on sensitive work. PanCode's own shell commands and native workers' commands run in an OS sandbox when one is available. External peers keep their own authority.

## Separate changes with a worktree

For supported headless dispatch, `--worktree` keeps a Git task branch for review. That helps you compare two proposed changes without mixing their working files.

A worktree is an organizational boundary. It does not confine a peer's filesystem or network access. Keep assignments narrow, inspect the branch and diff, and run the repository's checks before merging a result.

## Review before combining

**What to look for**

A useful result may be a diagnosis, a patch, or a failed attempt that reveals a missing dependency. Look for the files it touched, the checks it ran, and the limits of its report. A claimed test result and an observed check are different evidence.

When comparing agents, give them the same task and evaluate the actual output. Record the model, connector, setup, check results, and any costs you can substantiate. PanCode coordinating two peers does not make either one better.

**Boundaries**

- Supported modes differ by peer, and some cannot receive live steering. The Antigravity CLI over ACP can.
- A pane is an interactive handoff; it produces no run record.
- Peer accounts, subscriptions, and usage limits stay with each peer's own provider.

**Next steps**

- [Run it unattended within limits](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-it-unattended-within-limits.html)
- [Ask several agents at once](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/ask-several-agents-at-once.html)
- [Project quality checks](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/quality-policy.html)
- [Interoperability guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/interop.html)
- [How scheduling works](https://pancode.dev/research/scheduling.html)

# Keep a long coding task on track

> See what fills the context, carry your decisions through a handoff, and resume the right branch of a long task.

Long coding work needs more than saved chat history. You need the current objective, the decisions that still apply, the relevant files, and the checks left to run. PanCode gives you controls for inspecting that context and continuing after a session grows.

**Version scope**

This guide describes the context workflow. It does not promise that every detail survives summarization or that a model cannot misunderstand a handoff.

**Four controls for a long task**

1. Inspect (/context): Usage, reserved output, remaining headroom, and any pending handoff.
2. Reduce (/context compact): A focused summary that keeps what you name. Moves from the previous stage: history grows.
3. Hand off (/handoff): A continuation bound to this branch and its decisions. Moves from the previous stage: the work continues.
4. Recover (/context recover): Reduce or deliver, chosen explicitly by its ID. Moves from the previous stage: a transition stops.

*Inspect first; reduce, hand off, or recover only for a stated reason.*

## Give the project a starting point

A project handbook orients the model toward the repository's structure and rules. The context commands prepare a `PANCODE.md` handbook and a structural code index called the codemap.

```sh
pancode context init
pancode context index
```

Review generated project material as you would any other change. Keep build commands and verification expectations specific to the project: an incorrect handbook makes the wrong answer easier to repeat.

The codemap locates structural information without reading every file into the conversation. It does not replace reading a function before changing its behavior.

## Inspect before the context fills

In the terminal, `/context` shows usage, output reservation, remaining headroom, and any pending handoff. On the desktop alpha, the Session column has **Context** and **Branches** cards, and typing `/` in the composer offers `/context`, `/tree`, `/fork`, and `/handoff`.

![Terminal /context panel after one turn: 12.9k / 272k tokens in use (4.7%), split into system prompt, tool definitions, agent fleet, project context, messages, tool results and assistant output, with 205k free and a 54.4k autocompact reserve; autocompact runs at 80% with 12 active tools, and the next request has 226k of headroom.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-context.webp)

*/context: the window size, the tokens in use, and what fills them.*

![Terminal after /fork: a notice that the conversation forked into a new session while the original is unchanged and workspace files were not rewound, then the Session tree dock showing where the fork came from, a legend, and the first 10 of 35 turns (You, Panos, tool calls and tool results), with the selected turn's id, time and what Enter does.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-tree.webp)

*/tree after /fork: the branch records where it came from, and Enter continues from an earlier turn.*

The terminal's context window, and a forked conversation in /tree.

Watch what you are accumulating. A large test log, an old exploration branch, and a current design decision should not carry the same weight. Ask the agent to cite the file or tool result behind an important conclusion instead of a remembered paraphrase.

## Reduce with a stated purpose

```text
/context compact Keep the objective, decisions, changed files, test results, and remaining work.
```

**After compaction**

Read the continuation. Compaction reduces history; it does not prove that the model kept every fact. If an important constraint disappears, restate it with its source.

## Hand off a defined continuation

`/handoff <goal>` prepares a continuation around a stated goal. A useful goal says what the receiving session should do next and which work must stay intact.

**Example handoff goal**

> /handoff Fix the empty-input parser bug: keep the failing case in tests/parser.test.ts, the chosen approach of validating before tokenizing, and rerun the parser tests before finishing.

Handoffs are bound to the active conversation branch and its decisions. A fork can recall earlier notes without inheriting permission to resume its parent's pending transition. Use `/tree` and `/fork` deliberately, and confirm which branch you are continuing.

To return to a session after quitting, run the `pancode --resume <id>` line from the exit summary; a prefix works when it matches one session, and `pancode --continue` reopens the most recent one.

## Recover an interrupted transition explicitly

If `/context` shows a pending handoff, use its exact ID:

```text
/context recover <handoffId> reduce
/context recover <handoffId> deliver
```

These are two different recoveries, not two commands to run in turn. Choose **reduce** when the reduction has not committed and another attempt remains; choose **deliver** when the validated commit exists. The [continuity guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/context-continuity.html) explains those states.

A restarted process records an interrupted handoff as paused and waits for your command. Do not create a new handoff just because a pending one looks unfamiliar.

## Keep memory reviewable

Proactive memory is separate from the working context. Open `/memory` and use its **Review** tab to approve a proposed lesson with `a`, or press `x` twice to reject it; an observation about one repository should not quietly become a rule for every project.

Global, procedural, runtime, and agent lessons wait for you. A repository note can become a lesson automatically once two other sessions demonstrate it with no contradiction, and a later contradiction demotes it. `pancode memory consolidate` merges duplicate claims and demotes lessons that no longer hold, with no model call.

In `/settings`, under **Context and memory**, **Memory connection** and **Memory model** choose where memory's model calls run. Memory runs on rules by default, and its model steps are opt-in; with no route set, one you turn on uses your chat route. Turning **Proactive memory** off stops task memory, the memory section of the prompt and the `memory_note` tool.

Stored memory is not fine-tuning of the underlying model. Its value depends on selection, scope, and whether it is still relevant.

**Boundaries**

- A summary is a model's reduction, so check it against sources when it matters.
- A handoff belongs to the branch that prepared it; a fork recalls its notes but cannot resume it.
- Only lessons influence later sessions, and a repository note can become one automatically after two other sessions demonstrate it, so check `/memory`.

**Next steps**

- [Run a research campaign and a blind arena](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-a-research-campaign-and-a-blind-arena.html)
- [Continuity guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/context-continuity.html)
- [PanHub](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panhub.html)
- [How memory works](https://pancode.dev/research/memory.html)

# Check a change against your repository

> Name the checks that matter, run them through verify, and see whether a passing result still matches the files you are reviewing.

A useful coding result includes more than "done." You need to know what changed, which checks ran, and whether those results still apply to the files you are reviewing. PanCode can use your repository's declared checks and a project quality policy to make those questions explicit.

**What this establishes**

Recorded verification is evidence about named checks and named inputs. It is not proof of correctness; your tests still need to cover the behavior that matters.

## Before you start

- A Git repository with a test or build check it already declares, such as a package script or a CI step.
- PanCode with a model that supports tool calling.
- Time to read the resolved command each check runs.

## Start with checks the project already owns

The verifier derives checks from supported build systems, project scripts, and CI definitions. When it cannot resolve a requested check, it should not substitute an arbitrary command and call it a pass.

**Ask PanCode**

> Run this project's test check through verify. Report its exit status, failures, and anything you could not check.

![Terminal turn on gpt-6-luna in projects/lab-tools: asked to use verify with check test in examples/temperature-calibration and tabulate the reference temperatures, Panos runs the test check (exit 0, 19 lines), reads calibration.test.mjs, reports 7 tests and 0 failures, and shows freezing point, boiling point and absolute zero in Celsius, Kelvin and Fahrenheit, noting that no files were edited.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-verify-table.webp)

*The declared test check through verify, exit 0, then the reference temperatures read from the test file.*

The same request in the temperature-calibration example, with the check's working directory named.

Read the resolved command and working directory in the tool activity. A recognized test runner runs without a card, and other commands may ask first. `verify` is subject to command admission: naming a check does not grant permission to run it, and a denied command is not a validation result.

When a command does ask, the terminal approval card names the tool and the exact command. Its **effect** row says in plain words what a recognized command changes, and warns when PanCode cannot classify the command at all.

![Terminal approval card for bash git push origin main, after the request Run git push origin main: it is marked runs a command at default autonomy, with effect Publishes to origin and undo not guaranteed, Enter to allow, Esc to deny and Alt+X to stop the turn, and a note that no answer in 4:59 denies the call.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-approval-effect.webp)

*An outward command such as git push comes to you; the effect row says what it would change.*

The [tools guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html) covers discovery and execution. The [temperature-calibration example](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html) follows a small numerical correction with recorded test results.

## Declare what particular changes require

A quality policy selects required checks by changed path. At the Git workspace root:

```yaml title=.pancode/quality.yaml
version: 1
rules:
  - id: source
    paths: ["src/**", "tests/**"]
    inputs: ["src/**", "tests/**", "package.json", "package-lock.json"]
    checks: [test]
    allowLimitations: false
```

### Name the changes a rule covers

`paths` selects the rule: here, any change under `src/` or `tests/`.

### List every input the result depends on

`inputs` feeds freshness. Include fixtures, configuration, helper files, and lockfiles; this example assumes the root package declares a `test` script and keeps npm's lockfile. A pnpm or Yarn project lists `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `yarn.lock` instead. `verify` runs a package script as `npm run <id>` either way.

### Name existing checks, not commands

`checks` refers to declared checks. A policy cannot insert an arbitrary shell command or bypass approvals.

### Decide whether limitations are acceptable

`allowLimitations: false` means a reported limitation does not satisfy the rule.

PanCode does not write this policy for you. Review it as a repository contract: a command that passes a narrow subset of tests should not satisfy a policy that requires the full declared test check.

## Inspect freshness after editing

**When a passing check still counts**

1. Declared check (Your project): A package script, build target, or CI definition the project already owns.
2. Recorded pass (Results): Stored with source, check-declaration, and policy fingerprints. Moves from the previous stage: verify runs it.
3. Stale (Assessment): The earlier pass no longer describes the files. Moves from the previous stage: an input changes.
4. Current (Assessment): A result for the work that exists now. Moves from the previous stage: verify runs again.

*A recorded result belongs to the inputs it ran against; an edit to those inputs makes it stale until the check runs again.*

PanCode compares source, check-declaration, and policy fingerprints. A passing check becomes stale after relevant inputs change, and a later failure supersedes an earlier pass of the same check.

This matters during an iterative fix. The agent might run a test, make another edit, and then summarize the earlier success. The current assessment should describe the work that exists now, not the best result observed along the way.

Required checks run through `verify` without argument or working-directory overrides. Declare subproject checks with the correct working directory in the supported catalog or a root script. The [quality-policy guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/quality-policy.html) explains check identity and freshness.

## Read the result where you work

On the desktop alpha, the Session column's **Artifacts** card lists outputs and session records, **Changes** lists the files a turn changed, and **Evidence** appears once a run has a record. In the terminal, `/view` opens artifacts and run records.

![Terminal /view with the checked test row selected under Diffs & checks: the preview shows check test, cwd examples/temperature-calibration, exit 0 with 19 lines of output, the npm test script running node --test calibration.test.mjs, and passing tests for freezing point, boiling point, absolute zero, round trips and non-numeric input; the list also holds transcript details, message delivery, accountability, prompt manifests and 14 safety audit rows.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-view-result.webp)

*/view: the recorded check, with its working directory, exit status and output.*

**What to look for**

The actual check, its result, and any missing evidence. A sealed run record is an inspectable account of the run, and `pancode telemetry verify` checks its journals. It is not a certificate that every scientific or operational requirement was met.

**Boundaries**

- Snapshots need Git and a workspace at the repository root. They cover tracked and nonignored untracked source within the documented bounds.
- They do not establish the state of external datasets, installed dependencies, running services, or other hidden inputs.
- A valid policy selects high rigor by default and asks to continue for outstanding checks when recovery is possible; normal rigor makes the assessment advisory. Neither grants extra execution authority.
- Numerical comparisons, integration tests, and human review may still be necessary.

**Next steps**

- [Coordinate the coding agents you already use](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/coordinate-your-coding-agents.html)
- [A numerical change, checked with PanCode](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/temperature-calibration.html)
- [Run a research campaign and a blind arena](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-a-research-campaign-and-a-blind-arena.html)
- [Quality policy guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/quality-policy.html)

# Add skills and plugins deliberately

> Preview a project skill or plugin, inspect its package pin, and load only what your task needs; installing is not a permission grant.

PanHub contains skills, agents, prompts, playbooks, and plugins. You can add a procedure to one project or install it for your user. Preview what will be written, inspect the resource, and load it when a task needs it.

**Version scope**

PanHub recipes and extensions have different roles, and installing either is not a grant of authority.

**From the catalog to one task**

1. Browse (/hub or Alt+L): Catalog content that ships with PanCode; nothing is installed yet.
2. Preview (Install review): Destination, dependencies, scope, and the package pin. Moves from the previous stage: --dry-run.
3. Pinned copy (Project or user scope): Drifted content is blocked from loading. Moves from the previous stage: install.
4. Loaded for a task (One conversation): Recipes load on demand. Moves from the previous stage: /skill.

*Installing a package makes it available; a task loads what it needs. Neither step grants extra authority.*

## Browse what ships with PanCode

Open `/hub` in the terminal or press Alt+L. On the desktop alpha, the PanHub page lists the catalog with an **Installed only** filter. In the terminal, **Browse** shows available content and **Installed** manages your copies.

PanHub in the terminal is one place. `/hub skills` opens it on one kind, as do `prompts`, `agents`, `playbooks`, `plugins` and `extensions`. `/hub install <ref>` and the other verbs of `pancode hub` open the review that command would apply. `/hub interop` inspects the coding agents on your machine.

Inside PanHub, `b` switches between Browse and Installed and `s` between user and project scope. `i`, `u` and `x` open the review for installing, updating or removing the selected package; nothing is written until you apply it. `r` refreshes.

![Terminal PanHub in Browse mode on Skills, filtered to tdd at user scope: the tdd skill v0.4.2 and coding-standards v0.4.4 are not installed, and the detail pane offers [i] review install and describes tdd as building a feature or fix test-first, red to green.](/assets/guides/tui-hub-skill-tdd.webp)

*PanHub in Browse mode, filtered to the bundled tdd skill.*

## Preview a small addition

### Preview the install

Start with a resource you can evaluate, such as the shipped test-driven-development skill:

```sh
pancode hub install skill:tdd --project --dry-run
```

The plain output names the planned step and its scope. Add `--json` to see the rest of the plan: the destination, the version it writes, the source with its sha256, and the dependencies.

![Terminal: pancode hub install skill:tdd --project --dry-run --json prints the install plan with the destination .pancode/plugins/tdd, version 0.4.2, the bundled source with its sha256, publisher pancode, tier core, valid content and empty lists of required, missing and inactive dependencies.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cli-hub-dry-run.webp)

*A dry run plans the install without writing anything; --json prints the full plan.*

### Install it for this project

```sh
pancode hub install skill:tdd --project
```

The first project install in a workspace is yours, so PanCode approves the project's packages for that workspace. After that, a changed project package set, including one that arrives with a clone or a pull, is listed but not loaded until you review it with `pancode config trust plugins` and approve the digest it prints.

### Load it for one concrete task

```text
/skill tdd Add coverage for this parser before changing its behavior.
```

![Terminal PanHub in Installed mode at project scope: a notice says PanHub actions now select project scope, the tabs count Skills 1, Agents 10 and Playbooks 4, and the list shows 1 entry, with the tdd skill heading at the bottom edge.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-hub-installed.webp)

*Installed at project scope: the skill added to this project.*

**What installing establishes**

The skill is available and pinned. Installing it does not establish that it writes the right tests; review its instructions, the resulting changes, and the recorded checks. The [PanHub guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panhub.html) covers the current controls.

## Choose project or user scope

Project packages take precedence over matching user packages, and a disabled project copy also suppresses the user copy. A project can therefore keep a resource unavailable instead of inheriting it from one developer's setup.

| Scope | Who it serves | What takes precedence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Project | Everyone working in this repository | A matching project package, even when disabled |
| User | You, across projects | Used when the project has no matching package |

Scope helps reproducibility: another person can see which procedures belong to the project. It is not a filesystem sandbox, and the project's normal execution and tool controls still apply.

## Use plugins for related resources

A PanHub plugin groups related skills, prompts, agents, playbooks, and supporting files. The catalog ships with PanCode, but its content is not installed automatically.

```sh
pancode hub list --kind plugin
pancode hub install plugin:hpc --dry-run
```

![Terminal output of pancode hub list --kind plugin: eight bundled plugins, autotldr, cite-nexus, hpc, life-science, literature, science-data, wtfp and zulipchat, each with its version, the state available, its publisher and license, and a one-line description.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cli-hub-list-plugin.webp)

*The bundled plugins, listed without installing them.*

Review the bundle before installing it, and add `--project` when it should belong to the workspace. Local bundles use the same review flow; the [plugin guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/plugins.html) covers structure and lifecycle.

Installation records a pin over the complete package tree, and drifted content is blocked from loading. Verifying a pin is not a way to approve arbitrary edits to an installed package; use the documented update and review workflow.

## Keep discovery separate from loading

A large PanHub collection should not mean every resource enters every model request. The coordinator starts with a smaller attached toolkit and discovers secondary capabilities when a task calls for them, and recipes load on demand.

Write clear resource descriptions and narrow procedures. A skill that explains one project's numerical-test conventions is easier to select and inspect than a bundle that promises to solve every task.

After changes made by another process, `/reload hub` refreshes recipes and `/skill off` clears an active skill's armed tool surface. Neither erases earlier instructions from the conversation, and disabling a resource does not stop a tool already running.

## Know when you need an extension

PanHub plugins provide portable recipes. [Extensions](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html) are code that adds runtime tools, hooks, or interface behavior through `pancode extensions`, and load only after you approve the capabilities they declare.

Adding tool schemas requires a new session; reloading recipes does not change them. Project extensions follow the same trust rule through `pancode config trust extensions`, and PanCode names any it ignored when a session starts.

**Boundaries**

- Choose the least extensive mechanism that supplies the task.
- Workspace trust decides whether project packages load. It does not review them for you.
- Review executable code before using it, and account for its commands and network access under your own machine's permissions.
- A bigger collection helps only when it serves a better-defined task.

**Next steps**

- [Your first session with PanCode](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/first-session.html)
- [PanHub guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panhub.html)
- [Plugin guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/plugins.html)
