Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html

# Work from a laptop with remote workers

> Coordinate workers on other machines over SSH from your laptop, once each node has the same PanCode version and the project at the same path.

Your conversation can stay on your laptop while a worker runs tools on another machine. Register an SSH node, install the exact PanCode build if needed, verify its project and model route, then choose where the first bounded task runs.

**Version scope**

Remote workers use your existing SSH access. They do not grant access to institutional systems or replace their scheduler and data rules.

## Before you start

- Noninteractive SSH access to a machine you may use for work.
- PanCode on the node at exactly your client's version. For an automatic install, the node needs Node.js 22.19 or newer and npm on its noninteractive SSH PATH.
- The project at the same absolute path on the client and node, using shared storage or matching clean Git checkouts.
- A model route the worker can reach from the node.

## Choose where each part runs

**One remote task**

1. Session (Your laptop): The conversation, your approvals, and the dispatch.
2. Worker (Fleet node): Runs at default authority in the same absolute project path. Moves from the previous stage: SSH dispatch.
3. Inference (The worker's route): A localhost address resolves on the node, not on your laptop. Moves from the previous stage: model requests.

*The conversation stays on your laptop, the worker runs its tools on the node, and the worker's model route resolves from the node.*

Worker placement and inference are separate. A local worker calling a remote model endpoint runs tools locally. An SSH worker runs tools on the selected node. A target URL containing `localhost` refers to the worker's machine.

Choose a node for the compiler, filesystem, data or capacity the task needs. Declared labels such as `gpu` help describe it, but they do not prove observed hardware or available memory. A remote worker using a cloud target can send model input to that provider under the existing information policy.

## Add one SSH node

From your project root, register an SSH alias, hostname or address:

```sh
pancode fleet nodes add build-node --host build-node --max-workers 1
pancode fleet nodes list
```

The implicit `local` node already exists. Adding a node keeps unpinned work local. The new node starts as **not checked**.

Use an existing SSH alias to select the user, port and identity. You can also pass `--user`, `--port` and `--identity-file` explicitly. `--labels cpu,build` adds operator declarations. Start with one slot until you know the node's workload and resource limits.

In the terminal, `/settings workers` opens the **Workers** area; choose **Add SSH node** under **Machines**. The guided flow asks for a name and host, then offers to test and record readiness or preview an install. Open a node row to see evidence and timestamps, test it, preview an install or remove its saved entry. A test started here always records its result.

![Terminal Settings scrolled down Workers: under Machines, node local is ready with 0/8 busy, Add SSH node is selected above Discover with Tailscale, workers at once is Automatic and endpoint copilot has slots 0/4, then fleet retries 2; the side panel says Add SSH node adds a remote worker node with guided SSH setup and project verification.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/tui-settings-fleet.webp)

*Settings: worker routing, machines, and limits under Workers.*

### Use a LAN endpoint or optional Tailscale discovery

If the client and node share a network, prefer a LAN endpoint you have verified with SSH. Otherwise, a reachable Tailscale address or MagicDNS name can use the same worker transport.

```sh
pancode fleet nodes discover
pancode fleet nodes add travel-node --host travel-node.example-tailnet.ts.net
```

Discovery is opt-in. It reads `tailscale status --json` when the CLI is installed and signed in, lists MagicDNS names and IP addresses, and leaves the selection to you. The TUI's **Discover with Tailscale** lets you pick an endpoint and name the node. A discovered peer has no proven SSH access, runtime or project readiness. You can add an SSH host directly without Tailscale.

The endpoint can matter substantially. In one measurement on this project's development network, a 4 MiB SSH transfer ran at about **173 MiB/s over LAN and 1.4 MiB/s over Tailscale**. SSH setup and existing connection multiplexing affect those numbers; measure your own route. PanCode uses the host you configure and does not automatically switch between addresses.

## Install the exact client build

If the node lacks a matching PanCode runtime, preview a user-level install:

```sh
pancode fleet nodes install build-node
```

Review the package size, digest and destination. Then execute it:

```sh
pancode fleet nodes install build-node --yes
```

PanCode packs the build the client actually runs, transfers it over SSH, checks its SHA-256 digest, and installs it under the node's `~/.local/share/pancode/workers/<digest>/`. The install uses the node's existing Node.js and npm, verifies the version and updates the saved worker entry. The installer does not require sudo or modify services or shell profiles. Optional SDK dependencies are omitted.

You can also manage PanCode yourself, for example with the standard installer on a cluster login node, whose private Node.js is not on `PATH`. The default invocation is `pancode worker`. A custom `--entry` that ends in ` worker` is checked through its base command's `--version`; any other entry needs an explicit `--version-command`. The version check is never skipped.

## Prepare and verify the project

Choose one supported arrangement:

| Arrangement | What PanCode verifies | Available work |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared storage at the same absolute path | A transient client-side file challenge is visible from the node. | Read-only and mutating workers use that storage. |
| Independent checkout at the same absolute path | Both trees are clean, have the same Git HEAD and matching root history. | Read-only work; mutations through an isolated task worktree and SSH commit return. |

PanCode does not clone an arbitrary repository, map different paths, install project dependencies or stage datasets. Prepare those yourself. For independent checkouts, update both to the same clean baseline before testing.

### Observe first

```sh
pancode fleet nodes test build-node
pancode doctor
```

These commands observe the node without creating directories there or granting new dispatch eligibility. A plain test can identify a clean matching checkout; recording also permits the transient client-side challenge that proves shared storage.

Model facts distinguish network reachability, access to the model listing, model presence and runtime support. Unknown remains unknown; a catalog listing is not a successful generation or proof of a resident model.

Each registered node adds a `fleet node <id>` row to `doctor` with its host, remote version and project check. The recording shows the report on a fresh install, before any node or model is added; each warning names the command that clears it.

![Terminal recording of pancode doctor --fix and then pancode doctor on a fresh install of PanCode 0.9.1: a WARN row says chat cannot run yet because no model target is configured and names pancode configure, an OK row shows the version, and a WARN row says the herdr pane host 0.9.5 is not installed and names pancode panes install. The second report ends with 2 rows need attention, 42 checks passed, 13 notes, and points to pancode doctor --verbose for every row.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cli-doctor.webp)

*Doctor on a fresh install lists only the rows that need attention, each with the command that clears it.*

[Recording (asciicast)](https://pancode.dev/assets/casts/cli-doctor.cast), 0:08. Transcript:

```text
PanCode doctor on a fresh install
Recorded with PanCode 0.9.1. Each section is the terminal screen at that moment.

== repaired

~ $ pancode doctor --fix
WARN chat                   cannot run yet: no model target is configured; run `pancode configure` to choose one
OK   PanCode version        0.9.1
WARN external tool herdr    pane host 0.9.5 is not installed; run `pancode panes install`
chat is not set up: run `pancode configure`
2 rows need attention, 44 checks passed, 13 notes; `pancode doctor --verbose` prints every row
~ $

== healthy

~ $ pancode doctor
WARN chat                   cannot run yet: no model target is configured; run `pancode configure` to choose one
OK   PanCode version        0.9.1
WARN external tool herdr    pane host 0.9.5 is not installed; run `pancode panes install`
chat is not set up: run `pancode configure`
2 rows need attention, 42 checks passed, 13 notes; `pancode doctor --verbose` prints every row
~ $
```

### Record readiness for this project

```sh
pancode fleet nodes test build-node --record
pancode fleet nodes list
```

A passing recorded check makes the node **ready for this project**. A failed recorded check revokes previous eligibility. Records expire after one day and bind the entire connection configuration and client version. Changing the host, user, port, key or worker entry requires another recorded check.

`doctor --fix` can record all node checks, along with its broader local repairs. Run plain `doctor` first to review those repairs. The node-specific test is the focused route when you only want to record one node.

### Refresh after an upgrade or endpoint change

Install the new exact client build when needed, then repeat the recorded test from the project root. A pinned task with an invalid or expired check fails with a reason; it does not silently run elsewhere.

## Choose the first worker

Keep the first task read-only and familiar. For example, ask PanCode:

```text
Use a read-only Scout to inspect the README and explain this project's test command.
Before dispatching, ask me once where to run it, offering local and suitable verified fleet nodes.
```

Scout is PanCode's built-in read-only agent for finding your way around a codebase. When a verified node suits substantial work and no preference or pin exists, PanCode asks once for the session. The choice remembers the exact node id for later unpinned work. The question does not replace the existing dispatch-plan approval. If you explicitly request `build-node`, it can be pinned directly.

A **Standing worker node preference**, under **Machines** in the Workers area of `/settings`, persists across sessions. Placement priority is an explicit task node, a profile pin, the session choice, the standing preference, then local. Headless runs never ask; configure a preference or explicit pin before running them.

Remote workers run under their own permits. The safety judge does not answer for a remote placement, so at `default` a remote worker's ordinary ask is denied. Worker slots limit concurrency; they do not create a scheduler allocation. On a university or laboratory cluster, use an approved execution environment.

## Return edits from an independent checkout

An editing dispatch to an independent node checkout must use `worktree: true`. Ask PanCode to use an isolated task worktree, name the files the worker may change and declare the host checks you want before application.

A matching branch and worktree are created on the node at the approved baseline. After the worker exits, PanCode commits the worker's edits there, fetches the branch through the existing SSH connection and checks the returned baseline and permitted paths.

The commit is imported into the owned local task worktree before the existing host verification and guarded apply flow. `apply: "preserve"` keeps the result on the local task branch, and `pancode fleet land` lists and lands such branches later.

Transfer, verification and application failures preserve the node branch for recovery. The run record names the node, branch, worktree and returned commit when available. Inspect preserved work before merging or deleting it. A successful guarded merge permits remote cleanup. The node's original checkout stays at its old baseline, so update it deliberately before the next dispatch that needs the new commit.

## Follow the result

Open **Workers** with Alt+W to see queued, active, failed and completed work with its actual node. In a session with panes, the same key opens a [live dashboard](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/panes-and-docks.html) beside the conversation. Review the worker result, receipt and project changes. The CLI's `pancode fleet status` and `pancode fleet view <runId>` expose durable results from another terminal.

SSH nodes and delegated peers are separate execution paths. A delegated peer is not an SSH machine whose resources or project access PanCode has verified.

## On a cluster

```sh
curl -fsSL https://pancode.dev/install.sh | sh
```

The installer needs no root, refuses to run under sudo, and downloads one bundle that carries its own Node.js. On x64 login nodes with glibc from 2.17 to 2.27 it selects the bundle built for them. Behind a proxy, export `https_proxy` first; the cluster guide lists the variables for mirrored and offline installs.

That Node.js is not added to `PATH`. A node installed this way already has PanCode, so skip `fleet nodes install` there and keep its version equal to your client's.

PanCode does not submit jobs for its own workers. The agent submits scheduler work through the scheduler clients in `bash`, under review; the [cluster guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html) covers it.

**Boundaries**

- SSH access, exact PanCode version and the same absolute project path remain prerequisites.
- Project dependencies and datasets need your own staging; there is no arbitrary repository sync or path mapping.
- Independent-checkout edits require isolated task worktrees and the existing verification and application gates.
- Institutional access rules and schedulers still govern where work may run.
- Worker slots limit concurrency. They are not an allocation, and a login node is not a compute node.
- A remote worker sandboxes its commands only when bubblewrap is present on that node.
- A worker that uses a cloud model sends its input to that provider from the node.
- A worker on a node opens that node's own project store. Admission refuses store tag grants to a remote node, so run store-writing tasks locally.

**Next steps**

- [Your first session with PanCode](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/first-session.html)
- [Fleet guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [Install on a cluster](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)
- [Install PanCode](https://pancode.dev/#start)
- [How scheduling works](https://pancode.dev/research/scheduling.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/write-an-extension-with-declared-capabilities.html

# Write an extension with declared capabilities

> Scaffold, test, and install a small extension, and see exactly what approving its capabilities covers.

A plugin carries content such as skills and prompts. An extension is code: it runs in its own process, declares everything it may do, and loads only after you approve those capabilities. This guide scaffolds a small extension, tests it, installs it, and shows what the approval covers.

**Version scope**

This guide describes runtime api 2. The runtime runs inside bubblewrap on Linux or Seatbelt on macOS when a backend exists. Check `/extensions` for the confinement your host gives it.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, on Linux or macOS for a confined runtime.
- Node.js and a little TypeScript. The scaffold includes an entrypoint and a test.

### Scaffold a package

```sh
pancode extensions init lint-status --template status
```

This creates the package under `.pancode/dev/extensions/lint-status/` and prints the next commands; `--dir` puts it elsewhere. The templates are `status`, `hook`, `panel`, `tool`, and `workspace`. Each gives you a manifest, a TypeScript entrypoint, and a test.

### Read the manifest

`pancode-extension.yaml` holds the declaration. PanCode discovers and validates it without importing or executing package code. The `runtime` block is the capability envelope, which is the part you consent to.

### Validate and test

```sh
pancode extensions validate .pancode/dev/extensions/lint-status
pancode extensions test .pancode/dev/extensions/lint-status
```

Tests can use the package's test host, which drives the same registration code the runtime uses, with in-memory state and a fake clock.

### Install and review

```sh
pancode extensions install .pancode/dev/extensions/lint-status
```

The install prints what the package would be allowed to do, then records the digest of that envelope. If the manifest changes between review and apply, the install refuses and asks for a fresh review.

### Use and manage it

```text
/extensions
/reload extensions
```

`/extensions` shows each package's state, generation, failures, commands, and confinement. `/reload extensions` loads a reviewed install into the running session. From the shell, use `pancode extensions list`, `disable`, `enable`, and `remove`.

![Terminal output: extensions init creates lint-status from the status template under .pancode/dev/extensions; validate reports it valid with one warning that the licence is missing, then prints its capability envelope with the status command, session state, exec and net false, its SHA-256 and a passed registration check; extensions test reports one test passed and none failed.](https://pancode.dev/assets/guides/cli-extension-validate.webp)

*Scaffold, validate and test an extension; validate prints the capability envelope you consent to.*

**What you should see**

The extension listed with its confinement, and its status in the session. This shows it loaded under the approved envelope. It does not make the code safe, so review what you install as you would any dependency.

## Choose plugin or extension

| You want to | Use |
| --- | --- |
| Share skills, prompts, agents, or playbooks | A plugin |
| Add a hook on a tool call, a runtime tool, a panel, or a timer | An extension |
| Add both, under one name | A plugin paired with an extension |

A project's own extensions also need `pancode config trust extensions`. To try ideas without installing, a folder under `.pancode/dev/extensions/<id>/` is a dev extension for the terminal session, in a workspace whose project extensions you trust.

**Boundaries**

- Without a sandbox backend, an extension runtime runs with your permissions.
- Dev extensions load in terminal sessions. The desktop PanHub page shows the terminal command for extension lifecycle actions.
- Reinstalling changed content needs a fresh approval.

**Next steps**

- [Add skills and plugins deliberately](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/add-skills-and-plugins-deliberately.html)
- [Install plugins](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/plugins.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/diffusion-models.html

# Diffusion models in the terminal

> Connect Inception's Mercury models for chat and workers, and watch an answer refine as a whole instead of arriving token by token.

Most language models write an answer one token at a time. A diffusion language model starts from a rough version of the whole answer and refines it in a few passes. PanCode can use Inception's Mercury models this way, for chat and for workers, with tool calling.

**Version scope**

The frame-by-frame display exists only in the terminal, and diffusion models are less tested on long agentic work than the models most people use.

## Before you start

- An Inception account and API key, exported as `INCEPTION_API_KEY`.
- Permission to send this project's code to that provider.
- PanCode in the terminal, if you want to watch the answer refine.

## Connect Mercury

Run guided setup:

```sh
pancode configure
```

On a first run, choose **Guided setup**. If PanCode lists routes it found, pick **Set up something else**. Choose **An API key** and type `$INCEPTION_API_KEY`; setup reads the provider from the variable name, picks `mercury-3`, and sends one short test message before saving. When you add Mercury to an existing setup instead, choose **A provider account or API**, then Inception.

Or add the target directly:

```sh
pancode configure --id mercury --runtime inception --model mercury-3 --api-key-env INCEPTION_API_KEY
```

The runtime lists `mercury-3`, its default, `mercury-2.5`, `mercury-2`, and `mercury-edit-2`. Setup checks the model you name against the provider's model list and refuses one that is not on it unless you pass `--force`. `mercury-decide` answers typed decisions for System One only and cannot be a chat model.

## What you see

In the terminal, each update from the model carries the whole answer so far. PanCode replaces the visible text on every frame instead of appending to it, and dims the part that is still changing. There is no progress gauge.

Tool calls, permission cards, `/view`, and run records work as they do with any chat model. Headless runs, workers, the desktop app, and editors connected over ACP receive an ordinary stream of text.

## Where it fits

A quick whole-answer model suits short, bounded requests: a commit message, an explanation of one function, a first draft to compare. `/draft` uses the active chat model, so with Mercury active it returns several candidates quickly. You can also keep another model for conversation and route selected workers to the Mercury target.

Try it on a task you can check before trusting it with a long one. This page makes no speed or quality claim; measure both on your own repository.

**Boundaries**

- Mercury runs without a thinking level. For `mercury-2.5`, `mercury-2` and `mercury-edit-2`, PanCode pins the provider's fastest reasoning setting, because their default spends the output budget on hidden reasoning and can return an empty answer. `mercury-3` needs no pin.
- A provider content-filter refusal is shown as a refusal and does not count as a failed connection, so filtered workers do not take the target out of rotation.
- Inception is a cloud provider. Input you send leaves your machine, and usage is billed by Inception.

**Next steps**

- [Choose a model for your project](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)
- [Connection guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Bring a fast decision model with System One](https://pancode.dev/research/system-one-decisions.html)
- [How the drivers work](https://pancode.dev/research/drivers.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/panes-and-docks.html

# Panes and docks: files, workers, and music

> Show and hide a file browser, a live worker dashboard, and a focus radio beside the terminal conversation with one key each.

PanCode in the terminal can open panes of its own beside the conversation: a file browser below, a live view of workers on the right, and a small radio. Each is a dock. One key shows or hides it, and hiding keeps it running. Herdr, a terminal multiplexer, hosts the panes.

**Version scope**

Bare `pancode` in an interactive terminal opens its own private pane host, with no question to answer. The files and music docks are off until you enable them. Keys, commands, and settings may change. The pane host has builds for Linux, macOS, and Windows x64; elsewhere PanCode runs in the plain terminal.

## Before you start

- The pane host. The installer provisions it and a launch after an upgrade installs the new pin. After an npm or bun install, or when the installer could not fetch it, run `pancode panes install`; until then PanCode starts in the plain terminal and says so once.
- Yazi for the files dock: `pancode tools install yazi`.
- cliamp for music: `pancode tools install cliamp`.

## Turn panes on

Panes are on whenever the terminal allows them. Start PanCode in your project:

```sh
pancode
```

It opens its own pane host and hands the terminal back when you quit. The host is PanCode's own pinned copy of Herdr; a Herdr of yours on `PATH`, with its config and sessions, is never used or touched.

Inside your own Herdr session, bare `pancode` opens its host nested in that pane; `pancode --with-panes` joins your session as a guest instead. A session started inside tmux, Zellij, or screen stays in the plain terminal with no docks: `/files` becomes a one-time full-screen picker and Alt+W opens the worker list inside PanCode.

## Three docks, one habit

| Dock | Key | Where it opens | Also enable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workers | Alt+W | Right of the conversation | Nothing |
| Files | Alt+E | Below | `interface.panes.files.enabled` |
| Music | Alt+A | A thin strip below | `integrations.music.enabled` |

Press the key once to show a dock and again to hide it. A hidden dock moves to a parked tab and keeps its state: the file browser stays in its directory and the radio keeps playing. Press the key twice quickly to close the dock and end its program. Quitting PanCode closes all of them.

Drag a divider to resize a dock; the size is kept when you hide and show it. A dock never takes more than half the window, and one that cannot fit says how much room it needs. `/panes` prints which docks are visible, hidden, or closed. The same keys are under Ctrl+G, then `w`, `e`, or `a`.

## Pick files with Yazi

`/files` or Alt+E opens Yazi and moves the keyboard into it. Select files and press Ctrl+Y. PanCode appends them to your draft as `@path` references and returns you to the composer without sending anything. One pick carries up to 32 paths.

Yazi runs on a profile and theme that PanCode generates, so your own Yazi configuration is untouched. Set `interface.panes.files.profile: user` to use yours instead. `/files hide` and `/files close` do what the key does.

## Watch workers live

Alt+W opens a dashboard with one card per worker in this session: the agent and task, its state, the model, tool calls against its budget, tokens, cost when it is known, and what the worker is doing now. Running workers come first.

Move with the arrow keys and press Enter to fill the dock with one worker's live stream; Escape returns to the cards. `q` hides the dock. The dashboard only reads recorded run files, so it cannot change a run, and it does not open by itself when a worker starts.

## Play focus radio

`/music` or Alt+A opens cliamp in a strip tall enough for its spectrum bars and starts a lo-fi stream.

```text
/music pause
/music next
/music station Groove Salad
/music off
```

`next` steps through six built-in focus stations. `station` takes a stream URL or a station name; a name that is not built in is looked up in the public Radio Browser directory. PanCode keeps its player configuration separate from your own cliamp setup.

The model cannot touch the player unless you also set `integrations.music.agentControl: true` and restart. Then a `music` tool can play, pause, skip, and stop, but not choose stations. When to use it is up to your project instructions.

**Boundaries**

- As a guest in your own Herdr, docks need a recent protocol; an older Herdr can open panes but cannot hide them.
- Station lookup by name and the streams themselves use the network.
- `/panes peer <agent> [brief]` opens another coding agent in a pane for you to work in. It is a handoff with no run record.

**Next steps**

- [Files and terminal panes guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html)
- [Coordinate the coding agents you already use](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/coordinate-your-coding-agents.html)
- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/information-flow-rules.html

# Keep named files with the models you chose

> Declare which paths and tool results may reach which model targets, approve the policy, and see a request to any other destination refused.

Some files should reach only a model you chose. An information-flow rule names a source, such as everything under `secrets/`, and the destinations its content may go to. Once a session has read that source, PanCode refuses to send the conversation to any other model, in every permission mode.

**Advanced, described for 0.9.0**

Information flow does nothing until a project declares source rules and you approve them. The policy format is new and may change. It tracks what a session has read; it is not an operating-system sandbox.

## Before you start

- A project where specific paths or tool results must stay with specific models.
- A configured target for each allowed model, usually a local or institutional one.
- A restart after you approve the policy.

## Declare a source and where it may go

This policy keeps anything read under `secrets/` on one local model target:

```yaml title=.pancode/safety.yaml
version: 1
informationFlow:
  targets:
    local:
      runtime: llamacpp
      endpoint: http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1
  recipients:
    private-models: ["target:local"]
  sources:
    - id: secrets-local
      paths: [secrets/]
      recipients: ["group:private-models"]
```

A target is pinned by runtime and endpoint, so pointing the same name at another URL does not keep the approval. A source can also be a tool or an MCP server, and `recipients: []` means the content may go nowhere.

## Review and approve

### Show what would be approved

```sh
pancode config trust safety
```

This prints the policy files, their digest, and the exact approval command. It changes nothing.

### Approve those exact bytes

```sh
pancode config trust safety --hash <reviewed-sha256>
```

Approval belongs to this workspace and this content. Restart PanCode to load it.

An edit you have not approved can only restrict more: a new, unapproved rule labels content and allows no destination.

## What happens in a session

Reading `secrets/notes.txt` labels the session with `secrets-local`. Requests to the pinned `local` target continue. Switch to a cloud model and the next request is refused before it is sent, with the rule, the source, and the allowed destinations named.

The label follows the session through summaries, compaction, resume, branches, and worker results. Changing the model, the policy, or the permission mode does not clear it. To work without it, start a new session.

**Workers and other agents**

Native workers check each model request. Coding agents that make their own model calls, such as Claude Code or Codex, are refused at launch when any rule does not allow their target, and ACP agents and pane peers are refused.

**Boundaries**

- Labels apply to the whole session, not to individual passages.
- Shell commands are observed conservatively and incompletely. A read hidden in a script, a variable, or a `cd` is not reliably seen.
- A rule controls where content may go. Whether a file may be read at all is still decided by permissions.
- At `yolo`, `web_fetch`, `web_read` and MCP tool calls are not refused on a label. Model requests are still checked.
- Writes carry no label. A file a restricted session writes can later be read and sent anywhere.

**Next steps**

- [Tools and permissions](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html)
- [Information flow guide in the repository](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/0241470c83204f6dfb03baa5771a8d125fda3014/docs/guide/information-flow.md)
- [Choose a model for your project](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)
- [How protection works](https://pancode.dev/research/protection.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/semantic-context-and-recordings.html

# Search by meaning and record worker runs

> Index code, memory, and experiment folders with a local embedding model, and attach a redacted terminal recording to a worker's evidence.

PanCode can keep a local index of your project that you search by meaning instead of exact words. It covers code maps, wiki pages, approved memory, evidence bundles, recorded worker output, and folders of experiment data you register. PanCode can also record what a dispatched worker displayed, as a redacted terminal cast in that run's evidence. Both start off.

**Beta, described for 0.9.0**

Semantic context and worker recording are off by default. Commands, supported formats, and the index layout may change between releases. Ordinary startup scans and embeds nothing until you configure the feature.

## Before you start

- A PanCode target that serves the EmbeddingGemma 2 Q8 model through a llama.cpp embedding server or a LiteLLM proxy you already run. PanCode does not start one.
- The SHA-256 of the model file, and of its multimodal projector if you want images or audio.
- `ffmpeg` on `PATH` if you want still frames sampled from GIF or video files.

## Build an index

### Pin the model and check the route

```sh
pancode semantic configure \
  --target local-embed --model embeddinggemma-2-q8 \
  --asset-identity sha256:<model-sha256> \
  --projector-identity sha256:<projector-sha256> \
  --modality text --modality image --modality audio \
  --qualify
```

Use your own target and model names. `--qualify` sends fixed canary requests for each modality you chose and pins the text canary in the profile. It proves that the route accepts those requests and returns vectors of the expected shape. It does not measure retrieval quality, and it cannot read the model file's actual hash.

### Register a folder

```sh
pancode semantic inbox preview ./experiment-data
pancode semantic inbox add ./experiment-data --id experiments
```

Preview lists file types and the estimated work before anything is saved. PanCode honors ignore files, refuses symlinks and credential-shaped files, and applies the project's read policy. It never indexes a folder you did not register. Add `--scope user` to register an inbox for every project.

### Refresh and search

```sh
pancode semantic refresh
pancode semantic status
pancode semantic search "Which run produced the delayed oscillation?" --limit 5
```

`refresh` is an explicit, bounded job. An interrupted or partly failed refresh keeps the last complete generation and reports what is still pending. An unchanged refresh reuses its vectors.

## Read a result

Each hit names the exact path and, where it applies, the line, page, notebook cell, video frame, or audio offset. It carries a short excerpt and the generation it came from, and evidence and recording hits carry an evidence id. Search narrows where to look. PanCode still reads the original file, code, or receipt before it makes a claim.

In a session, the agent searches through its `context` tool with bounded filters for source kind, run, dates, media type, and count. A question that mixes a run manifest, a code symbol, and a plot works better as one search per source. If the embedding route is down, search falls back to lexical candidates from the last complete generation.

| Source | Indexed in this beta |
| --- | --- |
| Code and text | Source files, typed code map records, and wiki pages |
| Documents | PDF pages with extractable text, notebook sources and outputs |
| Images | PNG, JPEG, and WebP |
| Audio | Bounded mono 16 kHz WAV |
| Video | Timestamped still frames sampled from GIF, MP4, WebM, and MOV |
| Not supported | Raw video, reasoning across frames, scanned PDF OCR, and other audio formats |

## Keep the index current

Add `--background` to `semantic configure` to refresh at session start and after code map changes. It is off by default, yields to foreground inference, and checkpoints when interrupted. On a shared route that holds one model at a time, weigh the chat load before you turn it on.

The index lives in your cache directory, with one namespace per project and embedding profile. Code, memory, and evidence stay where they are, so deleting the cache removes only derived data.

A changed serving build, model file, projector, or preprocessing recipe needs a new qualification and gets its own namespace. `pancode semantic reembed --profile embeddinggemma-2-q8-768 --from <old-profile-identity>` embeds the old records again under the new profile. Old vectors are never copied into it.

## Record a worker run

```sh
pancode run --agent scout --record "Check the experiment on the worker node"
```

In a session, the dispatch tool accepts `record: true` for a call or a single task, including work placed on an SSH node. PanCode writes a bounded display stream beside the worker's own protocol. It copies a redacted `.cast` into the run's evidence bundle with the run, node, timestamps, byte count, and SHA-256.

A capture error or a partial run is labeled incomplete. The sealed run record, not the recording, decides whether the worker succeeded.

Capture needs no extra program. For playback, `pancode tools install asciinema` installs a checksum-pinned asciinema. `pancode fleet nodes tools install <node> asciinema` previews the same user-level install on a worker node, and `--yes` performs it without sudo. asciinema is GPL-3.0-or-later, and its license and exact source ship with the pinned install.

**Boundaries**

- Similarity finds candidates. It is not proof of a scientific result or of a worker's success, and run records and memory approval rules stay authoritative.
- Matching model and projector hashes do not make vectors compatible across serving stacks. Keep each stack's index separate.
- An extension can request embeddings only when its manifest declares the service and you approve it, and it never receives the target's credentials.
- A recording is bounded, timed terminal output. It is not a video of the screen.

**Next steps**

- [Semantic context beta guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/semantic-context.html)
- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)
- [Connect a model](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-on-a-local-model.html

# Run PanCode on a local model

> Connect a local server with no account or key, check what PanCode learned about it, and see what else to check if code must stay on your machine.

You can run PanCode with a model on your own machine, with no account and no API key. This guide connects a local server, checks what PanCode learned about it, and shows what else to look at if your code must not leave the machine.

**Version scope**

Supported local servers include Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, vLLM, SGLang, and Lemonade. Whether a given model handles long agentic work is yours to test, and setup does not test it for you.

## Before you start

- A local server running, with a model that supports tool calling loaded.
- PanCode installed, and a repository you know.

## Connect it

```sh
cd /path/to/your/project
pancode configure
```

Choose **Guided setup**. A server already running on a default local port is listed first, under **PanCode found a way to reach a model**. Otherwise choose **A model server or gateway** and enter its address, or choose **Connect by endpoint** when you already know the URL. LM Studio commonly serves at `http://localhost:1234`, and Ollama at `http://localhost:11434`.

Setup may pick the model for you: a detected server comes with the first model it lists. Use `/model` afterwards to choose one that supports tool calling. Setup checks that the server is reachable, reads its model list, and sends one short test request before saving. It does not test tool calling, so the first real test comes next.

## Check what PanCode learned

```sh
pancode targets --json
pancode doctor
```

In `targets --json`, `contextWindowProvenance` says where the window figure came from, such as a value the server reported or one you configured. A local server has no fallback number. If a figure looks wrong, set `targets[].capabilities.contextWindow`, or `ollama.numCtx` for Ollama, which is sent with every request.

## Ask something you can check

**Example**

> Read the build configuration and name the command that runs the tests. Run it and report the result. Do not edit files.

**What you should see**

Tool calls that really run, followed by an answer that matches your project. If the model writes out a command as text and never calls a tool, this model or server is not handling tool calls correctly, so try another before going further.

## Keep the work on your machine

A local chat route does not by itself make the whole session local.

- Memory uses the chat route when no memory connection is set, so it stays local unless you name another. Compaction does the same unless `context.compaction.model` names another.
- System One is off by default. A hosted route would send data out.
- Web tools, MCP servers, plugins, peers, and shell commands can still make network requests.

To enforce a boundary for named files, use [information-flow rules](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/information-flow-rules.html).

**Boundaries**

- Local inference costs no provider fee, though hardware and power still cost money. `pancode usage report` shows these calls as free.
- Local servers vary in how they handle tool calls, cache, and long context. Expect to try more than one model.
- Automatic discovery at startup checks default ports only, takes the first model listed, and uses a server it finds only after you say yes. Set a route with `pancode configure` to choose one.

**Next steps**

- [Choose a model for your project](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html)
- [Connection guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [When do several agents or small models pay off?](https://pancode.dev/research/fleets-and-local-models.html)
- [How the drivers work](https://pancode.dev/research/drivers.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/pre-register-a-benchmark.html

# Pre-register a benchmark before you measure

> Use the experiment-protocol skill to lock thresholds, tolerances, and verdict conditions into a contract you commit before any result exists.

A benchmark is easy to fool once you have seen the result. The `experiment-protocol` skill has PanCode write down the outcome, thresholds, tolerances, and verdict conditions before any measurement, and then keep to them. Use it for a performance study, a numerical comparison, a parameter sweep, or a solver comparison.

**Version scope**

This guide describes skill version 0.3.3. To find out why one output is wrong, use `scientific-debugging` instead, since that is a diagnosis and not an experiment.

## Before you start

- A repository with the code to measure and input data you can checksum.
- A chat route, in the terminal or a headless run.
- An environment you can pin: compiler, flags, package versions, and node class.

## Install the skill

```sh
pancode hub install skill:experiment-protocol --project --dry-run
pancode hub install skill:experiment-protocol --project
```

Read the dry run first. It shows the destination and the pin.

## Ask for a pre-registration

**Example**

> /skill experiment-protocol Compare the new solver against the current one on data/mesh-256.h5 for step time and accuracy. Stop after you write the contract so I can review it.

The contract goes in `.pancode/validation.yaml`, or `VALIDATION.md` at the repository root. A YAML contract that parses raises the repository's rigor to high, so a claim that the work is done must carry validation evidence or state a limitation. `VALIDATION.md` is read as advice and does not raise rigor.

## Review the contract

This is the step that matters, and it is yours. Check that the contract has each of these:

- **Outcome**: one sentence, with a number.
- **Thresholds**: a minimum below which the result is refuted, a target, and a stretch.
- **Tolerances**: absolute or relative, stated per metric. A bare `1e-6` is not a tolerance.
- **Environment pin**: compiler and flags, versions, node class, and scheduler context.
- **Input identity**: paths with checksums.
- **Verdict conditions**: what makes the result confirmed, refuted, or inconclusive.

Commit it before measuring anything, so the history shows it came first. In a headless run nobody can answer questions, so the skill records unstated details as explicit assumptions. Read those assumptions closely.

## Run it

The skill captures a baseline under the pinned environment, then changes one independent variable per run, and records job ids and node lists where a scheduler is involved. It compares results against the registered thresholds only.

**What you should see**

A verdict of confirmed, refuted, or inconclusive against the numbers you committed, with any deviation logged next to the result. Rejected approaches go in a dead-ends ledger. A refuted result plus a ledger entry is a successful experiment.

## Let a research campaign search under the contract

The contract's validators are prose until the project declares matching checks. Write them as checks in `.pancode/verifiers.yaml`, here a `bench` check whose command prints `{"step_ms": ...}` and an `accuracy` check of kind `numeric-compare` with the registered tolerance, and commit the file.

A `research` campaign can then search for improvements without moving the goalposts:

```sh
pancode research start --check bench --metric step_ms --direction min \
  --gate accuracy --max-iterations 5 --scope "src/solver/**" \
  --goal "reduce step time without changing any answer beyond the registered tolerance"
```

It first measures the base against itself and stops if that alone looks like a change, unless you pass `--allow-noisy`.

A candidate is kept only when the median improves by at least 5% (the default) with a 95% interval that excludes zero, and when every `--gate` check passes. A candidate that edits the check file or any file a check names is discarded unmeasured, so the thresholds you committed stay the ones that judge it.

**Boundaries**

- Watch for a threshold or tolerance edited after results appeared. The skill treats that as a red flag, and `git log` on the contract shows it.
- A single run on a shared machine does not establish a claim. Size repetitions to the noise.
- Findings outside the registered outcome are exploratory and need their own pre-registration.
- The skill checks process. Whether the tolerance is scientifically right is a judgment for someone who knows the field.

**Next steps**

- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)
- [Run a research campaign and a blind arena](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-a-research-campaign-and-a-blind-arena.html)
- [Check a change against your repository](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Research campaigns and arena](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html)
- [What would make a scientist trust an agent's change?](https://pancode.dev/research/scientific-and-hpc-workflows.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/keep-results-in-the-project-store.html

# Keep results outside the tree with the project store

> Store a result with a note, check it for drift, read it from a script, and let a worker write into one granted tag.

Results, datasets and checkpoints do not belong in Git, but scattering them across scratch folders loses track of where each came from. The project store keeps them outside the working tree, in named tags, with a record of what produced each file and whether it has changed since. You, the agent and its workers all see the same store.

**Version scope**

This tutorial describes the store's local backend. The output below is from the `pancode store` command run on Linux, where the store has been exercised.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, and a project in a Git repository.
- A result file to keep, here `run-042.csv`.

## Put a result in the store

From the project folder:

```sh
pancode store put results run-042.csv --note "baseline, 64 ranks"
```

**What you should see**

`stored results:run-042.csv (8 B) from /home/alice/proj/run-042.csv`. The `results` tag did not exist, so the put created it.

A tag is a named container and a blob is a file in it; `results:run-042.csv` names one blob. List what you have with `pancode store tags` and `pancode store ls results`. `pancode store where` prints the folder the store lives in, under PanCode's data directory, so it does not count against the repository and every checkout and task worktree of the project shares it.

## Check whether it changed

```sh
pancode store stat results:run-042.csv
```

**What you should see**

A `ref`, `path`, `bytes` and `sha256` line, and `drift     none`. Drift is `none` while the blob matches its record, `changed` when its bytes no longer match, `missing` when it is gone, and `unrecorded` when there is no record for it.

To check a whole tag at once, run `pancode store verify results`. It prints a count for each state, names any blob that is not `ok`, and exits 1 unless every blob is `ok`, so a job script can stop on it.

`pancode store history results:run-042.csv` lists every put, note and removal, with its hash, its source file and its note. The history is write-once.

## Read it from a script

`store get` prints the path of a read-only copy, so a script reads the stored bytes without any chance of changing them:

```sh
python3 analyze.py "$(pancode store get results:run-042.csv)"
```

Use `--to <path>` to copy the blob somewhere instead. In a session, ask for the same thing in words:

**Example**

> Plot the y column of results:run-042.csv against x and save the figure as fig-042.png. Put the figure in the results tag with a note naming the input.

The agent reaches the store through its `store` tool, and reading needs no approval.

When the figure comes from a script the agent ran with its `run_script` tool, the stored record keeps the script's hash and its declared inputs, and an input that came from the store is named by its `<tag>:<blob>`. Notes can be added later, and `derived_from` records which blobs a result was made from.

## Let a worker write results

A dispatched worker reads the store but does not write it unless its dispatch grants it tags. Ask for the grant by name:

**Example**

> Hand this to a researcher worker: rerun the analysis for runs 043 to 045 and put each figure in the results tag. Grant it the results tag only.

The tag must exist before the dispatch. The worker may then `put` and `note` into `results` and nowhere else in the store. A read-only run, an ACP agent or a worker on a remote node cannot be granted tags.

## Replace and remove with care

The store keeps no earlier versions of a blob, and no workspace snapshot covers it.

When the agent would replace a blob or remove one, it asks you first and names the blob. From the shell, `pancode store put` over an existing blob replaces it and says `replaced`. `pancode store rm results:run-042.csv` only prints what it would delete; add `--yes` to delete it. The blob's records remain.

**Boundaries**

- The store lives on one host. A worker on another node through an SSH fleet sees that node's own store.
- `put` copies bytes. A large dataset takes its size again in the store.
- Above 64 MiB the record omits the hash; `pancode store verify results --hash-large` hashes such blobs and records the digest as a note.
- `pancode reset --data`, `reset --all`, and `uninstall` without `--keep-data` delete the store, and nothing recovers it.

**Next steps**

- [Keep results in the store](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panstore.html)
- [The store tool and its limits](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/tool-usage.html)
- [Workers and fleets](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [Install on a cluster](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/set-up-a-lab-from-one-setup-file.html

# Set up a lab from one setup file

> Write one YAML file that connects every lab member to your model gateway, check what it may carry, and test the route.

A lab or site that runs its own model gateway can connect every member's PanCode with one small YAML file. You publish it once; each member imports it, sees where their prompts will go, and confirms. The file can name models and where to find a key, but it can never carry a key or change what PanCode is allowed to do.

**Version scope**

The output below is from `pancode configure --import` run against a fresh PanCode home.

## Before you start

- An OpenAI-compatible model gateway your members can reach, here `https://llm.lab.example.org/v1`.
- A way to give each member a key, which they keep in an environment variable.
- An `https` address or a shared path where you can publish the file.

## Write the setup file

```yaml title=lab-pancode.yaml
notes: "Lab gateway. Ask #research-computing for a key; export it as LAB_API_KEY."
targets:
  - id: lab
    runtime: openai-compat
    url: https://llm.lab.example.org/v1
    defaultModel: gpt-oss-120b
    capabilities: { contextWindow: 131072 }
    auth: { apiKeyEnvVar: LAB_API_KEY }
chat: { target: lab }
fleet: { target: lab, model: gpt-oss-120b }
```

`targets` lists the model endpoints. `chat` and `fleet` choose which target the main session and its workers use. `notes` is shown to the member before they confirm, so use it to say how to get a key.

## Know what the file may carry

A setup file may hold only `targets`, `chat`, `fleet` and `notes`. A target may hold only `id`, `runtime`, `url`, `defaultModel`, `wireModels`, `capabilities`, `pricing` and `auth`, and `auth` only names an environment variable (`apiKeyEnvVar`) or an OAuth profile. Anything else refuses the whole file. A literal key is the usual mistake:

```yaml title=bad.yaml
targets:
  - id: lab2
    runtime: openai-compat
    url: https://x/v1
    auth: { apiKey: sk-123 }
```

**What you should see**

`error: setup file refused; nothing changed:` followed by `targets[0].auth.apiKey is not allowed in a setup file`, and exit code 1.

The same rule refuses request headers and safety settings, so a member never has to read a setup file for hidden permissions.

## Try it on your own account first

```sh
pancode configure --import lab-pancode.yaml
```

In a terminal, the command prints what the file will change and asks `Apply these changes? [y/N]`. Answer `n` and nothing changes. `--yes` applies without asking. With `--yes`, and no `LAB_API_KEY` exported yet, the import printed:

**What you should see**

```text
Setup file lab-pancode.yaml will:
Lab gateway. Ask #research-computing for a key; export it as LAB_API_KEY.

  add target lab (openai-compat)
    prompts go to https://llm.lab.example.org/v1
    model gpt-oss-120b; key from $LAB_API_KEY
  chat uses lab / gpt-oss-120b
  fleet uses lab / gpt-oss-120b
Imported 1 target.
  lab reads its key from LAB_API_KEY, which is not set in this shell.
```

After `Imported`, each target gets one line: `lab: ready`, or what is still missing, as here.

A plain `http` address to anything other than this machine or a private network address adds a warning that prompts and keys cross the network unencrypted.

Importing saves the settings without sending a request to the model. Check the route yourself:

```sh
export LAB_API_KEY=...
pancode doctor
pancode targets --probe --target lab
```

The `chat` row of `doctor` should end in `endpoint reachable`, and the probe's `health` column should not read `down`.

## Publish it

Put the file at an `https` address or a path members can read. A fetched file must be `https` all the way, a redirect to anything else is refused, and the file may be at most 64 KiB.

## What a member sees

A member who has never run PanCode runs `pancode`. At **What do you have?** they choose **A setup file from my lab or team**, type the address at **Where is the setup file?**, and see the same preview under **This setup file will:** with **Apply** and **Back**. A member who already uses PanCode runs:

```sh
pancode configure --import https://lab.example.org/pancode/setup.yaml
```

Only the `lab` target and the chat and fleet routes change. Their other targets, project settings and stored keys stay as they were.

Importing the same file again prints `Setup file already imported; nothing changed (lab-pancode.yaml).` with the status line, so it is safe to put in a login script with `--yes`. Without a terminal and without `--yes`, the command prints the preview and exits 2 without saving.

## Change the file later

If you change the settings of a target a member already has, their import is refused with `lab already saved with different settings; nothing changed.` and the command to rerun with `--replace`. Tell members when you change it. A new target id imports without `--replace`.

**Boundaries**

- Importing does not test the model. Members should run `pancode doctor` after setting their key.
- The file cannot hand out keys. Each member still gets a key and exports it in their shell.
- A member can change their route afterwards with `/model` or `pancode configure`; the file is not enforced.

**Next steps**

- [Connect PanCode on an HPC login node](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)
- [Setup files and model targets](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Run on a local model](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-on-a-local-model.html)
- [How the drivers work](https://pancode.dev/research/drivers.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/share-a-folder-with-a-teammate-or-a-second-terminal.html

# Share a folder with a teammate or a second terminal

> Run two sessions in one project, keep each person's state private, and commit project settings that can only make PanCode stricter.

Two people can work in one project folder with PanCode, and so can you in two terminals. What they share is the folder: its files and the project settings committed under `.pancode/`. Each session, its transcript, its credentials and its approvals stay with the person who started it, and the project settings can make PanCode stricter for everyone but never looser.

**Version scope**

The output below is from PanCode run against a fresh PanCode home and a new Git repository; paths are shortened to the default layout.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed for each person, in their own account.
- A project folder each of you can open: a shared filesystem, or a clone of the same repository.

## Open a second terminal

Run `pancode` in the folder from a second terminal while the first is still open. The second launch never joins the first one's session. It prints:

```text
PanCode: this folder already has a PanCode in another terminal; this one has its own panes.
```

It then starts its own private pane host, with its own session and its own docks. A folder can have up to four pane hosts at once. A fifth terminal runs without panes, still with its own session, until one of the four exits.

The two sessions see each other's work only as changed files on disk. Give each one a different part of the tree, and read `git diff` before you commit what either produced.

## Keep your state yours

Each person's sessions, transcripts and approvals live in their own PanCode home, never in the project. `pancode paths` shows where:

```text
config   /home/you/.config/pancode
data     /home/you/.local/share/pancode
state    /home/you/.local/state/pancode
cache    /home/you/.cache/pancode
project  /home/you/lab-model
```

These directories are created owner-only (`0700`), and session transcripts are under `state/sessions`. On a shared machine, keep `PANCODE_HOME` and the state directory out of shared project space. If a state directory is open to other users, `pancode doctor` says so:

```text
WARN state dir mode         /home/you/.local/state/pancode is 755: group or other users can enter it and read session transcripts (run `pancode doctor --fix`, or `chmod 700` it when the directory is not PanCode's alone)
```

`pancode doctor --fix` closes it and reports `tightened to 700`.

## Commit project settings that only tighten

`.pancode/settings.yaml` holds settings for everyone who opens the folder. Here a project lowers the session spending ceiling and tries to loosen two other controls:

```yaml title=.pancode/settings.yaml
version: 2
safety:
  autonomy: yolo
  limits:
    sessionCostUsd: 2
    chatToolCallsPerTurn: 200
```

Nobody's PanCode reads this file until that person approves it. Run `pancode config trust settings` to see the captured bytes and the command that approves exactly those bytes:

```text
Review the captured files above. Approve exactly these bytes with:
pancode config trust settings --hash 8917fe3bce74889bee87a978044311d803678e1ae96dbd6f19d3af95c796a061
```

After the approval, `pancode config inspect` shows what the project actually changed:

```text
! settings project: /home/you/lab-model/.pancode/settings.yaml: safety.autonomy: project autonomy may only tighten the level in user settings; project value ignored
! settings project: /home/you/lab-model/.pancode/settings.yaml: safety.limits.chatToolCallsPerTurn: a project may only tighten a limit from user settings; project value ignored
safety.limits.sessionCostUsd = 2  [project]
```

The lower spending ceiling applies. `yolo` and the higher tool-call limit were dropped, because the user's own settings allow less. A project can tighten `yolo` to `default`, never the reverse, and the same rule covers the sandbox, snapshots, worker permissions and every safety and fleet limit.

**What the approval covers**

The approval is yours, for this folder and these bytes. It is stored in your config directory, so a teammate approves the same file separately. If the file changes, PanCode ignores it again until each of you reviews the new bytes.

## Keep personal overrides out of Git

`.pancode/settings.local.yaml` is a second project layer for overrides of your own. The first time PanCode generates a file in `.pancode/`, it writes an allow-list `.pancode/.gitignore` that keeps `*.local.yaml` and generated files out of Git while authored settings, skills and rules can be committed.

Project layers never carry credentials. Keys such as `auth`, `apiKey`, `token`, `secret` and `password` are dropped with a diagnostic, and a project target that points at a URL is never sent your stored or environment keys. Each person keeps their key in their own settings or credential store.

**Boundaries**

- Approval is per person, per interface and per folder. Approving settings does not approve the project's hooks, safety rules, extensions or plugins.
- Two sessions in one folder do not coordinate their edits. Split the work, and review the diff before committing.
- A pane host per terminal is verified on Linux only.

**Next steps**

- [Settings layers and project trust](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/configuration-and-targets.html)
- [Panes and the pane host](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/panes-and-files.html)
- [Connect PanCode on an HPC login node](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/hpc-clusters.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-a-research-campaign-and-a-blind-arena.html

# Run a research campaign and a blind arena

> Keep a speed-up only when a measurement proves it and the answers still match, then compare model answers without knowing which model wrote them.

You changed some code and it feels faster, or one model's answer looks better than another's. PanCode has two commands that replace that impression with a record. `pancode research` keeps a change only when a measurement shows a real gain and every correctness check still passes. `pancode arena` shows you answers from several models without their names, and records your vote.

**Version scope**

The output below comes from one recorded session on a small Python project. The campaign's agent ran on Claude Haiku 5.5 through the `anthropic-max` route, and the arena put Claude Haiku 5.5 against GPT-6 Luna on the `openai-codex` route. One match is enough to learn both commands. It is not enough to rank models, and the arena section shows why. The cover image comes from a later match on PanCode 0.9.0-dev: an A/A match with both contenders on GPT-6 Luna through GitHub Copilot, each asked to make the Kelvin conversion in a small JavaScript project clearer.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed, with a connected model.
- A Git repository with a check that prints a number as JSON, and a second check that proves the answers are still right.
- Whatever the checks need installed before you start. The agent cannot install it during the campaign.

## Declare what to measure and what must not break

The project here has a `summary()` function that returns a mean, a median and a variance. It is correct and slow. `bench.py` times it on 3000 values and prints `{"wall_ms": ...}`. `check.py` prints the answers for a holdout input, and `tests/reference/stats.json` holds the expected values.

```yaml title=.pancode/verifiers.yaml
version: 2
checks:
  - id: bench
    description: Wall time of summary() on 3000 values (min is better)
    tags: [perf]
    kind: command
    command: [python3, bench.py]
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
  - id: correct
    description: summary() answers match the reference on a holdout input
    tags: [correctness]
    kind: numeric-compare
    command: [python3, check.py]
    reference: tests/reference/stats.json
    tolerance: { relative: 1.0e-9 }
    cwd: .
    timeoutMs: 60000
```

Every check needs `id`, `description`, `command`, `cwd`, `timeoutMs` and `tags`; an empty `tags: []` is allowed. Commit the catalog and every file the checks run or name. Each campaign worktree starts from `HEAD`, so an uncommitted `bench.py` or reference file is not there.

Keep build output such as `__pycache__/` out of Git: a tracked `.pyc` rewritten by a check run counts as a change outside `--scope`, and the iteration is archived without being measured.

The tolerance is your definition of the same answer. Here, a relative difference up to one part in a billion still passes.

## Run a short campaign

```sh
pancode research start --check bench --metric wall_ms --direction min \
  --max-iterations 2 --gate correct --scope stats.py --max-wall-minutes 25 \
  --goal "make stats.py faster without changing any answer"
```

`--scope` limits which files the agent may change, and an iteration that changes anything outside it is archived without being measured. The checks and every file they name are protected the same way, so the agent cannot speed up the benchmark by editing it.

**What the session printed**

```text
campaign r20261114-233756-1d28 (stopped: max-iterations)
objective: min wall_ms from check bench; min improvement +5.00%, 5 pairs
gates: correct; scope: stats.py
protected: .pancode/verifiers.yaml, bench.py, check.py, tests/reference/stats.json
agent: autonomy default
branch: pancode/research/r20261114-233756-1d28 at f94cd0f0c1dc (base f68a37ce7951, 2 ratchets)
budget: 2/2 iterations, 25 min wall; spend ~$0.0032 est
A/A: quiet; unchanged, median delta +0.55%, 95% CI [-8.30%, +4.42%]
  it-0001  ratcheted; improved, median delta -57.05%, 95% CI [-57.83%, -55.97%]; gates correct pass; cost ~$0.0018 est
  it-0002  ratcheted; improved, median delta -99.44%, 95% CI [-99.45%, -99.38%]; gates correct pass; cost ~$0.0014 est
stopped: max-iterations: ran 2 of 2 iterations
```

## Read the result line by line

Start with the A/A line. Before any change, PanCode timed the unchanged code against itself in five interleaved pairs. The medians moved 0.55%, and the 95% interval spans zero, so the noise stayed under the 5% threshold. If the base against itself already looked like a change, the campaign would have stopped there unless you passed `--allow-noisy`.

Each iteration counts as improved only when the median moves at least 5% the right way and the bootstrap interval excludes zero. The first iteration cut the time by 57.05%. The second, measured against the first iteration's commit, removed almost all of what was left. Both passed the `correct` gate.

`~$0.0032 est` is an estimate, marked as one. The `anthropic-max` route is a subscription, so PanCode priced its tokens from its catalog instead of a bill.

On a route with no price at all, such as a gateway target without `targets[].pricing`, the line reads `spend not measured`, because PanCode does not count unknown spend as zero. With `--max-cost-usd` on such a route, the campaign stops as `budget-unenforceable` unless you also pass `--allow-unpriced`.

## Audit it and take the change

```sh
pancode research report r20261114-233756-1d28
git diff HEAD pancode/research/r20261114-233756-1d28
```

`report` regrades the A/A check and every iteration from the stored samples with the recorded seed. In the recorded session each line ended `agrees with the journal`, and the command exited 0. It exits 1 when a grade disagrees.

The result lives on the branch `pancode/research/<id>`, and your checkout is never touched. Here the branch replaced an insertion sort with `sorted()` and stopped `variance` from recomputing the mean for every element. Review the diff and merge it yourself.

## Compare answers blind

```sh
pancode arena run --suite speed --check correct \
  --contender anthropic-max/claude-haiku-5-5 --contender openai-codex/gpt-6-luna \
  -- "Make summary() in stats.py faster without changing any answer. Keep the change minimal."
```

A contender is `<target>/<model>`. Each one runs as a normal `pancode run` in its own worktree from `HEAD`, and `--check` runs the named check on each result. Naming the same model twice instead makes an A/A match, which shows how much two runs of one model differ before you read anything into a difference between two models.

To name your own contenders, `pancode targets` lists each target id with its model, a local server's target included.

| | Contender A | Contender B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Change | `variance` reuses the mean it already computed | The same edit, line for line |
| Diff | `+1 -5` | `+1 -5` |
| `correct` check | Pass, every answer bit-identical | Pass, every answer bit-identical |
| Work shown | 10 turns, 13 tool calls | 4 turns, 5 tool calls |
| Its own timing claim | `correct` and `bench` checks passed | Speed not measured, said so |

Both contenders made the same edit and both left the quadratic insertion sort alone, citing the minimal-change instruction. What separated them was how they reported: one claimed a passing benchmark, the other said plainly that it had not timed anything.

## Vote, then reveal

```sh
pancode arena show 20261114-233756-7102
pancode arena vote 20261114-233756-7102 tie --note "same one-line fix, both exact; B said up front it did not time it"
pancode arena show 20261114-233756-7102 --reveal
pancode arena standings --suite speed
```

Before a vote, `show` lists A and B in a seeded random order and hides the target, model, duration, tokens and cost. `--reveal` before a vote is refused. PanCode never grades a contender; the vote is yours, and so is the note.

**What the session printed**

```text
recorded tie for match 20261114-233756-7102; arena show 20261114-233756-7102 reveals who is who
```

The reveal named the contenders:

```text
   A = openai-codex/gpt-6-luna  22.5s  tokens 77.4k  cost ~$0.0020 est  session 31viz4dfrb0k
   B = anthropic-max/claude-haiku-5-5  10.3s  tokens 51.7k  cost ~$0.0019 est  session 36ja80a9wg03
```

`standings` then printed:

```text
TARGET/MODEL                    VOTES  WINS  LOSSES  TIES  BOTH-BAD  ELO
anthropic-max/claude-haiku-5-5  1      0     0       1     0         n/a (<5 votes)
openai-codex/gpt-6-luna         1      0     0       1     0         n/a (<5 votes)

1 voted of 1 matches in suite speed. These are your recorded votes; PanCode does not judge.
```

That is the inconclusive result, reported as it is. Two models gave the same code, and one tie says nothing about either. A rating appears once a model has 5 votes, and one vote is one person's judgment on one prompt. A match that pits a model against itself is never counted in standings.

**Boundaries**

- A campaign is only as good as its checks. A benchmark that measures the wrong thing will be optimized anyway.
- The `correct` gate checks one holdout input. Iteration answers that pass it can still differ elsewhere.
- Research runs one candidate per iteration and optimizes one number at a time.
- A single vote is an anecdote. Standings mean something only after many matches with different contenders.

**Next steps**

- [Work from a laptop with remote workers](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/work-from-a-laptop-with-remote-workers.html)
- [Research campaigns and the arena](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/research-and-arena.html)
- [Check a change against your repository](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html)
- [Pre-register a benchmark](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/pre-register-a-benchmark.html)
