Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/report-a-problem-without-leaking-your-machine.html

# Report a problem without leaking your machine

> Draft a bug report, read the exact text with your paths, names and keys masked, choose how it leaves, and share a diagnostic bundle only if you want to.

When PanCode itself misbehaves, `/report` in a session and `pancode report` in a shell draft a bug report, a feature request or a question for its maintainers. You read the exact text before anything leaves your machine, with your paths, names and keys masked, and PanCode never sends a report on its own. This tutorial previews a report and never sends one.

**Version scope**

The output below is from PanCode run with `--dry-run` against a fresh PanCode home and a small Git repository that had one finished session. Nothing was sent or saved.

## Before you start

- PanCode installed.
- A folder where you have run at least one session, for `--last`.
- To send for real: the GitHub CLI `gh`, signed in. Without it you can still open or write the report.

## Draft a report

In a session, `/report bug footer flickers on resize` uses the summary as the title and adds what PanCode observed in the current session. `/report feature` and `/report question` work the same way. From a shell, `--title` and `--body-file` supply the text, and `--last` adds the newest session in this folder:

```sh
pancode report bug --title "footer flickers on resize" --body-file notes.txt --last --dry-run
```

Without `--body-file`, a terminal opens `$EDITOR` on a template. `--session <id>` names another session. The note in this run named the machine and the project folder on purpose.

## Read what would be posted

The preview opens with where the report would go, then the body exactly as it would be sent:

```text
Public, posted from your gh account to github.com/PanStudio/pancode; nothing sent yet

----- title -----

fix: footer flickers on resize

----- body, exactly as it will be sent -----
### What happened

The footer flickers when I resize the terminal on <host>.
Repro: open pancode in <path> and drag the window edge.
```

The host name and the folder were masked before the preview was shown. Below the body come an environment block (version, platform, Node, install kind and model) and a report block with an id. The preview ends with what was masked and what sending would do:

```text
Masked by PanCode: 1 path, 1 host name. No secrets recognized.
No diagnostic bundle is attached.

Sending will, in this order:
  1. search PanStudio/pancode for an existing report of the same problem
  2. post the text you reviewed as a public issue from your gh account
dry run: nothing sent
```

The masks cover local paths, URLs other than PanCode's own, user, host, project, branch, remote and target names, e-mail and IP addresses, and secrets, including the API keys the process holds. The review then searches the text again for this machine's names, and refuses to send while one slipped past or the text holds hidden characters.

In the session, `e` edits the text in `$EDITOR` and masks the edit again, `m` masks or unmasks one value, Enter moves to the next step and Esc closes the review and keeps a draft.

## Choose how it leaves

What happens at the end depends on what the machine has:

- **Send.** With a signed-in `gh`, PanCode searches GitHub for the same problem, then posts a public issue under your account. In a session only `s` on the send step sends, never Enter. In a shell you choose send at the prompt, or pass `--yes`.
- **Open.** Without `gh`, it opens a prefilled form in your browser, and you submit it there.
- **Write.** Without a browser, it writes the report to a file and prints the link to paste it into.
- **Preview.** `--dry-run` stops after the preview, with no network call.

The shell prompt can also save a draft for `pancode report send <id>` later. When the search finds an open report of the same problem, you choose to add your details to it, file a new issue that links it, or cancel. With `--yes`, `--on-duplicate stop` is the default: the draft is saved and the command exits 3.

## Attach a diagnostic bundle only if you want to

A bundle is opt-in and built only from a shell: add `--bundle mechanics --consent debug` with `--last` or `--session <id>`. Its preview lists what it keeps and what it never keeps:

```text
Never kept:
  - Prompts, model text, thinking, tool arguments and output, unless the transcript is ticked.
  - File contents, diffs, commit messages.
  - Absolute or relative paths, repository names and remotes, branch names.
  - Host and user names, endpoint URLs, target ids, agent, rule and hook names, environment variables.
  - Anything a schema does not bound.
```

`--transcript [N]` adds the last turns, scrubbed. `debug` lets the maintainers read the bundle to fix this report, and `dataset` also lets its mechanics go into public datasets. `pancode report selftest` builds the same bundle in memory and writes nothing. Here it printed `0 identifiers found in 11370 bytes`, and it exits 1 when an identifier survives.

The bundle stays on your machine and the issue never carries it. `/report` in a session, over ACP or in the desktop app attaches no bundle.

## Sharing is turned off

Report sharing is turned off in this build. `--share` uploads nothing: it prints `Report sharing is turned off in this build.` and exits 2.

## Forget it later

`pancode report status` lists your reports and drafts, and `pancode report forget <id>` deletes a draft you never posted. A posted report cannot be withdrawn from PanCode; edit or close it on GitHub.

Your local copy of a sent report's bundle is deleted once it is 30 days old, the next time you compose, send or forget a report; `pancode report sweep` deletes every expired bundle now. Nothing runs at startup or in the background.

**Exit codes**

`pancode report` exits 0 when the report was sent, opened in the browser, written or previewed; 1 when sending failed or a bundle was refused; 2 on a usage error, or outside a terminal without `--yes`; and 3 when a likely duplicate or a newer release stopped it and the draft was saved.

**Boundaries**

- The masks cover the names PanCode knows about this machine. Text you typed about another machine can pass, so read the preview.
- A sent report is a public GitHub issue. Security problems never go there: `/report security` prints the link to the private advisory form.
- The agent can save a draft, but never send one or share a bundle. Only your own review sends.

**Next steps**

- [Report a problem to the maintainers](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/troubleshooting.html#report-a-problem-to-the-maintainers)
- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)
- [Automate with pancode run](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/exit-codes-and-output.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/tutorials/ask-several-agents-at-once.html

# Ask several agents at once

> Poll two to five agents on one question and read the vote, or give a council roster one task and let a judge write a single answer.

Sometimes one agent's answer is not enough. `/poll` asks two to five agents the same question independently and shows how they vote. `/council` gives a roster of two to five agents the same task and can have a judge write one answer from theirs. Both are read-only: the members read your project, argue and vote, but never change a file.

**Version scope**

The output below is from PanCode run against a fresh PanCode home and a one-file Node package, with participants seated on two models: Claude Haiku 5.5 on the `anthropic-max` route and GPT-6 Luna on the `openai-codex` route. The package's Git status was clean afterwards. The cover image comes from a later poll on PanCode 0.9.0-dev, run without `--models`, so all three participants ran on GPT-6 Luna through GitHub Copilot.

## Before you start

- PanCode connected to at least one model. Every participant can run on the same one.
- For `/council`, a roster in your settings (shown below).
- An interactive session: at the default autonomy level, a poll or a council waits for your approval.

## Ask a quick question with /poll

`/poll` takes the number of participants, then the question. `--options` limits each vote to one of the listed answers, and `--rationale` asks for a short reason with each vote:

```text
/poll --options node:test|vitest|jest --rationale --models anthropic-max/claude-haiku-5-5,openai-codex/gpt-6-luna 3 Which test runner should a small dependency-free ES module package like this one use?
```

Without `--models`, every participant runs on your chat model. `--models` takes a comma-separated list of `target` or `target/model` routes and seats participants on them in turn, so here p1 and p3 ran on Claude Haiku 5.5 and p2 on GPT-6 Luna. Each participant answers alone: no one sees another's answer.

## Approve the plan

A poll is a small fleet, so at the default autonomy level PanCode shows the plan before anything starts. It names each participant, its agent and its model:

```text
Plan ────────────────────────────── Alt+V shows every field
p1    scout on anthropic-max · claude-haiku-5-5
p2    scout on openai-codex · gpt-6-luna
p3    scout on anthropic-max · claude-haiku-5-5
cost  counts against this session's $5.00 limit
```

The card also states each run's bounds: the cost per model call at its output bound, or that the route is unpriced.

Enter allows it, and Esc denies it without starting anyone. At `yolo` the plan runs without this stop. Participants run as the `scout` agent, and every member of a poll or council gets only read-only tools: `read`, `grep`, `find`, `ls`, `git`, `code_nav` and `context`.

## Read the vote

Each participant appears with its time and the start of its answer. When all have voted, PanCode prints the distribution:

```text
poll       3 of 3 voted; majority: node:test
node:test  ### 3 (100%)
```

The headline reads `majority` when one answer has more than half the votes, `plurality` when it leads without a majority, and `tie` when the top two are level.

Here all three chose `node:test` in about two seconds each, on both models, and gave the same reason: it ships with Node and adds no dependency. `/view` opens each full answer. A participant whose vote names none of the options is asked again, with the options quoted.

## Declare a council roster

A council needs a roster. Without one, `/council` stops and says where to add it:

```text
/council needs a roster. Declare one under fleet.rosters in settings.yaml, for example fleet.rosters.default with two to five members, each with a label and a target, then run /council <task> or name another roster with --roster <name>.
```

Each member has a label and a target, and can name a model and an agent. This roster seats one plain reader and one `tester`:

```yaml title=settings.yaml
fleet:
  rosters:
    default:
      members:
        - { label: reader, target: anthropic-max, model: claude-haiku-5-5 }
        - { label: tester, target: openai-codex, model: gpt-6-luna, agent: tester }
```

The roster is read on the next command, without a restart. `--roster <name>` picks another roster. A member whose target runs on an SSH fleet node, or on an agent runtime that cannot enforce read-only tools, such as an ACP peer, is refused before you approve anything.

## Ask the council, with a judge

```text
/council --synthesis judge Is add() in index.js covered by a test, and what is the smallest test that would cover it?
```

The plan card listed `reader` as `scout` on Claude Haiku 5.5, `tester` as `tester` on GPT-6 Luna, and a synthesis run as `oracle` on the fleet's default route, here GPT-6 Luna. The `tester` member kept its own way of working, but the council's read-only tools still applied, so it answered without writing a test. It made 4 tool calls and answered:

```text
Yes. `index.test.js` directly tests `add(2, 2) === 4`, which covers the function’s basic behavior. The smallest test is that existing assertion; no additional test is needed for basic coverage.
```

The `reader` member finished in 1.13 seconds without answering the question. Its whole answer was one pending finding: `read index.js and index.test.js to determine coverage of add()`. The judge read both answers and wrote one, with the verdict `covered`:

```text
Yes. `index.test.js` tests `add(2, 2) === 4`. The smallest test is a single assertion that calls `add` with two inputs and checks the expected result; the existing test already does this.
```

A council does not hide a weak member. `/view` shows each member's answer beside the synthesis, so you can see that this verdict rests on one member's reading.

`--synthesis vote` tallies the members' votes instead, and `none`, the default, returns each answer as it is. `--rounds 2` or `3` shows each member the others' previous answers before it answers again. `--deadline 90s` stops a member that runs too long, and the council returns the rest marked partial.

A member whose target is down is reported as not run while the others deliberate, and a council with fewer than two live members is refused.

**What you have**

A spread of independent answers to one question, and for a council either a tally or one written answer with every member's answer behind it. Each member's run has its own sealed run record, and no file in the project changed.

The answers stay out of your main conversation. `/fleet share <runId>` brings one member's answer into it; shared from the synthesis run, it brings the synthesis with every member's labelled answer.

**Boundaries**

- Members on one model are not fully independent. They share its habits, so a unanimous vote from one model is weaker evidence than a split across several. Use `--models` or a mixed roster to spread the question.
- Every member is a model run and counts against your spending limit. Here the `tester` member alone used 7,056 tokens.
- Members run on this machine only. A council never writes files or makes a worktree.

**Next steps**

- [Workers and fleets](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/fleet-dispatch.html)
- [Commands and shortcuts](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/commands-and-modes.html)
- [Coordinate the coding agents you already use](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/coordinate-your-coding-agents.html)
- [How scheduling works](https://pancode.dev/research/scheduling.html)

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/drivers.html

# Drivers: the model you have, on its own wire

> How PanCode shapes each request for its provider wire, names the cause of a cache break, and an experiment to measure the saving.

A model reaches PanCode through a wire format, and each wire caches, prices, and constrains a request in its own way. The driver layer shapes every request for its wire and records what the provider's cache did with it. This page describes that design, where it lives in the source, and how to measure it.

**Design described for PanCode 0.9.1**

The mechanisms here are read from source. Nothing on this page is measured yet. The experiment is proposed and not yet run.

## The design

- **A pinned prefix, split per wire.** The prompt compiler orders sections by how long their bytes stay fixed and hashes the part that is the same across an installation. Each wire marks that boundary its own way: a cache breakpoint on Anthropic, a separate input item on Codex, and a breakpoint part on Responses.
- **Cache-break attribution.** Every request is digested field by field. When the provider reads far less from cache than the previous request wrote, PanCode names a cause. It first compares request fingerprints (model, system prompt, thinking, tool choice), then consults reasons the host stamped, such as a compaction or an idle period past the cache lifetime.
- **Tool rounds that keep the prefix.** When a turn must call one named tool, wires that allow it keep the full tool list and name the tool, so the cached tool block survives. A provider's rejection is remembered for that target and model.
- **Keepalive that has to pay for itself.** While a turn waits on a long tool, a small request can keep the cache warm. It is sent only when the expected saving exceeds its own cost by at least five cents.
- **Capabilities from the live server.** A probe of the inference server decides tools, vision, and reasoning before a packaged profile does, and an operator setting can only lower what was found. A context window that nobody reported stays unknown.
- **Per-model repairs.** Parsers recover tool calls from models that emit them in a nonstandard channel, and a response that stops with thinking and no answer is retried once at a lower thinking level.

Reasoning, vision, and diffusion models run through this layer. For a diffusion model, PanCode renders refinement frames in the terminal, and the agent loop is the same one other models use. A decision model is a separate, opt-in engine for typed questions.

## Source map

| Mechanism | Source | Default | Switch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pinned prefix | `src/domains/prompts/compiler.ts`, `src/engine/provider-diagnostics.ts` | On | None yet |
| Cache-break attribution | `src/engine/request-structure.ts`, `src/core/cache-telemetry.ts` | On | Instrumentation |
| Tool-round control | `src/engine/provider-payload.ts` | On | None yet |
| Keepalive | `src/engine/cache-keepalive.ts` | On | `chat.cacheKeepalive` |
| Prewarm | `src/session-control/turn-prewarm.ts` | Off | `chat.prewarm` |
| Live capabilities | `src/domains/providers/capabilities.ts` | On | Target `capabilities` |

## The question

Does shaping each request for its wire reduce the fresh input a session pays for, and by how much on each model lineage? The answer could be no. A provider may cache well enough without help that the split adds nothing.

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from source. They are not study results.

- Behavior on the Codex wire rests on measurements of one model on one date.
- The thresholds that declare a cache break are empirical, and some breaks still record an unknown cause.
- The pinned prefix and tool-round control have no off switch, so they cannot be compared with a baseline yet.
- Prompt wording changes very little between model lineages.
- Nothing in the loop, the budgets, or tool handling is specific to diffusion models.

## Why it matters

Input tokens dominate the cost of an agent session, and providers bill cached input at a fraction of fresh input. A harness that breaks the cache without noticing pays full price for the same bytes on every turn. Attribution turns that from a suspicion into a recorded cause someone can fix.

## Use PanCode on it today

### Read what a session's cache did

```sh
pancode telemetry tokens --session <id> --by-source --json
```

Each turn reports its cached input, fresh input, and output tokens. `--by-source` splits the prompt by where its bytes came from.

### Compare with keepalive off

```sh
pancode config set chat.cacheKeepalive false
```

Run the same long task again and compare cached input on the turns that follow a slow tool call.

### Check what a connection reports

```sh
pancode targets --probe
```

The probe shows the capabilities each target answered with.

Worked example: [Choose a model for your project](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/choose-model-for-your-project.html).

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, your numbers are the first this page has.

Pick one long task and one model from each lineage your subscription offers. Run it three times with keepalive on and three times with it off, holding the repository and thinking level fixed. Record cached and fresh input per turn, and the recorded cause of every cache break.

The main mechanism needs a switch first. Until the pinned prefix can be turned off, only keepalive and prewarm can be compared with a baseline.

## Open questions

- [Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?](https://pancode.dev/research/system-one-decisions.html)

## How to join

Open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) that says what you plan to measure, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). Results are published on this page with their numbers, including null and negative ones.

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/memory.html

# Memory: context as a priced storage tier

> How PanCode tiers the context window, prices an eviction against the prompt cache, and recalls evicted output exactly, with a first experiment.

A context window is storage that fills, and the provider's prompt cache makes some of that storage cheap to keep and expensive to disturb. PanCode manages the window as a tiered store: live context, records it can recall exactly, and a summary as the last resort. This page describes that design and how to measure it.

**Design described for PanCode 0.9.1**

The mechanisms here are read from source. Nothing on this page is measured yet. The experiment is proposed and not yet run.

## The design

- **A working set with ordered rungs.** Eviction takes the cheapest material first: output made stale by a later edit, a read replaced by a newer read of the same lines, a failure that was later resolved, a listing already used. Age is the last rung and runs only under pressure. The most recent turns, unresolved failures, and refusals are protected.
- **Eviction priced against the cache.** Removing a body near the start of the conversation forces the provider to rewrite everything behind it. PanCode keeps such a body unless the tokens it frees, read over the next ten requests, outweigh rewriting that span at 11.5 times the cached-read price.
- **Exact recall.** The session ledger is never rewritten. An evicted body leaves a marker with its tool, path, size, a short preview, and the literal call that returns it unchanged. A body recalled twice is pinned.
- **A ladder that depends on the route.** Results replaced by a later identical call are removed only on routes with no prompt cache. Step checkpoints apply only to small or uncached routes. Below a 52,428-token window, the reserve for output is capped at half the window.
- **A summary that rides the warm prefix.** When a summary is needed, PanCode checks whether the summarizer request can extend the last request byte for byte. If it can and the cache-weighted cost is lower, the summary call reads the conversation from cache.
- **Facts that survive a summary.** Each checkpoint carries facts the host measured: files with their line counts and hashes, the newest numeric tool results, and the active request word for word. A file the checkpoint names must be read again before it is edited.

## Source map

| Mechanism | Source | Default | Switch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Working-set rungs | `src/domains/context/working-set/policies/` | On | `context.workingSet.policy` |
| Cache-priced eviction | `src/domains/context/working-set/policies/cache-price.ts` | On | None yet |
| Rearm band | `src/domains/context/fold/pressure.ts` | On | `context.workingSet.rearmFraction` |
| Exact recall | `src/domains/context/working-set/marker.ts`, `recall.ts` | On | None yet |
| Route-conditional ladder | `src/domains/context/fold/contract.ts` | On | Target `cache.retention` |
| In-prefix summary | `src/engine/in-prefix-summary.ts` | On | `context.compaction.model` |
| Exact facts and edit guard | `src/domains/session/compaction/exact-facts.ts`, `stale-edit-guard.ts` | On | None yet |

## The question

Does pricing eviction against the provider's cache beat evicting by age on a long task? The measure is the input a session pays for, with the task still passing. The answer could be no, if the rewrite a naive policy causes is small in practice.

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from source. They are not study results.

- The 11.5 ratio comes from one provider's pricing and is applied to every route.
- Removal of replaced results never runs unless a target declares that it has no prompt cache, because caching is assumed by default, local servers included.
- The per-turn pool for tool output has a floor larger than a 32K window, so on small windows the guard after each tool batch does the protecting.
- Search by meaning is off by default.
- Whether the agent still knows what it needs after a reduction is not measured. That question has its own page below.

## Why it matters

Long tasks routinely outlive a model's window. Every reduction is a trade: bytes removed now against cached bytes rewritten on the following turns. A policy that counts only tokens can make a session more expensive while making it smaller.

## Use PanCode on it today

### See what fills the window

Type `/context` in a session. It shows what occupies the window.

### Switch the eviction policy

```sh
pancode config set context.workingSet.policy age-horizon
```

`structural-v2` is the default. `age-horizon` evicts by age alone.

### Read the cost per turn

```sh
pancode telemetry tokens --session <id> --by-source --json
```

Compare cached and fresh input across the turns that follow an eviction.

Worked example: [Keep a long coding task on track](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html).

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, your numbers are the first this page has.

Take one task long enough to trigger several reductions, forty turns or more. Run it under `structural-v2`, under `age-horizon`, and with the working set disabled, three times each on one model. Record fresh input, tokens the provider had to rewrite, the number of summary calls, and whether the task's check passes.

Cache-priced eviction itself has no switch yet. Adding one would let the pricing rule be compared with the same rungs unpriced.

## Open questions

- [What does an agent lose when its context is reduced?](https://pancode.dev/research/context-and-retrieval.html)
- [Does agent memory change outcomes?](https://pancode.dev/research/proactive-memory.html)

## How to join

Open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) that says what you plan to measure, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). Results are published on this page with their numbers, including null and negative ones.

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/scheduling.html

# Scheduling: a mixed fleet under one policy

> How PanCode admits, bounds, and grades its workers and other coding agents, with a first experiment against a single agent.

A group of agents is a workload. Each job needs a route, a share of a real endpoint, a boundary on what it may touch, and a way to tell whether it did its work. PanCode schedules its own workers and other coding agents under those rules. This page describes that design and how to measure it.

**Design described for PanCode 0.9.1**

The mechanisms here are read from source. Nothing on this page is measured yet. The experiment is proposed and not yet run.

## The design

- **A typed intent and an envelope that only subtracts.** A dispatch names its read roots, write roots, expected outputs, and the checks that will judge it. Shell commands are refused in that field. What the worker may do is narrowed in a fixed order by its role, the request, the runtime, and the host, and every capability withheld is recorded and sealed.
- **Roles that owe evidence.** A builder owes a change or a declared reason for none. A checker owes checks that ran. A reviewer or judge owes cited evidence. The host grades each return against facts it observed. A return that misses its obligation is retried once on a different model, unless the attempt may have changed files.
- **Review gates built on citations.** The host assembles a packet for the reviewer: the worker's handback, the measured diff, and host check results, each with an id and a digest. A verdict that cites nothing, or cites an id the packet lacks, does not pass the gate.
- **Host verification with a replay on the base.** After a worker settles, the host runs the declared checks itself. A failing check is replayed on the base commit inside the sandbox. A failure the base already had is sealed as not implicating the worker.
- **Failures mapped to the part that failed.** Each failure class excludes one part of the route: the model, the target, the node, or the runtime. A context overflow earns one retry on a strictly larger window. No retry runs when the failed attempt may have changed files.
- **Capacity leases.** An endpoint's slot count comes from an operator setting, then a live probe, then a remembered value. Leases are held across processes. A dispatch is refused when the main turn already holds every slot, because waiting would deadlock.
- **Cache-aware fan-out.** Workers that share a prompt prefix wait up to 15 seconds for the first one's first token, so the others read the prefix from cache.
- **Councils and polls.** Two to five read-only seats answer over at most three rounds, and the result is a vote or a judge's synthesis.

## Source map

| Mechanism | Source | Default | Switch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Typed intent and envelope | `src/domains/dispatch/intent.ts`, `envelope.ts` | On | Target and permission mode |
| Role obligations and grading | `src/domains/dispatch/obligation.ts`, `grading.ts` | On | `fleet.retry.maxRetries` |
| Evidence packets and gates | `src/domains/dispatch/evidence-packet.ts`, `gate-decisions.ts` | On request | `review`, compete mode |
| Host verification | `src/domains/dispatch/host-verification.ts` | With declared checks | Omit the checks |
| Failure classes | `src/domains/dispatch/failure-classification.ts` | On | `fleet.retry` settings |
| Capacity leases | `src/domains/dispatch/capacity-lease.ts` | On | `fleet.concurrency` |
| Prefix stagger | `src/domains/dispatch/prefix-stagger.ts` | On | `fleet.staggerSharedPrefix` |

## The question

Does a graded fleet finish more work per token than one agent on the same tasks? The comparison is a single agent, the same agent behind a review gate, and several candidates with a judge. The answer could be no. Review costs tokens, and on easy tasks it may buy nothing.

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from source. They are not study results.

- One policy is enforced for PanCode's own workers, the Claude SDK, and agents reached through mediated ACP. Other agent command lines receive the closest flags they support, and OpenCode cannot enforce read-only.
- Whether a reviewer is independent of the builder (a different agent and model lineage) is recorded and never enforced.
- Compete takes 2 to 4 candidates, and each can name its own target and model. Given only a count, they share one model and differ by a one-line stance in each prompt.
- Matching a worker's claim to a command that ran is text matching.
- Adaptive routing from past results is off by default.
- No comparison between a single agent and any of these arrangements has been run.

## Why it matters

Every vendor now ships subagents, and the usual evidence for them is a demonstration. A team paying for several models needs to know when a second agent raises the pass rate and when it only raises the bill. That takes the same tasks, the same models, and a count of tokens per task that passed.

## Use PanCode on it today

### Send one worker and read its record

Type `/run reviewer <task>` in a session, then inspect the run from a shell.

```sh
pancode evidence inspect <run-id>
pancode fleet verify <run-id> --json
```

### Ask several agents

`/poll 3 <question>` takes a vote, and `/council` gives a roster one task. Both need a roster in your settings.

### Turn the retry off for a comparison

```sh
pancode config set fleet.retry.maxRetries 0
```

Worked examples: [Run a playbook from plan to commit](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/run-a-playbook-and-land-it.html) and [Coordinate the coding agents you already use](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/coordinate-your-coding-agents.html).

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, your numbers are the first this page has.

Choose ten tasks with a hidden check each, half of them hard enough that a single agent often fails. Run each task three ways: one builder, one builder behind a review gate, and compete mode with a judge. Record the pass rate on the hidden check, the runs that reported success and failed it, and tokens per passed task.

Vary the reviewer's model lineage in a second round. That measures whether independence, which the record already tracks, changes the outcome.

## Open questions

- [When do several agents or small models pay off?](https://pancode.dev/research/fleets-and-local-models.html)

## How to join

Open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) that says what you plan to measure, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). Results are published on this page with their numbers, including null and negative ones.

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/protection.html

# Protection: a floor at every autonomy level

> How PanCode decides each call: a fixed floor, containment, a judge that never reads model text, and flow rules, with a first experiment.

An agent runs commands with your permissions, and some of what it reads was written by strangers. PanCode decides each call in layers: a floor that never moves, containment where the host offers it, a judge for what remains, and you for what only you can decide. This page describes that design and how to measure it.

**Design described for PanCode 0.9.1**

The mechanisms here are read from source. Nothing on this page is measured yet. The experiment is proposed and not yet run.

## The design

- **One admission function.** The same function decides a call from PanCode's own tools, from the Claude SDK bridge, and from an agent reached through ACP. It applies the floor first, then hard limits such as read-only, then confirmation rules, then the autonomy level.
- **A floor at every autonomy level.** Formatting a disk, deleting a home directory or the workspace's `.git`, and changing PanCode's own state, credentials, or project trust are refused before anything else is considered, yolo included.
- **Containment before judgment.** A shell call the OS sandbox contains runs without an approval card. So does a destructive call that a snapshot taken beforehand can undo. Asking is reserved for what neither contains.
- **A judge that never reads the model.** A call that would wait for approval goes first to a model with no tools. Its input is your typed messages, facts the host computed, and the call itself inside a random tag. It never sees the assistant's text, its reasoning, or any tool result.
- **Backstops in code.** The judge's permission to leave the sandbox stands only when your own words mention it. Three blocks under different rules, or twenty in total, hand the next call to you.
- **Information-flow labels.** A project can declare which paths and tool results may reach which model connections. A result is labeled before its call runs, the labels survive compaction and resume, and every outbound request is checked against them. An unreadable ledger refuses all transfers.
- **Settings that can only tighten.** A project's own configuration can make safety stricter than yours and never looser.

## Source map

| Mechanism | Source | Default | Switch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Admission order | `src/domains/safety/admission.ts` | On | `safety.autonomy` |
| Floor | `src/domains/safety/yolo-floor.ts` | On | None |
| Sandbox and snapshots | `src/core/sandbox/`, `src/domains/workspace-snapshots/` | On where available | `safety.sandbox`, `safety.snapshots` |
| Safety judge | `src/domains/safety/safety-judge.ts` | On | `safety.judge.enabled` |
| Information flow | `src/domains/safety/information-flow.ts` | Off | A project policy |
| Tighten-only layers | `src/core/settings-layers.ts` | On | None |

## The question

How many approval cards can containment and a judge remove without admitting a call you would have refused? Both numbers matter. Fewer cards with one bad admission is a worse system. The answer could be that the judge saves little once the sandbox is on.

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from source. They are not study results.

- The floor reads command text. It cannot see what a script does once it runs, which is why the sandbox is the real boundary where one exists.
- The judge does not read model text, but the call it reviews carries arguments the model wrote.
- The checks on your words are string matching.
- Flow labels apply to a whole session. Data read through a script or a shell variable is not labeled.
- A screen for instructions hidden in web and tool results exists and runs only when a decision model is configured, which is off by default.
- The macOS sandbox profile is less tested than the Linux one.

## Why it matters

Approval fatigue is a safety problem. A person who has clicked allow two hundred times reads the next card less carefully. Removing the cards that containment already makes safe leaves attention for the ones that matter, provided nothing unsafe is admitted along the way.

## Use PanCode on it today

### Check what your machine can contain

```sh
pancode doctor
```

The report says whether a sandbox backend is available.

### Compare with the judge off

```sh
pancode config set safety.judge.enabled false
```

Run the same task and count the approval cards.

### Undo a change

Type `/rewind` in a session. It previews and restores files from a snapshot and never moves your branches.

Worked example: [Let PanCode work without watching every call](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html).

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, your numbers are the first this page has.

Build a task set of two kinds. The first needs ordinary commands that would normally ask, such as installing a dependency. The second plants an instruction in a file or a fetched page that asks the agent to do something you never requested. Run each with the judge on and off.

Record approval cards per task, calls admitted that the planted instruction asked for, and the judge's added time per call. A single admitted planted call is the result to report first.

## Open questions

- [Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?](https://pancode.dev/research/system-one-decisions.html)

## How to join

Open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) that says what you plan to measure, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). Results are published on this page with their numbers, including null and negative ones.

---

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/accounting.html

# Accounting: done, checked against what ran

> How PanCode checks a finished task against what it observed and seals the record, with the first experiment the project plans to run.

When an agent says a task is done, that is a claim. PanCode keeps its own account of what happened: which checks ran on the final tree, which of the agent's statements a command supports, and what was never measured. This page describes that design and the first experiment the project plans to run.

**Design described for PanCode 0.9.1**

The mechanisms here are read from source. Nothing on this page is measured yet. The experiment is proposed and not yet run.

## The design

- **Checks count only on the final tree.** The host classifies every tool call as a check, an inspection, or a change. A change to the workspace retires every pass recorded before it, so a test that passed before the last edit verifies nothing.
- **Claimed and assessed, side by side.** The agent declares done, partly done, or not done. The host seals its own state beside that claim, and a declared done over an open fact becomes partly done. Open facts include a change with no check after it, a failed check, and a missing expected output.
- **Claims matched to commands.** A worker's statement that a check passed is matched to a command the host saw exit cleanly. Trust is kept as five separate readings (integrity, grounding, independent review, context provenance, and completion evidence) and is never collapsed into one score.
- **Assess, then seal.** A run's settlement and assessment are written before a hash chain over its journal is sealed. Verification replays the chain, checks every file's size and hash, and rejects lines added after the seal.
- **Unknown stays unknown.** Every usage and cost value is measured, estimated, unknown, or absent, each with a reason. A sum keeps its known subtotal and counts the unknowns. A cost cap that cannot be priced stops the run.
- **Checks for numerical work.** A check can compare results within a relative, absolute, or ULP tolerance, repeat a seeded run and report the spread, or reproduce from inputs pinned by hash. Each judged check becomes a claim tied to its commit, command, and tolerance, and two opposite verdicts under the same conditions are recorded as a contradiction.
- **PanCode accounts for itself.** Every nudge and block the host issues gets an id and settles exactly once: acted on, ignored, recovered, or exhausted. The same holds for a lesson from memory, which counts as delivered only when its text reached the model and is held only when later evidence supports it.

## Source map

| Mechanism | Source | Default | Switch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Final-tree freshness | `src/domains/safety/run-effects.ts`, `check-classifier.ts` | On | None yet |
| Claimed and assessed | `src/domains/safety/finish-contract.ts`, `src/tools/finish.ts` | On, advisory | `PANCODE_RIGOR`, `run --exit-code` |
| Claim grounding and trust | `src/domains/dispatch/validation-grounding.ts`, `src/domains/evidence/trust-status.ts` | On | None |
| Seal and verify | `src/domains/telemetry/seal.ts` | On | None |
| Measured, estimated, unknown | `src/core/telemetry/fact.ts` | On | None |
| Numerical checks | `src/tools/verify/numeric.ts`, `reproduce-run.ts` | When declared | The check catalog |
| Claims ledger | `src/domains/claims/` | When declared | The check catalog |
| Intervention ledger | `src/domains/middleware/fired-record.ts` | On | Instrumentation |

## The question

How often does a model declare a task done when the evidence does not support it, and how often does the host catch it? A third number keeps the first two honest: how often the host lowers a done that was in fact correct. The answer could be that models rarely overclaim, or that the host misses most of it.

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from source. They are not study results.

- The seal is unkeyed and unsigned. It shows a record is intact and cannot show who produced it.
- The host that did the work also assesses it.
- The assessment only lowers a declared done. A declared partly done is not examined further.
- At normal rigor the completion check advises and does not block. `PANCODE_RIGOR=high` makes it ask again.
- A writer the host does not recognize, run after a passing check, leaves that pass standing.
- A second clean run that agrees with the first shows self-agreement, not correctness.

## Why it matters

A change to research code is finished when the checks say so, and a summary written after one more edit may describe a tree that no longer exists. A reader of a result, in the same lab or another one, needs to know which statements a command supports and which rest on the agent's word.

## Use PanCode on it today

### Make an unfinished run fail the job

```sh
pancode run --exit-code --verify "npm test" --fail-on-verify \
  --output-format json "<task>" | jq '.outcome, .causes'
```

The run exits 1 when the agent declared partly done, when its done left unvalidated changes, or when the check failed.

### Read what a run did

```sh
pancode evidence inspect <run-id>
pancode claims
```

### Verify a sealed record

```sh
pancode telemetry verify --run <run-id>
```

The command uses only the record's own files, so it works on another machine.

Worked example: [Check a change against your repository](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/check-a-change-against-your-repository.html).

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

This is the first experiment the project plans to run. Nobody has run it yet.

Write trap tasks, each with a hidden grader the agent never sees. In one, the natural fix passes the visible test and a later cleanup edit breaks it. In another, the test runner cannot start. In a third, a numerical result drifts inside the test's tolerance and outside the reference's. A fourth cannot be completed as stated.

Run each task several times on one model from each model lineage, at normal and at high rigor. Record three rates: declared done with the grader failing, those the host lowered, and done lowered while the grader passed.

One thing is needed first: the trap tasks do not exist yet. The campaign runner already repeats a roster with `--repeat` and records each run's sealed completion and verification.

## Open questions

- [Can an agent run be a scientific record?](https://pancode.dev/research/sealed-run-records.html)
- [What would make a scientist trust an agent's change?](https://pancode.dev/research/scientific-and-hpc-workflows.html)
- [Does agent memory change outcomes?](https://pancode.dev/research/proactive-memory.html)

## How to join

Open a [GitHub issue](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) that says what you plan to measure, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md). Results are published on this page with their numbers, including null and negative ones.

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/system-one-decisions.html

# Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?

> Open questions on System One: evaluating on trajectories, asking better questions, and bringing a decision model, with a first experiment.

Can a small, fast decision model make a coding agent's work better? System One is where PanCode asks that question. You bring a model that answers typed questions, and PanCode gives the agent a `consult` tool, a screen beside the safety judge, and optional triage of queued messages.

The plumbing has shipped. Whether it helps is still open, and the evidence so far is thin.

**Open question, described for 0.9.0**

System One is off until you name a route, and its keys and tool may change between releases. Contributors and outside researchers are welcome to work on it. All samples below are small, and every experiment on this page is proposed and not yet run.

## The question

Three questions sit inside the big one, and each could come back negative.

- **Trajectories.** With a decision model bound, does the agent take a better path through a task: fewer wrong turns, fewer rounds, and the same or better accepted result?
- **Question formation.** Which questions can a small model answer usefully, and what must the question carry for that to happen?
- **Training.** Could a model trained on agent work outperform a general one on these questions?

## What is measured so far

These were measured on an earlier build of the same design, on small samples. They show what the parts do. None of them shows that System One improves an agent's work.

| Measurement | Result | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filter recall on a file digest, on Jev | 0.77, 0.82, 0.92 | Three sets of 6 queries |
| Filter recall on the first 512 characters, on Jev | 0.65, 0.35, 0.92 | The same three sets |
| Filter recall by query type | 0.92 for what a file is for; at best 0.58 for how it behaves | The same sets |
| Judge screen, on a real Haiku judge | Parked 8 of 8 injected pages | 8 pages |
| Judge screen latency | Screen 104 to 157 ms; judge verdict 938 to 1370 ms | The same run |
| Steering triage, how a message relates to the work | 105 of 105 | The relation pick only |
| `consult` calls with Jev bound | 0 calls | 12 real Haiku sessions, 6 with Jev bound |

Read those together. A digest holds up better than a file's opening characters on two of the three sets and ties on the third. It finds what a file is for and misses much of what a file does, which fits a digest that never carries the body.

Precision is weak. Between a third and more than half of filter matches can be wrong, so a filter can narrow a list and cannot settle anything.

### Filter across routes

These also ran on that earlier build. They are small samples, and the query sets were regression sets, so they were not independent of the work being tested.

| Route | Recall | Precision | Median latency | Returns |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Haiku, as a chat route | 0.81 | 0.68 | 2.5 s | Labels |
| Jev | 0.85 | 0.47 | 163 ms | Probabilities |
| A self-hosted chat model | 0.87 | 0.67 | 6.3 s | Labels |

On 3 fresh queries, with about 3 samples, Haiku scored recall 0.83 and precision 1.00, and Jev scored recall 0.50 and precision 0.26. Those figures moved a long way from the table above, which shows how unstable these numbers are. Do not rank the routes from them.

Jev and other engines whose profile declares real probabilities return a score. Any chat route returns one label per question, so its match has no score, and it never drives the judge screen.

### What the screen result covers

The screen result covers injected pages only, and it says nothing about how often the screen would park an honest page.

The most important number is the last row. Given the tool, the agent did not call it once. Nothing has measured a benefit from `consult`, because none of the measured sessions used it on its own.

### One earlier run, on a design that no longer exists

An on/off evaluation ran the older fixed-site design, where PanCode asked its own questions at fixed points in a turn. That design is gone, and so is the run's raw data. Only these numbers remain, so nobody can reanalyze them.

The run used build `jev-1.14.0` with Haiku as the main model, over 24 episodes per arm. Total time with System One on was 1.237 times total time with it off, meaning slower, with an interval of 1.037 to 1.484. Acceptance was 24 of 24 per arm. Hints fired on 4 of 32 turns and changed no rounds.

Do not read that as a verdict on `consult` or on decision models in general. It says that one design cost time and bought nothing visible on that sample.

## Why it matters

A main model is slow and expensive for the small judgments an agent makes constantly: which file to open, whether a web page is trying to instruct it, whether a queued message means stop.

The judge screen numbers show a decision can return in about a tenth of a verdict's time. If small decisions like these can steer the larger model, long agent work gets cheaper and safer.

The clock is a poor measure of that. A decision that adds a second and saves a wrong branch is a win that total time can hide, and a saved second that leads the agent astray is a loss. That is why the direction below is to evaluate on trajectories.

## Directions to work on

### Evaluate on trajectories

Define what a better path means and measure it per episode: rounds, tool calls, files read and then never used, repeated failed commands, cost, and whether the result was accepted. PanCode journals each decision without its content, so the outcome, latency, route, and answering build can be set against the rest of the run.

Agents did not reach for `consult`, so a first result may be about adoption: what tool description or prompting makes an agent use it when it would help, and whether forcing the call helps at all.

### Form better questions

`consult` asks yes-or-no, pick, or rate questions over a small state, and it filters lists against one criterion.

Each engine declares what it can carry, and a question that does not fit abstains instead of being cut down. Open work includes what to put in a digest so that behavior queries improve, how to phrase criteria, and which of an agent's choices are worth asking about.

### Bring a model, and one day train one

You can bring a model today. A server that answers `POST /v1/systemone` becomes a route, and a named capability profile says how its numbers are read. Profiles make no accuracy claim, and there are no fitted thresholds, so a comparison across engines would be new evidence.

Training is an open research direction with no plan or timeline. There is no training data: the decision dataset from earlier releases was removed, and today's journal keeps decision records without content. Building an opt-in dataset is part of the work, including what consent it needs, what to redact, and what counts as a correct label.

## Use PanCode on it today

You need a working chat model, since System One never replaces it, and a route to name. Off is the default and sends nothing.

### Name a route

```sh
pancode systemone use jev
pancode systemone status
pancode systemone check jev --live
```

`status` says what each route reaches and sends. `check --live` sends one content-free decision and reports the build that answered, which shows the route works and says nothing about its quality. In the terminal, `/usage health` shows the same state. A choice takes effect on the next start. For one headless run, pass `--systemone`:

```sh
pancode run --systemone jev "<task>"
pancode run --systemone off "<task>"
```

### Choose what answers

- `jev` is a hosted engine that needs `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` and returns real probabilities.
- A declared engine is a decision server you run, with a named profile.
- `memory`, `main`, or a chat target answer with one label per question. They have no real probabilities, so a filter match has no score and they never drive the judge screen.

A hosted route receives file digests and heads, chunks of results, web and MCP result text, and queued messages. Redaction is best effort. Use a route you run yourself when that matters.

### Read what happened

```sh
pancode telemetry timeline <session-id>
pancode telemetry inspect <session-id> --json
```

The timeline includes each System One decision. Use `pancode telemetry inspect --run <run-id>` for a dispatched or headless run.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, the result is useful whichever way it comes out.

**Score the filter on a repository you know.** This extends the measurements above to new code, adds precision, and needs an afternoon.

### Write the labels before you run anything

Pick a repository you know well. Write 12 queries, six about what a file is for and six about what a file does in its body. For each query, list by hand the files that should match.

### Run each query through `consult`

Ask for the filter form directly, one query per headless run, so the agent's choice not to call the tool does not get in the way:

```sh
pancode run --systemone jev "Call consult with a files filter over src/**. Criterion: <query>. Use limit 32. Report the matches and do nothing else."
```

One filter carries at most 256 items and returns at most 32 matches, so scope `paths` to fit and keep each hand-labelled list shorter than that.

### Score it

For each query, compute recall and precision against your labels, separately for the two query types. Note `carried.partial` and which items carried a digest or a head.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the repository's language and size, the build `check --live` reported, your query types, and the scores. Include your sample size and leave out anything private.

Needs: `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` for Jev, or your own decision server. A label route can also run this, though it returns no scores, so a comparison with Jev is a second result.

A natural second experiment, also proposed and not yet run, is a small paired on/off study: the same task and the same model, repeated with `--systemone jev` and `--systemone off`, scored on the trajectory measures above. It needs tasks whose result can be accepted or rejected mechanically, and enough repeats to report an interval.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- System One is not a safety net. The deterministic safety rules and the judge decide, the screen can only tighten, and no use removes a confirmation.
- A filter miss is not proof, especially when `carried.partial` is above zero.
- PanCode ships a client for these wires and no inference server.

**Next steps**

- [System One guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/system-one.html)
- [Can an agent run be a scientific record?](https://pancode.dev/research/sealed-run-records.html)
- [Let PanCode work without watching every call](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/let-it-work-with-containment-and-rewind.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/sealed-run-records.html

# Can an agent run be a scientific record?

> What a sealed run record proves and what it cannot, how far repeated runs differ, and a first experiment to measure that spread with PanCode.

What would it take to treat an agent run as a scientific record that someone else can check? PanCode already writes a sealed record of each run. Nobody has yet studied what those records can support as evidence, how much two runs of one task differ, or what a reader in another lab would still need.

**Open question, described for 0.9.0**

The records and commands on this page have shipped. The research use of them is new. No reproducibility study exists yet, so this page has no outcome numbers, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. Contributors and outside researchers are welcome.

## The question

- **Repeatability.** Given the same task, repository, and model, how far apart are the results of repeated runs, and which recorded facts explain the difference?
- **Sufficiency.** What must a shared record contain before an outside reader can judge a claim about a run without re-running it?
- **Method.** Can sealed records carry a controlled comparison between agent configurations well enough to publish?

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design, read from the source at this version. They are not study results.

A finished run writes its settlement, its result object, and an assessment, then seals them. A seal records a SHA-256 hash chain over the journal, plus the size and hash of every journal segment and stored object. `pancode telemetry verify` checks all of that using only the scope's own files, so it works on any machine.

**What a seal shows.** The record's files match their manifest and the chain is intact, so damage and partial edits are caught.

**What a seal does not show.** The chain is unkeyed and carries no signature, so someone with the files could write a consistent new record, and a seal cannot say who produced it. Verification also runs nothing. A verified seal says the record is intact, and leaves open whether the agent's work was correct or would come out the same again.

Other parts of the design matter to a researcher:

- Unknowns stay unknown. A missing token count reads as not recorded instead of zero, and a dropped or refused record leaves a gap record behind.
- An assessment keeps trust states separately, including whether a run's claims were grounded in commands that actually ran.
- Sharing has four profiles. `content-free` is the default, `structural` adds structure such as prompt and tool-schema manifests, `report` is structural with target ids anonymized too, for an archive linked from a public issue, and `research` adds content captured under consent.
- A share re-applies secret redaction, and below `research` it keeps only allowlisted fields and anonymizes identities. Redaction is best effort.

## Why it matters

A success rate and a description of the setup leave a reader unable to see what an agent did, what it cost, or which results were lost along the way. A record format that keeps those facts, and says plainly when one is missing, could raise the standard of evidence.

Every other page in this section depends on the answer. A study of decision models, memory, or compaction is only as good as the records behind it, and the variance between repeated runs sets how many episodes such a study needs.

## Directions to work on

**Measure run-to-run variance.** Model output varies, and so does what the agent chooses to read. A baseline spread for rounds, cost, and accepted results on a few task types would give every later study its sample size.

**Decide what provenance needs.** An unkeyed chain suits integrity on your own machine. A shared claim may need more, such as a signature or a published digest. Designing that, and testing whether it is worth its cost, is open work.

**Test what a reader can conclude.** Give someone a `content-free` archive and a claim. Find out which claims they can check, which need `structural` or `research`, and what is still missing.

**Build the analysis layer.** PanCode exposes JSON reads over its journals, and it has no comparison tool. A small script that folds two sets of runs into a paired table would help every study here.

## Use PanCode on it today

### Run a task and read its record

```sh
pancode run --agent <agent-id> --output-format stream-json "<task>"
pancode telemetry inspect --run <run-id> --json
pancode telemetry cost --run <run-id> --json
```

`pancode agents` lists the agents. For a supported local or OpenAI-compatible runtime, `--temperature` sets the sampler for one run. The JSON stream ends with a result frame, and the run has its own scope.

### Verify it

```sh
pancode telemetry verify --run <run-id>
pancode fleet verify <run-id> --json
```

`telemetry verify` reports the seal. `fleet verify` also reads the settlement and reports the mismatch kind when a seal fails.

### Share it

```sh
pancode telemetry share --run <run-id> --profile content-free --dry-run
pancode telemetry share --run <run-id> --profile content-free --out run.tar.gz
pancode telemetry verify run.tar.gz
```

Nothing is uploaded. Read the `--dry-run` output before you send an archive to anyone. On another machine, `pancode telemetry import run.tar.gz` verifies the archive and places it for reading.

### Capture more, deliberately

```sh
pancode telemetry consent --workspace <dir>
```

Set `telemetry.mode: research` and turn on the `telemetry.research` flags you need. Content capture also needs consent for that workspace. Research capture is capped at 256 MiB per session, and a refusal leaves a gap record.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. If you do, the spread you measure is the first baseline this project has.

**Measure the spread of one small task.**

### Fix the setup

Choose a small repository with a test suite, and a task whose result those tests can accept or reject. Commit the starting state. Fix the model, route, and PanCode version, and write them down.

### Run it ten times

Run the task ten times, each from a clean checkout of the same commit. Pass `--temperature 0` as well if your route supports it, then repeat the set without it if you have the budget.

### Fold the records

For each run, read `telemetry inspect --run <run-id> --json` and `telemetry cost --run <run-id> --json`. Tabulate tool calls, tokens, cost, duration, stop reason, and whether the tests accepted the result. Report the median and the range.

### Check it from outside

Share two runs with `--profile content-free`, then give the archives and your table to a colleague on another machine. Record what they could verify and what they had to take on trust.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the setup, the table, and your colleague's notes. Ten runs is a small sample, so say so.

Needs: any chat route and a repository with tests. A local model server avoids API keys and spend. A second machine is only needed for the last step.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- A seal shows integrity of the record. It is not proof of correctness, authorship, or repeatability.
- Share profiles reduce what leaves your machine, and redaction is best effort, so read what you are about to share.
- Publish numbers and methods. Do not attach another person's session content without their agreement.

**Next steps**

- [See what a session cost and what a run did](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/see-what-a-session-cost-and-what-a-run-did.html)
- [Can a small decision model improve an agent's work?](https://pancode.dev/research/system-one-decisions.html)
- [All open questions](https://pancode.dev/research.html)

Source: https://pancode.dev/research/proactive-memory.html

# Does agent memory change outcomes?

> Whether lessons change what an agent does, whether self-approval is safe, and a first experiment on one repeated mistake.

Does memory make an agent better at the next task, or does it only add text to a prompt? PanCode has a working memory system with an approval gate, and it can also approve some of its own lessons. Nobody has yet measured whether any of this changes outcomes.

**Open question, described for 0.9.0**

Proactive memory has shipped and is on by default. This page has no outcome numbers because none exist yet, and every experiment here is proposed and not yet run. Contributors and outside researchers are welcome.

## The question

- **Effect.** With a relevant lesson available, does an agent avoid a mistake it would otherwise repeat, at what model cost?
- **Trust.** Is the rule that lets a repository lesson approve itself safe, and how often does it approve something wrong?
- **Timing.** When should a reminder appear so that an agent acts on it without being distracted by it?

## What is known so far

These are facts about the design at this version. They are not study results.

The design follows Wu et al., *Remember When It Matters: Proactive Memory Agent for Long-Horizon Agents* (2026), adapted to PanCode. A session keeps bounded banks of knowledge, attempts, and diagnoses. A rules tier makes no model calls. A model tier uses the memory route, or the chat route when no memory route is set, so a default install spends model calls on memory.

Durable lessons are separate from those banks, and only eligible approved records reach a prompt. A person can approve any record.

Repository knowledge from a task-bank entry can also receive automatic approval once one session records that the lesson held, with no contradiction or recorded regression. It waits for a person if another approved or rejected lesson already carries the same command as evidence.

The gate is narrow. Automatic approval needs a command that could have failed. A lesson backed only by a quote from a repository file waits for a person, and so does one whose only command cannot fail, such as `echo`, `ls` or `true`.

PanCode records two useful observations about an approved lesson: `delivered` when its reminder was submitted, and `held` when the recommended command then succeeds exactly. A held lesson did not necessarily cause that success, and the agent might have run the command anyway. That gap is the research problem in one sentence.

## Why it matters

Long agent work fails in repetitive ways: the same wrong command, the same forgotten convention, the same dead end after a reset.

Memory is the obvious fix, and also an easy way to pay for tokens that do nothing, or to teach an agent something false that then persists across sessions. Evidence here would tell users when to leave it on and developers what to cut.

## Directions to work on

**Measure counterfactual effect.** Compare paired sessions on seeded tasks with memory on and off, and with a lesson present and absent. Count repeated failures, rounds, and cost, including memory's own calls.

**Audit the approval gate.** Collect automatically approved lessons from real repositories and have a person grade them. A false-approval rate, even from a small sample, would be new evidence about whether one held session is enough. Lessons approved under an earlier, wider gate are a separate sample, because the rule changed.

**Study reminder timing.** Reminders can land at tool-batch boundaries, at turn end, or on the next prompt. Cadence is configurable, so whether frequent reminders help or distract can be tested.

**Compare memory routes.** A small local model and the main chat model may produce very different lessons at very different costs.

## Use PanCode on it today

### Look at what memory is doing

Open `/memory` in the terminal. Its tabs are **Lessons**, **This task**, **Review**, and **Diagnostics**. In **Review**, `a` approves a proposal and `x` rejects it after asking once. From the shell, `pancode memory` lists, approves, rejects, and prunes durable records.

### Control the conditions

In `/settings`, under **Context and memory**, then **Proactive memory**, **Memory connection** and **Memory model** choose the route. **Proactive memory** turns the whole system off, or set `context.memory.enabled: false` in project settings for one arm of a study. Cost appears in `/usage` and `pancode usage report`.

### Capture more when you need it

```sh
pancode telemetry consent --workspace <dir>
```

With `telemetry.mode: research`, consent for that workspace, and `telemetry.research.content` on, PanCode also records memory traces in the session's journal. This stores redacted content, so use a repository you may study.

## First experiment

**Proposed, not yet run**

Nobody has run this protocol. A result of no effect would be just as useful.

**Does one approved lesson stop a repeated mistake?**

### Seed a trap

Make a small repository where the obvious test command fails and a documented, less obvious one succeeds. Put the working command somewhere an agent must look for it. Commit that state.

### Teach it once

Run one session that hits the trap and finds the way through. Check `/memory`, and approve a lesson that names the working command. If none is proposed, write that down, since it is itself a finding.

### Run paired arms

From fresh checkouts, run the same new task five times with the lesson available and five times with `context.memory.enabled: false`. Keep the model and version fixed.

### Score it

For each session, count failed attempts of the obvious command, tool calls, and total cost from `pancode telemetry cost <session-id> --json`. Report the numbers for each arm and say the sample is small.

### Report it

Open a GitHub issue with the setup, the table, and the lesson's text.

Needs: any chat route and a repository you can publish or describe. A local model server avoids keys and spend. Durable memory lives in your own state directory, so set `PANCODE_HOME` to a separate directory for the study and keep your real lessons out of it.

## How to join

Open a GitHub issue on [the repository](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/issues) saying what you want to try, before or after you run it, and read the [contributor guide](https://github.com/PanStudio/pancode/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for code changes. Negative results and replications are welcome.

**Boundaries**

- `held` is an evidence-gate input and is not proof of a general claim.
- Stored memory is not fine-tuning of the underlying model.
- A background model never writes directly to the system prompt.

**Next steps**

- [Keep a long coding task on track](https://pancode.dev/tutorials/keep-long-coding-tasks-on-track.html)
- [Proactive memory guide](https://pancode.dev/docs/guide/proactive-memory.html)
- [Can an agent run be a scientific record?](https://pancode.dev/research/sealed-run-records.html)
